**Choosing the spread.** Each side earns money from noise traders and loses money to informed traders. I estimated both for several widths around 11.5:
- At 3 either side of fair value, the expected profit is about 0. Losses to informed traders roughly cancel the noise-trader edge.
- At 5 to 7 either side, the expected profit is about 0.40 to 0.44 per quote.

**Why the quote is asymmetric.** Die 2 rolls 0 or 1 with combined probability 0.3, so the value has a fat lower tail. Informed traders therefore cost more on the bid side.
- On the ask side, the expected profit is about the same at 16.5 and at 17.5 (about 0.28 each), so 17 sits between them.
- On the bid side, the expected profit peaks at about 4.5 to 5.5 (about 0.16 each), so 5 sits in that range.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.0}

The first trade, a buy at 17, makes it more likely the value is high. I'll lift my fair value to about 14, keep the ask above the likely top values, and set the bid where losses to informed sellers are small.

**Prior fair value**
- Die 1 averages (2+3+4+4+6+6+7+8)/8 = 5.
- Die 2 averages 0(.2)+1(.1)+6(.1)+7(.1)+10(.4)+11(.1) = 6.5.
- So the starting fair value was 11.5.

**Updating on the buy at 17**
- The sum is above 17 only when the total is 18 or 19. That has a prior probability of 0.075.
- If the sum is above 17, a buy is likely: 0.5 for the informed counterparty plus 0.5 × 0.121 from noise, about 0.56.
- If the sum is 17 or less, only noise traders buy at 17, with probability about 0.06.
- The posterior probability that the sum is above 17 is about 43%.
- The posterior fair value is about 14.05.

**Ask**
- If the sum is above 17, it is mostly 18, with some chance of 19.
- An ask around 18 to 19 avoids most sales to informed buyers.
- Noise traders still buy with probability 15–20%.
- The expected profit is about +0.36 per quote across asks from 18.1 to 19.

**Bid**
- The trade-off is losses to informed sellers on low sums against gains from noise traders selling.
- Expected profit per quote by bid level:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5 | +0.058 |
| 6 | +0.064 |
| 8 | +0.05 |

- A bid around 6 is best.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 18.5}

Die 2 is 10, so the value is 10 plus die 1. That makes it one of 12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17 or 18.

**What the stage‑1 trade tells me.** Someone bought at 17.
- An informed trader buys at 17 only if the value is above 17. With die 2 = 10, that means die 1 = 8 and the value is 18.
- A noise trader in stage 1 valued the contract at the old fair value, about 11.5, plus noise. It buys at 17 only about 12% of the time.
- Putting those together, the value is 18 with probability about 0.57. Each other face has about 0.06.
- That gives a public fair value of about 16.5.

**Ask.**
- At 18, an informed trader never buys: even at value 18 it is not strictly above my ask.
- A noise trader buys about 38% of the time, and I earn roughly 1.5 per trade. That is positive expected value at no risk from informed traders.

**Bid.**
- At 13, an informed trader sells only if the value is 12. That has probability about 0.06 and costs me 1.
- A noise trader sells about 23% of the time, and I earn about 3.5 per trade.
- I compared bids of 12, 13 and 14, and 13 gives the best expected profit.

{"bid": 13, "ask": 18}

With die 2 revealed as 10, the settlement is 10 plus die 1. That gives eight equally likely values: 12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17, 18. The fair value is 15.

The buy at 18 on quote 3 must have come from a noise trader. An informed trader buys only if the value is above the ask, and the value can't exceed 18. So that trade tells us nothing, and the fair value stays at 15.

**Choosing the quotes**
- **Ask at 18 or above:** an informed trader never buys, because the value can't be above the ask. Only noise traders buy.
- **Bid at 12 or below:** an informed trader never sells, because the value can't be below the bid. Only noise traders sell.
- **Noise-trader edge:** the expected profit from one side is roughly (distance from 15) × P(noise > distance). With noise standard deviation 4.7, this peaks at a distance of about 3.5.
  - Ask 18.5: 3.5 × 0.228 ≈ 0.80.
  - Ask 18.0: 3.0 × 0.262 ≈ 0.79.
- **Inside the range:** moving the quotes closer, such as an ask of 17.9 or a bid of 12.1, starts losing to informed traders and gives a smaller noise edge.

So I quote symmetrically, 3.5 from fair value on each side.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 18.5}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (8 faces, each equally likely): 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/10), 6 (prob 1/10), 7 (prob 1/10), 10 (prob 1/10), 10 (prob 1/5), 10 (prob 1/10), 11 (prob 1/10).
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 11.5, but its distribution is lumpy and skewed, so I set the bid and ask separately rather than as one symmetric spread.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 (faces 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8): mean is 5, variance is 3.75.
- Die 2 (loaded): mean is 6.5, variance is 18.45.
- Sum: mean is 11.5, variance is 22.2, standard deviation is about 4.7.

**How I set each side**
For each side, I compared two expected effects per counterparty:
- **Noise trader gain:** the chance a noise trader crosses my price times how far that price is from fair value.
- **Informed trader loss:** the expected amount by which the true sum lies beyond my price.

**Ask side (expected net per counterparty)**

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14.5 | 0.79 | 0.63 | ≈ 0.08 |
| 15.5 | 0.79 | 0.36 | ≈ 0.21 |
| 16.5 | 0.72 | 0.16 | ≈ 0.28 |
| 17.5 | 0.61 | 0.05 | ≈ 0.28 |

The best ask is around 17.

**Bid side**
Low outcomes are concentrated where die 2 shows 0 or 1, so the bid needs to sit fairly low.

| Bid | Net |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | ≈ 0.13 |
| 5.5 | ≈ 0.16 |
| 4.5 | ≈ 0.16 |

The best bid is around 5.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.0}

I quote the same as last time: bid 5, ask 17. The aim is to profit from noise traders while limiting losses to informed traders.

**Expected settlement value**
- Die 1 averages 40/8 = 5.
- Die 2 averages 0(0.2) + 1(0.1) + 6(0.1) + 7(0.1) + 10(0.4) + 11(0.1) = 6.5.
- The expected sum is **11.5**. It can range from 2 to 19.
- The last quote (5 / 17) did not trade, which barely changes this estimate.

**Choosing the ask.** For each ask, I compare the expected gain from noise traders with the expected loss to informed traders.

| Ask | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | ≈ +0.37 | ≈ −0.39 | ≈ −0.02 |
| 15 | ≈ +0.40 | ≈ −0.24 | ≈ +0.16 |
| 16 | ≈ +0.38 | ≈ −0.12 | ≈ +0.26 |
| 17 | ≈ +0.33 | ≈ −0.04 | **≈ +0.29** |
| 18 | ≈ +0.27 | ≈ −0.01 | ≈ +0.27 |

The best ask is about 17.

**Choosing the bid.** The low end only matters when die 2 shows 0 or 1.

| Bid | Net |
|---|---|
| 6 | ≈ +0.15 |
| 5 | **≈ +0.17** |
| 4 | ≈ +0.16 |

The best bid is about 5.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 17}

Die 2 is revealed as 10, so the settlement value is 10 plus die 1. Die 1 is uniform over 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 6, 7, 8, which averages 5. That gives a fair value of 15, with possible values 12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17, 18.

The best quotes are 11.4 and 18.6:
- **Ask:** At 18 or above, an informed trader never buys, since the most the contract can be worth is 18. Noise traders value it at 15 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 4.7. Expected profit per noise trader is the edge times the chance they trade, which peaks at about 0.8 with an ask near 18.6.
- **Bid:** By symmetry, at 12 or below an informed trader never sells, since the contract is worth at least 12. The bid's profit also peaks at about 0.8 near 11.4.
- **Tighter quotes are worse:** Moving inside 12–18 lets informed traders pick us off, which costs more than the extra noise trades earn. For example, a bid of 13 is worth about 0.27 per quote against about 0.40 at 11.4.

{"bid": 11.4, "ask": 18.6}

Die 2 is revealed as 10, so the settlement value is 10 plus die 1.

**Settlement range.** Die 1 has an average of 5. The settlement value can be 12, 13, 14, 14, 16, 16, 17 or 18, each with probability 1/8. So the public fair value is 15.

**What the last quote tells us.** At quote 3 my bid was 11.4 and my ask was 18.6. Every possible settlement value lies between those, so an informed trader could not have traded. The lack of a trade tells us nothing new.

**Choosing the ask.**
- If my ask is at or above 18, an informed trader never buys from me.
- A noise trader buys if their valuation is above my ask. My expected gain from noise traders is then about x × P(noise > x), where x = ask − 15.
- With noise standard deviation 4.7, this is largest at about x = 3.5, giving about 0.80 × 0.5 ≈ 0.40 expected profit from that side.
- An ask of 17 loses money to informed traders when the value is 18 and earns less from noise traders. Its expected profit is about 0.27, so it is worse.

**Choosing the bid.** The same reasoning applies on the buy side. The lowest possible value is 12, so a bid of 11.5 means an informed trader never sells to me.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 18.5}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Before anything is revealed, fair value is 21, since each card averages 7 and there are 3 cards.

**How uncertain the settlement is.** One card has a variance of 14. Because the cards are dealt without replacement, the sum of 3 cards has a variance of 3·14·49/51 ≈ 40.4. That gives a standard deviation of about 6.35.

**Choosing the spread.** Both kinds of counterparty have valuations spread about 6.4 around 21:
- Informed traders know the actual sum.
- Noise traders use 21 plus noise with a standard deviation of 6.4.

So I treat both as roughly normal around 21 with σ ≈ 6.4, and write the half-spread as s = z·σ. With probability 0.5 the counterparty is noise and I earn the half-spread s. With probability 0.5 it is informed and I lose the amount by which its value passes my quote. Per side, expected profit is proportional to 2z(1−Φ(z)) − φ(z). Here Φ is the standard normal cumulative distribution and φ is its density.

Setting the derivative to zero gives 2(1−Φ(z)) = z·φ(z), which is satisfied at z ≈ 1.2. That means a half-spread of about 1.2 × 6.4 ≈ 7.7 points, so I quote 13.3 bid and 28.7 ask.

{"bid": 13.3, "ask": 28.7}

Card 1 is a 9, so expected settlement is about 9 + 2 × (355/51) ≈ 22.9. The two hidden cards add roughly 5.2 standard deviation. Balancing the profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders gives a best half-spread of about 7.

{"bid": 15.9, "ask": 29.9}

Card 1 is a 9, so fair value is about 22.9, and the past quotes give no reason to shift it. I'm quoting about 6 on each side: bid 16.9, ask 28.9.

**Fair value**
- The full deck sums to 4 × 91 = 364. Removing the revealed 9 leaves 355 across 51 cards, an average of about 6.96 per card.
- The two hidden cards are worth about 13.9 together, so expected settlement is 9 + 13.9 ≈ 22.9.
- Nobody traded at quote 3 (bid 15.9 / ask 29.9). An informed trader would have traded if the value were outside that range, so the value is probably inside it. That range is centred on fair value, so fair stays near 22.9.

**Spread**
- The two hidden cards have a standard deviation of about 5.2, and noise traders scatter by 6.4 around fair value.
- I compared expected profit per side at several distances from fair value:

| Distance from fair | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | ~0.53 | ~0.23 | ~0.30 |
| 5 | ~0.55 | ~0.13 | ~0.42 |
| 6 | ~0.52 | ~0.04 | ~0.48 |
| 6.5 | ~0.50 | ~0.03 | ~0.47 |

- The no-trade result means the value is probably no lower than 15.9 and no higher than 29.9. That keeps losses to informed traders small at this width, so about 6 is best.

{"bid": 16.9, "ask": 28.9}

Card 3 comes from the 50 unseen cards. Their mean is 7.0, so before looking at trades the settlement would be expected at 14 + 7 = 21.

**What the quote-4 sale tells us.** At quote 4 the counterparty sold to me at 16.9.
- **Informed trader:** sells only if the true sum is below 16.9. With 14 already showing, card 3 must be 1 or 2.
- **Noise trader:** public fair value then was about 22.9. A noise trader sells below 16.9 with probability about 0.17.

**Updated belief.**
- The chance that card 3 is 1 or 2 rises from 0.16 to about 0.56.
- The posterior mean of card 3 is about 4.4, so fair value is about 18.4.
- The settlement sum is concentrated on 15 and 16, with a thin tail up to 27.

**Choosing the quotes.** I compared expected profit at a few prices, counting informed and noise counterparties.

| Side | Price | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| Ask | 24 | about +0.41 |
| Ask | 25 | about +0.43 (best) |
| Ask | 26 | about +0.42 |
| Bid | 14.9 | about +0.51 |
| Bid | 13.9 | about +0.54 (near best) |
| Bid | 12.9 | about +0.54 |

Bid profits are flat between 12.9 and 13.9, so I bid 13.5 and ask 25.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 25.0}

The last quote should be **bid 15.0, ask 27.0**. These sit just outside the most likely settlement values, so an informed trader never trades at a loss to me, and noise traders still trade at a good edge.

**Base value.** Cards 1 and 2 sum to 14. The other 50 cards have a mean value of 7.0, so with public information alone the expected settlement is 21.

**What the trading history tells me about card 3:**
- At quote 4 someone sold at 16.9. This makes it more likely that cards 2 and 3 were small, so card 3 is more likely to be 1 or 2.
- At quote 5 someone bought at 25. An informed buyer would only do that if the total were above 25, so card 3 is more likely to be 12 or 13.
- Working out how likely each trade was for each possible card 3, the posterior is roughly:

| Card 3 | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 or 2 | 15 or 16 | about 0.36 |
| 3 to 11 | 17 to 25 | about 0.23 |
| 12 or 13 | 26 or 27 | about 0.41 |

- The public fair value is therefore about 21.3.

**Choosing the ask.**
- At 27.0, an informed trader never buys, because the settlement is at most 27.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 19%, and I earn about 5.7 on that sale.
- The expected profit is about 0.53. That is better than an ask of 26, which loses to an informed buyer when the total is 27, and better than 28.

**Choosing the bid.**
- At 15.0, an informed trader never sells, because the settlement is at least 15.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 16%, and I earn about 6.3 on that purchase.
- The expected profit is about 0.51, which beats a bid of 14.5 or 15.5.

{"bid": 15.0, "ask": 27.0}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The expected sum of three cards is 3 × 7 = **21**.

The standard deviation is about 6.35:
- One card's variance is (13² − 1)/12 = 14.
- For three cards dealt without replacement, the variance is 3 × 14 × 49/51 ≈ 40.4.
- So the SD is about 6.35, almost the same as the noise traders' SD of 6.4.

**Choosing the spread.** Both counterparty types value the contract around 21 with an SD of about 6.4. On each side, the expected profit per quote is proportional to 2k(1−Φ(k)) − φ(k), where k is the half-spread divided by the SD. Here Φ is the standard normal distribution function and φ is its density. This is maximised near k ≈ 1.2, which gives a half-spread of about 7.6. The expected profit at that spread is small but positive.

**Quote:** bid 13.4, ask 28.6.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 28.6}

After one fill at my bid, the market's fair value has dropped to about 15.7. My quotes are bid 8.5 and ask 25.5, set to make money from noise traders while limiting losses to informed traders.

- **Prior:** the sum of 3 cards has mean 21 and standard deviation about 6.35.
- **Update from the fill:** a counterparty sold at 13.4. An informed trader sells only if the true sum is 13 or less, which has probability about 0.12. A noise trader sells with about the same probability (about 0.12). So the sale is roughly a 50/50 signal between "informed, with a low sum" and "noise, with no information."
- **Posterior:** if informed, the expected sum given it is at most 13 is about 10.4. If noise, it stays at 21. The new public fair value is therefore about 0.5 × 10.4 + 0.5 × 21 ≈ 15.7.
- **Bid:** noise traders now value the contract around 15.7 ± 6.4. Informed sellers come from the low part of the sum distribution, which now carries more weight. Bids around 8 to 9 gave the best expected value, about +0.33 per quote.
- **Ask:** the high side of the sum is still exposed to informed buyers. Asks around 24 to 27 have only a small positive expected value, so I set it at 25.5.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 25.5}

The fair value is about 13.4, even though cards 2 and 3 alone would average about 18.1. The quote-1 trade is the main reason for the drop.

**Fair value without history.** Card 1 = 4 leaves 51 cards averaging 360/51 ≈ 7.06. Two unseen cards give about 14.1, so the sum would be about 18.1.

**What the quote-1 sale tells us.** Someone sold to me at 13.4.
- An informed trader sells only if the true sum is below 13.4. With card 1 = 4, that means cards 2 and 3 sum to 9 or less.
- A noise trader sells about 12% of the time, whatever the true sum is.
- Before the trade, a two-card sum of 9 or less has about a 21% chance.
- After the trade, low sums are weighted about 9.5 times more than high sums. That lifts the chance of a low sum to about 72%.

**Updated fair value.**
- If the two cards sum to 9 or less, they average about 6.7, so the contract settles near 10.7.
- If they sum to 10 or more, they average about 16.0, so it settles near 20.
- Weighting the two cases gives a fair value of about 13.3–13.5.
- The quote-2 no-trade only slightly reduces the weight on extreme sums.

The value is bimodal, so an informed trader on either side has a large edge. I set each side where the noise-trader profit most outweighs the expected loss to informed traders.
- **Ask:** profit is highest around 19–22, at about 0.25–0.29 per quote.
- **Bid:** profit is highest around 7–9, at about 0.45–0.50 per quote.

I hold +1, so I lean the ask slightly lower to make selling a bit more likely.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 20.5}

Card 1 = 4, so before looking at trades the fair value is about 18.1: 4 plus two cards averaging about 7.06 each.

**Updating on the trade history:**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at 13.4. That is roughly 9.5 times more likely if the true value is below 13.4.
- **Quote 2:** there was no trade between 8.5 and 25.5. This mildly favours a value inside that range.
- **Quote 3:** after the reveal, there was no trade between 8.5 and 20.5. This again favours a value inside that range.

Combining these with the distribution of the last two cards puts most of the weight on a value of about 9–13. The updated fair value is about 13.0.

**Checking the quote:**
- **Ask at 15:** an informed buyer would arrive with probability about 0.2, costing me about 1.8 per unit. A noise buyer would arrive with probability about 0.38, earning about 2. The expected edge is positive.
- **Bid at 10:** an informed seller would arrive with probability about 0.12, costing me about 1.5. A noise seller would arrive with probability about 0.32, earning about 3. The expected edge is positive.

I'm long 1, so I keep the quote centred slightly at or below fair value.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 15.0}

Card 3 is the only unknown, and both the card counts and the trading history say it is probably low.

**Card 3 before using the history**
- After removing the 4 and the 7, the remaining 50 cards sum to 364 − 11 = 353.
- So card 3 averages about 7.06, and the sum averages about 18.06.

**What the trades tell us**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold to me at 13.4. An informed trader sells there only if card 3 is 1 or 2 (sum 12 or 13). A noise trader sells there only about 12% of the time. So this sale is strong evidence for a low card.
- **Quote 3:** no trade at 8.5 / 20.5. An informed trader would have bought if card 3 were 10 or higher. This is mild evidence against a high card.
- **Quote 4:** no trade at 10 / 15. An informed trader would have traded unless card 3 is 4 or lower. This is further evidence for a low card.
- Combining these, card 3 is 1 or 2 with about 86% probability. Its expected value is about 2.05, so the fair value of the sum is about 13.05.

**Choosing the quote**
- **Bid:** the lowest possible sum is 12, so an informed trader will not sell to me at any bid below 12. The best bid sits about 5 below fair value, which gives a bid of about 8.0. This balances the edge per noise trade against how often noise traders sell.
- **Ask:** if card 3 is high, an informed buyer costs me money, but that is now unlikely. Checking different asks, expected profit peaks at about 18–19. At those levels I still sell to noise traders with valuations above the ask about 20% of the time, at a large edge.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 18.5}

The third card is drawn from the 50 cards left after the 4 and the 7. Those 50 cards sum to 364 − 11 = 353, so their mean is 7.06. The fair value of the contract is therefore 11 + 7.06 = **18.06**.

The settlement value can only fall between 12 (card 3 is an Ace) and 24 (card 3 is a King). This is the last quote, so I set each side to earn the most from noise traders while losing little or nothing to informed traders.

- **Ask at 24:** no informed trader buys, because the settlement value cannot exceed 24. Noise traders buy about 17.7% of the time, each time earning about 5.94 against fair value. The expected profit on this side is about 0.525, slightly more than at nearby prices such as 23.1 or 24.5.
- **Bid at 12:** no informed trader sells, because the settlement value cannot fall below 12. Noise traders sell about 17.2% of the time. The expected profit on this side is about 0.52.

Buying would take my position from +1 to +2, which is within the ±5 limit.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 24}

| Bid | 19.1 | 0.651 | 0.053 | 0.60 |

The best prices sit just at whole-number settlement values, because an informed trader doesn't trade when the value equals my price. Quoting 19.0 and 27.0 means only settlements of 17 and 18 are hit on the bid, and only 28 and 29 on the ask.

My position is +1, well inside the ±4 limit, so inventory doesn't change the quotes.

{"bid": 19.0, "ask": 27.0}

The third card is drawn from the 50 cards left after a 12 and a 4. Before any trading, its mean value is 348/50 = 6.96. That puts the fair value of the sum at 16 + 6.96 ≈ 22.96.

**What the sale at 19 tells us.** At quote 5 the counterparty sold to me at 19.
- An informed trader sells only if the total is below 19, which means card 3 is an Ace or a 2.
- A noise trader sells at 19 with probability about 0.2.

Updating on this sale, an Ace or 2 becomes more than twice as likely as before. Card 3's expected value drops to about 6.07, so fair value is now about **22.1**.

**Choosing the quotes.** This is the last quote, so each side should simply maximise its expected edge. Noise traders' valuations are centred near 22.1 with standard deviation 4.8. Informed traders trade only when the true total is outside my quotes.

| Side | Price | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| Ask | 25 | about 0.51 |
| Ask | 26 | about 0.57 |
| Ask | 27 | about 0.56 |
| Bid | 17.5 | about 0.61 |
| Bid | 18 | about 0.62 |
| Bid | 18.5 | about 0.59 |

The ask's best value lies between 26 and 27, so I quote 26.5. The bid peaks at 18. My position is +2, so buying one more takes it to +3, which is within the limit.

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 2, 2, 6, 8, 9, 11.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 11, 11.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The fair value is the expected sum of the three dice.

**Expected values of each die:**
- Die 1: (2+2+6+8+9+11)/6 ≈ 6.33
- Die 2: (1+2+11+11)/4 = 6.25
- Die 3: (3+4+5+7+7+12)/6 ≈ 6.33
- Fair value ≈ 18.92

**Uncertainty in the settlement value:**
- Die 1 variance ≈ 11.6
- Die 2 variance ≈ 22.7
- Die 3 variance ≈ 8.6
- Total variance ≈ 42.8, so the standard deviation is about 6.5.

**Choosing the half-spread:** Half the counterparties are informed, and they win when the true value lands outside my quotes. Noise traders have a standard deviation of 9.8, which is wider than the value's 6.5, so a wide quote still catches many of them. Treating the value as roughly normal, the net edge per quote is about:

| Half-spread | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | 1.53 | 0.84 | 0.69 |
| 7 | 1.66 | 0.48 | 1.18 |
| 8 | 1.66 | 0.35 | 1.31 |
| 9 | 1.61 | 0.26 | 1.36 |

The best range is a half-spread of about 8 to 9. I'll use about 8.5 around the fair value of 18.9.

{"bid": 10.4, "ask": 27.4}

Fair value is about 14.9. Before any trade the expected sum was 18.92 (6.33 + 6.25 + 6.33). The sale at my bid of 10.4 lowers that estimate. An informed seller means the sum is at most 10, and that happens with probability 17/144. Given that it happened, the expected sum is about 8.2. A noise seller would have sold here with probability about 0.19.

The sum has two clusters. Die 2 shows 11 half the time, which puts the sum high (16 or more). Otherwise the sum is often 10 or less. Because of that gap, informed traders will hit a tight quote on whichever side fits.

I'm already long 1, so I'll keep the spread wide and set it slightly toward selling.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 20.0}

Fair value now is about 10.4, which is well below the 18.9 prior mean.

**Distribution.** The total is bimodal.
- If die 2 shows 1 or 2, and dice 1 and 3 are low, the total sits around 6–10.
- If die 2 shows 11, the total sits around 16–34. Its mean in that case is about 20.4.
- The prior chance of a total below 8.5 is only about 7%.

**What the two sales say.** Both counterparties sold to me at low bids (10.4, then 8.5).
- An informed trader sells there only if the true value is below the bid.
- A noise trader sells there only about 19% of the time.
- Updating on both sales gives roughly:
  - 69% that the total is about 7 (die 2 low, dice 1 and 3 small).
  - 8% that it is about 9–10.
  - 23% that it is in the high cluster, about 20.

**Ask.** An informed buyer appears only in the high cluster (about 20), so the ask should sit near that level. I tested several asks against both counterparty types. Expected profit peaks around 19–21.

**Bid.** An informed seller only sells if the value is below my bid. The low cluster bottoms out at 6, so a bid below 6 never trades with an informed seller. A bid around 4–5 also gives a good edge on noise-trader sales. I'm already long 2, which is another reason to keep the bid low.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 19.5}

Given die 3 = 5 and the two sells at 10.4 and 8.5, the trade history points strongly to a low total.

**Where the settlement probably is.** The settlement value is S = die1 + die2 + 5. I weighted each of the 24 die1/die2 combinations by how likely it was to produce the stage-1 history. That history is the sells at 10.4 and 8.5 and the no-trade at 4.5 / 19.5, with half the traders informed and half noise.

| S | Posterior probability |
|---|---|
| 8 | ≈ 0.72 |
| 9 | ≈ 0.13 |
| 12–18 | ≈ 0.13 |
| 22–27 | ≈ 0.03 |

The expected value of S is about 9.6. My position is +2.

**Bid.** Informed traders sell whenever S is below my bid. S cannot be below 8, so any bid under 8 is never hit by an informed trader. Below that, a lower bid earns more per noise trade but gets hit less often. Expected edge per quote is about 0.83 at a bid of 3, versus 0.80 at 4 and 0.80 at 2.

**Ask.** Informed traders buy only when S is above my ask. Asks below about 14 lose money because the 12–18 and 22–27 outcomes are bought by informed traders. Expected edge rises to about 0.73 at an ask of 18 and falls to 0.68 at 20, so I'll quote 18.5.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 18.5}

Die 3 = 5, so settlement is 5 + die 1 + die 2.

**Prior on the unrevealed dice**
- Die 1 averages 6.33.
- Die 2 averages 6.25.
- Before any trading, the expected settlement was about 17.6.

**What the trading history implies (rough estimate)**
- Quotes 1 and 2: counterparties sold to me at 10.4 and then at 8.5. This points strongly to a low sum. The likeliest case is die 1 = 2 and die 2 = 1, giving S = 8.
- Quotes 3 and 4: no trade at 4.5/19.5 or at 3/18.5. That makes very high sums (22 or more) less likely.
- Putting this together:
  - P(S = 8) ≈ 0.66
  - P(S = 9) ≈ 0.16
  - P(S between 12 and 18) ≈ 0.16
  - P(S ≥ 22) ≈ 0.01
- The public fair value is therefore about 9.7. This rests on my approximations of the earlier public fair values, so it is not exact.

**Choosing the quote**
- **Ask:** If informed, the counterparty buys only when S is above my ask, and that is unlikely above about 17. Noise traders would still buy at about 17 roughly 20–23% of the time, at a large margin over the 9.7 fair value. My estimated expected profit is about 0.75 at an ask of 17 and about 0.33 at 13.
- **Bid:** No informed trader sells below 8, because the lowest possible sum is 8. A bid around 5 still gets hit by noise traders at a good edge, for an estimated expected profit of about 0.7.
- **Position:** I am long 2 with a limit of 4, so there is room on both sides.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 17}

Die 3 = 5 is now known, so the settlement value is 5 + die 1 + die 2. That leaves 24 equally likely combinations, ranging from 8 to 27.

**What the trading history implies.** I weighted each of the 24 outcomes by how likely the observed trades were under it.
- **Stage 1 sales:** counterparties sold to me at 10.4 and then at 8.5. Under that weighting, the value is very likely low, at 8 or 9. That means die 1 = 2 and die 2 is 1 or 2.
- **Later quotes:** there were three quotes with no trade at asks of 19.5, 18.5 and 17. These also point away from high values.
- **Result:** my rough estimate is that the value is 8 or 9 with about 90% probability. The posterior mean is about 8.9.

**Quote choice.**
- **Ask:** the main risk is an informed buyer if the value is 12 or more, which I put at about 10%. An ask of about 13 still gets good edge from noise buyers. Selling here also helps, because I'm long 2 units bought at an average of 9.45.
- **Bid:** no outcome is below 8, so an informed seller is no threat at a bid well under 8. Even so, I want a wide margin before adding to my long position, given that my estimate is uncertain. A bid near 3.5 still earns decent edge from noise sellers.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 13}

Die 3 = 5 and die 1 = 2, so the settlement is 7 + die 2. That makes it 8, 9 or 18, with 18 having half the prior weight.

**The no-trade history points to a low value.**
- At quotes 5 and 6 (asks 17 and 13), an informed trader holding 18 would have bought. A low value (8 or 9) fits no trade much better, by a combined factor of about 18 to 1.
- The two stage-1 sells at 10.4 and 8.5 also point to a low value.
- So P(18) is only a few percent. The fair value is about 8.6–9.

**Quote choice:**
- A bid below 8 keeps informed traders from selling to me. An ask above 9 keeps them from buying, unless the value is 18, which is rare.
- Against noise traders (standard deviation 9.8), the best edge is about 7 on each side.
- So I'll bid about 2 and ask about 15.5.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 15.5}

Revealed so far: die 3 = 5 and die 1 = 2, so 7 is known. Die 2 is still hidden and is 1, 2, 11 or 11. The settlement is therefore 8, 9, 18 or 18, and the public fair value is 7 + 6.25 = 13.25.

The sale at my bid of 2 on quote 7 must have come from a noise trader, because an informed trader values the contract at 8 or more. So that trade tells us nothing and the fair value stays 13.25.

**Ask:** If I post an ask below 18, informed traders buy whenever the value is 18, which happens half the time. That costs too much. At or above 18, only noise traders buy. Their expected profit to me is 0.5 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 13.25), which peaks at about 0.83 for an ask around 20–21.

**Bid:** If I bid at 8 or below, informed traders never sell, since the lowest possible value is 8. The expected profit is 0.5 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (13.25 − bid), which peaks at about 0.83 for a bid around 6–6.5.

My position is +3, so I can still buy one unit.

{"bid": 6.3, "ask": 20.5}

**Fair value.** Die 3 = 5 and die 1 = 2 are known, so 7 is locked in. Die 2 is still hidden and is equally likely to be 1, 2, 11 or 11. That makes settlement 8, 9, 18 or 18, with a fair value of 0.25·8 + 0.25·9 + 0.5·18 = **13.25**.

**Stage-3 trades tell us nothing.** At quote 7 someone sold at 2, which no informed trader would do because the minimum value is 8. At quote 8 someone bought at 20.5, which no informed trader would do because the maximum value is 18. Both were noise trades, and an informed trader would not have traded at those prices whatever the value. So the trades don't change the odds, and fair value stays at 13.25.

**Ask side.**
- An ask at 18 or above can only fill against noise traders. The expected profit is 0.5·(a−13.25)·P(noise valuation > a).
- This is highest when a sits about 0.75σ above fair value, so a ≈ 20.6. The expected profit there is about 0.83.
- Asking below 18 lets informed traders buy whenever the value is 18, and that loss outweighs the extra noise trades.

**Bid side.**
- A bid at 8 or below never fills against informed traders. Because the payoff is symmetric, the best bid is about 0.75σ below fair value, so b ≈ 5.9. The expected profit is about 0.83.
- Bidding at 8 gives only about 0.78.
- Bidding above 8 gets picked off by informed sellers when the value is 8.

**Position.** My position is +2, so buying one more unit stays within the +4 limit. Since I am maximising expected profit, the inventory doesn't change the quotes.

{"bid": 5.9, "ask": 20.6}

game.title: Dice sum
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 2, 2, 6, 8, 9, 11.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 11, 11.
- Die 3 (6 faces, each equally likely): 3, 4, 5, 7, 7, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of all the dice.

info.raw:
The expected settlement value is about 18.9:

- Die 1 averages 38/6 ≈ 6.33.
- Die 2 averages 25/4 = 6.25.
- Die 3 averages 38/6 ≈ 6.33.

The total has a standard deviation of about 6.5 (variances of roughly 11.6, 22.7 and 8.6).

I weighed the profit from noise traders, who are spread with standard deviation 9.8, against losses to informed traders. Treating the total as roughly normal, the best half-spread comes out at about 9 to 10. That is where expected profit per side levels off at about 1.36 in my calculation.

So I am quoting about 18.9 ± 9.5.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 28.4}

Fair value with nothing revealed is about 18.9, the sum of the three die means (6.33 + 6.25 + 6.33). The settlement value has a standard deviation of about 6.5.

**Choosing the spread.** I approximated the sum as normal to find the best half-spread h:
- Noise traders (valuation spread 9.8) pay me about P(noise > h) × h per side.
- Informed traders cost me about E[(value − fair − h)⁺] per side.
- The net profit per side is flat at about 0.68 for h between 9 and 10, and is lower for tighter spreads.

So I keep the quote wide and centred near 18.9. I tighten it slightly from last time, which drew no trade.

{"bid": 9.8, "ask": 28.0}

Expected sum ≈ 6.33 + 6.25 + 6.33 ≈ 18.9. Die 2 makes the distribution bimodal: one cluster around 14–15 and one around 24.

The quote that maximises expected profit is wide on both sides:
- **Ask:** an ask of about 28 earns about 0.69 per quote. Noise traders buying above fair value add about 0.80, and informed traders cost about 0.11, because the value rarely goes above 28.
- **Bid:** a bid of about 9–10 earns about 0.71 per quote. Noise traders add about 0.8, and informed traders cost only about 0.06–0.10, because the low tail below 10 is thin.

{"bid": 9.8, "ask": 28.3}

Die 3 = 7, so the settlement is 7 + Die 1 + Die 2. There are 24 equally likely combinations, giving values from 10 to 29 with a mean of about 19.6.

**Effect of the stage-1 trade.** Someone bought at 28.3, which only an informed trader would do if the total is 29. Two quotes earlier saw no trade, which counts slightly against 29. Taken together, the probability of 29 is about 9%, close to the prior of 8.3%. The public fair value is therefore about 19.6.

**Choosing the quotes.** Expected profit on each side is roughly 0.5 × P(noise trades) × edge, minus 0.5 × the expected loss to informed traders.
- **Ask:** profit peaks around 28, about +0.78 per quote. Only a total of 29 can beat it, and that has about a 1-in-12 chance.
- **Bid:** profit peaks around 11, about +0.77 per quote. Only totals of 10 or 11 are below it.
- **Position:** I am short 1, so a fill on the bid would also reduce my inventory risk.

{"bid": 11.0, "ask": 28.0}

Die 3 = 7, so before trading the expected settlement is 7 + 6.33 + 6.25 = 19.58. The sale to me at 11 in quote 4 is evidence for the lowest outcome (10). Updating on that trade drops my estimate of fair value to about 16.7, with about 36% weight on 10.

- **Bid:** Any bid above 10 gets hit by informed traders who know the value is 10 or 11. Bidding 9.9 avoids that and still trades with noise traders (about +0.8 expected).
- **Ask:** I balanced losses to informed buyers against profit from noise buyers. The best range is about 26.9–27, where only the 27 and 29 outcomes beat me (about +0.7 expected).

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 26.9}

Fair value is about 17.2, so I'm quoting a bid of 9.9 and an ask of 29.1.

**Prior.** Die 3 = 7, so the settlement is die 1 + die 2 + 7. The possible values, out of 24 equally likely outcomes, are:

| Value | Count |
|---|---|
| 10 | 2 |
| 11 | 2 |
| 14, 15, 16, 18, 19 | 1 each |
| 17 | 2 |
| 20 | 5 |
| 24, 26, 27, 29 | 2 each |

The prior mean is about 19.6.

**Updating on the trade history:**
- **Quote 3:** a counterparty bought at 28.3. An informed trader only buys there if the value is 29. This makes 29 about 6 times more likely than before.
- **Quote 4:** a counterparty sold at 11. An informed trader only sells there if the value is 10. This makes 10 about 6 times more likely than before.
- **Quote 5:** no trade at 9.9 / 26.9. This makes 27 and 29 somewhat less likely.

The posterior is roughly 35% on 10, 13% on 29, and the rest spread over the middle. The posterior mean is about **17.2**.

**Choosing the quote:**
- **Bid:** keep it below 10, so the heavy mass of informed sellers at value 10 cannot hit me. At 9.9 only noise traders sell, with a gain of about 7.3 per trade.
- **Ask:** at 26.9 or 28, informed buyers at value 29 cost me money. At 29.1 no informed trader buys, and noise traders still give a good edge. The expected profit of the ask is about the same across these choices, so I take the safe one.

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 29.1}

**Settlement outcomes.** Dice 3 and 1 are revealed, so the sum so far is 7 + 2 = 9. Die 2 is still hidden, so the contract settles at:
- 10 if die 2 shows 1
- 11 if die 2 shows 2
- 20 if die 2 shows 11

**What the trades tell me about die 2.**
- **Quote 4:** The counterparty sold to me at 11 when only die 3 was known. An informed trader sells only if the true value is below 11. Given die 1 = 2, that means die 2 = 1 (value 10).
  - At that time the public fair value was about 19.6. A noise trader would have sold at 11 only about 19% of the time.
  - So the sale is about six times more likely if die 2 = 1 (0.5 + 0.5×0.19 ≈ 0.595) than otherwise (0.5×0.19 ≈ 0.095).
- **Quotes 5 and 6:** No trade at 9.9 / 26.9 and 9.9 / 29.1. An informed trader would not have traded in any of the three cases, so these tell me nothing.
- **Quote 3:** The buy at 28.3 must have been a noise trader, since the total can be at most 20. It also tells me nothing.

**Updated odds.**

| Die 2 | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10 | about 0.675 |
| 2 | 11 | about 0.108 |
| 11 | 20 | about 0.216 |

This gives an expected value of about 12.3.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Bid:** Any bid above 10 gets hit by an informed trader holding value 10, which is the most likely case. At a bid of 10.0, informed traders never sell to me. Noise traders still sell about 41% of the time, for an expected gain of about 0.92 per noise trader.
- **Ask:** At an ask of 20.0, an informed trader holding value 20 does not buy, since a buy needs a valuation strictly above the ask. Noise traders buy at about 20 roughly 21% of the time, with a margin of about 7.7. This is close to the best balance between margin and trade frequency.

{"bid": 10.0, "ask": 20.0}

With dice 1 and 3 revealed (2 + 7 = 9), the settlement is 9 plus die 2. Die 2 is 1, 2, 11 or 11, so the settlement is 10, 11, 20 or 20, each with probability 1/4. The fair value is about 15.25.

**Quote 7 told us nothing.** I quoted 10 / 20 and nobody traded. An informed trader needs a valuation strictly above the ask or strictly below the bid. None of 10, 11 or 20 meets that, so an informed trader would never have traded. The no-trade gives no information and the fair value stays at 15.25.

**Keep informed traders out.** With the bid at or below 10 and the ask at or above 20, an informed trader never trades with me. The only trades are then with noise traders, whose valuation is 15.25 plus noise with standard deviation 9.8.

**Choose the spread.** For each side I want to maximise the edge times the chance a noise trader crosses it.
- The best edge is about 0.75 standard deviations, or roughly 7.4 points.
- That gives an ask near 22.6 and a bid near 7.85.
- Expected profit is about 0.84 per side.
- This beats quoting right at 10 / 20, which gives about 0.75–0.78 per side.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 22.5}

The contract now settles at 9 plus die 2, so it is worth 10, 11, 20 or 20, each equally likely. Fair value is 15.25.

The no-trades at quotes 7 and 8 tell us nothing. An informed trader would not have traded at those prices whatever the true value was. Noise traders centre on the public fair value, which does not depend on the truth.

**Ask:**
- Any ask below 20 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 20, which is an outright loss.
- Above 20, only noise traders buy. Expected profit is 0.5 × P(noise buys) × (ask − 15.25).
- That profit peaks at about 0.83 near an ask of 23.

**Bid:**
- A bid above 10 gets hit by informed traders when the value is 10 or 11, which costs money.
- At 10 or below, only noise traders sell. Expected profit is 0.5 × P(noise sells) × (15.25 − bid).
- That profit peaks at about 0.83 near a bid of 8.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 23}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Fair value is 21, since each card averages 7. The sum's standard deviation is about 6.35 (cards drawn without replacement). Noise traders' valuations scatter around 21 with standard deviation 4.8.

I estimated the expected profit per side as noise-trader earnings minus losses to informed traders, for a few half-spreads:
- **Half-spread 3:** about 0.38 per side.
- **Half-spread 4:** about 0.44 per side.
- **Half-spread 5:** about 0.44 per side.

The best is around 4.5, so I quote 21 ± 4.5.

{"bid": 16.5, "ask": 25.5}

Fair value is still 21 with no cards revealed: three cards averaging 7 each. Quote 1 produced no trade, which tells us almost nothing new.

**Uncertainty.** A single card's value has variance (13² − 1)/12 = 14. Drawing 3 cards without replacement gives variance 3 × 14 × 49/51 ≈ 40.4, so the sum has a standard deviation of about 6.35.

**Choosing the half-spread (a).** For one side of the quote, expected profit is:
- From noise traders: 0.8 × a × P(noise > a), with noise standard deviation 4.8.
- Minus the loss to informed traders: 0.2 × E[(V − 21 − a)⁺], treating the sum as roughly normal.

| a | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 3 | ≈ 0.38 |
| 4 | ≈ 0.44 |
| 4.5 | ≈ 0.45 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.44 |

The best half-spread is about 4.5, so I'll quote 21 ± 4.5 again.

{"bid": 16.5, "ask": 25.5}

Card 1 is a King (13), so my fair value is about 26.9, and I'm quoting 24.0 / 30.0 around it.

**Fair value**
- The full deck sums to 4 × 91 = 364.
- With the King removed, the other 51 cards sum to 351, an average of about 6.88 per card.
- The two unseen cards are therefore expected to add about 13.76, for an expected total of about 26.76.
- In stage 1 the counterparty bought at 25.5. That hints the value may be a bit higher, but the signal is weak. I put fair value at roughly 26.9.

**Choosing the spread**
- The two unseen cards together have a standard deviation of about 5.2. Noise traders' valuations have a standard deviation of 4.8.
- I compared a half-spread of 3 with a half-spread of 4:

| Half-spread | Expected gain per side from noise traders | Expected loss per side to informed traders | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3 | about 0.65 | about 0.18 | about 0.47 |
| 4 | about 0.65 | about 0.13 | about 0.52 |

- A half-spread of about 3 to 4 works best. I'm only short 1, so I don't need to skew the quote much.

{"bid": 24.0, "ask": 30.0}

The revealed King (13) leaves 51 cards worth 351 in total, so each unseen card averages about 6.88. That puts the public expected sum at about 13 + 2(6.88) ≈ 26.8.

**Effect of the buy at 30 (quote 3)**
- A noise trader values the contract at about 26.8 ± 4.8, so it buys at 30 roughly 25% of the time.
- An informed trader buys only if the true sum is above 30. That needs the other two cards to sum to more than 17, which has a probability of about 24%.
- So a buy is about twice as likely when the true value is high (0.4 vs 0.2).
- Updating on that raises the fair value to roughly 28. The earlier buy at 25.5 nudges it slightly higher, to about 28.2.

**Quote choice**
- I'm short 2 units, so I lean the quote slightly toward buying back.
- I keep enough width to cover the risk of trading against an informed counterparty, who appears 20% of the time.

{"bid": 26, "ask": 31}

Card 3 posterior: card 3 comes from the 50 cards left after removing the K and the J. Their mean value is 340/50 = 6.8. That gives a naive fair value of 24 + 6.8 = 30.8.

The two stage-2 buys shift this up. They happened at asks of 30 and 31, after card 1 = 13 was known. An informed buyer would only buy there if card 3 were high, so the buys are evidence of a high card. A Bayesian update on that evidence puts E[card 3] at about 8.8, so fair value is about 32.8.

Quote: I am short 3, so I can sell one more unit at most. I'll centre roughly on 32.8 and leave room for informed traders.
- **Ask 35.0:** an informed buyer buys only if card 3 is Q or K (value 36 or 37), about a 24% posterior. The adverse-selection loss on those trades is modest.
- **Bid 30.5:** an informed seller sells only if card 3 is 6 or lower, about 19% posterior.
- Both sides should still catch noise traders profitably.

{"bid": 30.5, "ask": 35.0}

**Fair value before trading.** Cards 1 and 2 total 13 + 11 = 24. Card 3 comes from the 50 remaining cards, whose values sum to 364 − 24 = 340. So card 3 has a mean of 6.8, and the fair value is 30.8.

**Update for the quote 5 trade.** The counterparty sold to me at 30.5.
- An informed trader sells only if the settlement is below 30.5, which means card 3 is 6 or less.
- A noise trader sells with probability of about 0.475.
- So a sell had probability 0.58 when card 3 is 6 or less, and 0.38 when it is above 6.
- If card 3 is 6 or less, its mean is 3.5. If it is above 6, its mean is about 9.85.
- Weighting by these probabilities gives a card 3 mean of about 6.13.
- The fair value is now about **30.1**.

**Choosing the quote.** I compared the expected profit at each price against both trader types. Informed traders cost me money on the discrete card outcomes. Noise traders pay me the spread.
- Ask 34.5 gives about +0.585, the best of the asks checked (33.5 gives +0.566 and 35 gives +0.572).
- Bid 26.0 gives about +0.625, slightly better than 25.5 or 26.5 (both about +0.61).

My position stays within limits on either side: it would move from −2 to −1 if I buy or to −3 if I sell.

{"bid": 26.0, "ask": 34.5}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Before any card is revealed, the expected sum is 3 × 7 = **21**.

The sum's standard deviation is about 6.35:
- One card has variance (13² − 1)/12 = 14.
- For three cards dealt without replacement, the variance is 3 × 14 × 49/51 ≈ 40.4, so the standard deviation is √40.4 ≈ 6.35.

**Choosing the spread.** I want the half-spread *h* that balances what I earn from noise traders against what I lose to informed traders. Expected profit per side is:

0.65 · h · P(noise > h) − 0.35 · E[(V − 21 − h)⁺]

| h | Profit per side |
|---|---|
| 4 | ≈ 0.17 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.21 |
| 6 | ≈ 0.21 |
| 7 | ≈ 0.18 |

Profit peaks at a half-spread of about 5.5, so I quote 15.5 bid and 26.5 ask.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 26.5}

Card 1 is a 10, so the remaining 51 cards average 354/51 ≈ 6.94. Before any trading, the expected sum of cards 2 and 3 is about 13.9, which puts fair value near 23.9.

The buy at 26 in stage 1 also tells me something. A buyer at 26 is much more likely when the true sum is above 26, because informed traders (35%) would buy then. For the sum to beat 26, cards 2 and 3 must total 17 or more, which has a prior chance of about 31%.

Updating on the buy:
- If cards 2 and 3 total 17 or more, a buy happens with probability 0.35 + 0.65 × P(noise buys) ≈ 0.45.
- Otherwise, only noise traders buy, with probability about 0.10.
- So the chance that cards 2 and 3 total 17 or more rises to about 0.67.

Given they total 17 or more, their expected sum is about 19.8; otherwise about 11.2. The posterior expected sum is roughly 0.67 × 19.8 + 0.33 × 11.2 ≈ 17.0, so fair value is about **27**.

Uncertainty is still large and 35% of counterparties are informed, so I'll quote a wide spread around 27. I'm short 1, so I'll skew slightly upward.

{"bid": 24.8, "ask": 29.8}

**Fair value.** Card 1 is 10, so 51 cards remain, with a total value of 364 − 10 = 354. That gives an average of about 6.94 per card. The two unseen cards should add about 13.9, so the expected sum is about 23.9.

**Adjusting for trades.** Someone sold to me at 24.8 this stage, which points slightly lower: an informed trader sells there if the value is below 24.8. The buy at 26 in stage 1 tells me little now that card 1 is revealed. My adjusted fair value is about 23.6.

**Spread.** The two-card sum has a standard deviation of about 5.3, and there is a 35% chance the trader is informed. A spread of roughly ±2.3 around fair value fits that risk. I am flat, so I quote both sides symmetrically.

{"bid": 21.4, "ask": 25.9}

**Fair value of the contract**

- Cards 1 and 2 are revealed as 10 and 2, so the settlement value is 12 + card 3.
- Card 3 comes from the 50 cards left in the deck. With no other information, its average would be 352 / 50 = 7.04, giving a fair value of about 19.0.
- The trading history lowers that estimate. The counterparty sold to me at 21.4 in stage 2. An informed trader would only do that if the total is below 21.4, which means card 3 is 9 or less.
- The earlier sale at 24.8 also counts slightly against card 3 being a King (13).
- I weighted each possible card 3 by how likely those trades were for it. That puts the average of card 3 at about 5.9, so the contract's fair value is about 17.9.

**My quote**

- Card 3 could be anything from 1 to 13, so an informed trader has a big edge. That calls for a fairly wide spread.
- I am long 1, so I shift both prices slightly down to make selling more likely than buying.

{"bid": 15.2, "ask": 20.0}

Settles at 12 + card 3. Before trading, card 3 averages 7.04 (50 cards left, total value 352), so fair would be about 19.04.

**Last trade (quote 5).** The counterparty sold at my 15.2 bid.
- An informed seller does that only if card 3 is 3 or lower. That covers 11 of the 50 cards: 4 aces, 3 twos and 4 threes, averaging 2.
- A noise trader sells there about 21% of the time.
- After the sell, the chance that card 3 is low is about 50%. When card 3 is high (4 to King) it averages about 8.46.
- The new fair value is about 12 + 0.5×2 + 0.5×8.46 ≈ **17.2**.

**Ask.** I checked how far up to set the ask so that noise-trader profit outweighs losses to informed buyers. Expected profit per quote:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 19.5 | +0.19 |
| 20.5 | +0.32 |
| 21.5 | +0.37 |
| 22.5 | **+0.41** |
| 23.5 | +0.35 |

22.5 is best: only Jacks, Queens and Kings make an informed buyer pay it, and those lose me little.

**Bid.** At 13.0, an informed seller never sells, because the lowest possible total is 13. Noise traders sell about 19% of the time at about 4.2 below fair, worth roughly +0.52. Bidding any higher lets informed sellers with an ace hit me.

{"bid": 13.0, "ask": 22.5}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Before any card is revealed, the fair value is the expected sum of three cards: 3 × 7 = 21. One card has variance 14, so the 3-card sum, drawn without replacement, has a standard deviation of about 6.35. The first quote at 15.5/26.5 didn't trade. That tells us little and is symmetric, so fair value stays 21.

For each side, I compared expected noise-trader profit against expected losses to informed traders at different half-spreads (h):

| Half-spread h | Expected net profit per side |
|---|---|
| 4 | about 0.17 |
| 5 | about 0.21 |
| 6 | about 0.205 |

The best half-spread is about 5 to 5.5, so I'll keep the same 15.5/26.5 quote.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 26.5}

Card 1 is an 8, and the stage-1 buy at 26.5 pushes my estimate up, so I'm centring around 25.3 with a wide spread.

**Prior with card 1 = 8 known.** The other 51 cards sum to 356, which averages about 6.98 per card. Cards 2 and 3 are therefore expected to sum to about 13.96, so the fair value before the trade is about 21.96.

**Updating on the stage-1 buy at 26.5.** Before any reveal, fair value was 21.
- An informed trader buys only if the total is above 26.5. Given card 1 = 8, that means cards 2 + 3 sum to at least 19.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > 5.5/4.8), which is about 0.126.
- So the chance of a buy is about 0.432 if cards 2 + 3 sum to 19 or more, and about 0.082 otherwise.

**Updating the card distribution.** The sum of cards 2 and 3 has mean about 13.96 and standard deviation about 5.2.
- The prior chance that the sum is 19 or more is about 0.19.
- After the buy, that chance rises to about 0.55.
- If the sum is 19 or more, it averages about 21.4; otherwise it averages about 12.2.
- The expected sum of cards 2 and 3 is now about 17.3, so the total is expected at about 25.3.

**Quote.** I'm centring around 25.3 with a wide spread, because informed traders are common and uncertainty is high. I'm skewing slightly up because I'm short 1.

{"bid": 22.0, "ask": 28.5}

Card 1 = 8. Before trading, the expected value of each unseen card is 356/51 ≈ 6.98, so the expected sum is about 22.

Both buys came at high asks, and each one is strong evidence that the other two cards are high:

- **Quote 3 (buy at 28.5):** an informed trader buys only if cards 2 and 3 sum to at least 21. This has a prior probability of about 12%. A noise trader buys with probability of only about 9%.
- **Quote 2 (buy at 26.5):** with card 1 known to be 8, an informed buy needs cards 2 and 3 to sum to at least 19.

Combining both buys gives these estimates for cards 2 + 3:

| Sum of cards 2 + 3 | Posterior probability | Conditional mean |
|---|---|---|
| 21 or more | about 79% | about 22.8 |
| 19–20 | about 8% | about 19.5 |
| Below 19 | about 13% | about 12.3 |

The posterior expected sum of cards 2 + 3 is about 21.2, so fair value is about 29.

I'm short 2, so I set the quote around 29 with a slight upward skew and a reasonable spread against informed flow.

{"bid": 27.5, "ask": 31.5}

**Fair value of card 3 before using the trade history.** 50 cards remain after removing an 8 and a Queen. Their values sum to 364 − 8 − 12 = 344, so the average is 6.88. The baseline fair value is 20 + 6.88 = 26.88.

**Updating on quote 5.** Someone bought at 31.5.
- An informed trader buys at 31.5 only if card 3 is a Queen or King (3 Queens and 4 Kings remain).
- A noise trader buys at 31.5 with probability about 0.17.
- So a Queen or King makes a buy about 4× as likely as any other card (0.46 vs 0.11).
- After this update, Queen or King has probability about 41%. The expected value of card 3 is about 8.65, so public fair value is about **28.65**.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared asks around 32 to 33.5. At 33.0, an informed buyer never trades, because the value is at most 33. Noise buyers still trade about 18% of the time, giving an edge of about +0.52, which is the best of the asks checked.

**Choosing the bid.** At 24, about 17% of noise sellers hit me, giving an edge of about +0.50. Informed sellers when card 3 is an Ace to 3 cost about 0.12. Net expected value is about +0.39, which is at or near the best bid.

{"bid": 24.0, "ask": 33.0}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A standard 52-card deck is shuffled. Card values: Ace = 1, 2-10 face value, Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Three cards from 1–13 have an expected sum of 21 and a standard deviation of about 6.35. The best half-spread trades the edge earned from noise traders against losses to informed traders. Noise valuations have a standard deviation of 6.4, and the optimum comes out at about 1 standard deviation, which is roughly ±6.4 around 21.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 27.4}

With no cards revealed, fair value is the expected sum of three cards: 3 × 7 = **21**.

**Uncertainty.** One card has variance (13² − 1)/12 = 14. Because the three cards are drawn without replacement, the variance of the sum is 3 × 14 × 49/51 ≈ 40.4. That gives a standard deviation of about 6.35. This is almost the same as the noise traders' standard deviation of 6.4.

**Spread.** On each side I chose the half-spread h, in units of z = h/6.4, to maximise:

- the gain from noise traders who cross, proportional to (1 − Φ(z))·z,
- minus the expected loss to informed traders, proportional to 0.35·φ(z).

Comparing values:

| z | Expected profit per side (relative) |
|---|---|
| 0.8 | 0.068 |
| 1.0 | 0.074 |
| 1.2 | 0.070 |

The best value is near z = 1, so h ≈ 6.4.

**Last quote.** The quote of 14.6 / 27.4 did not trade. That gives no directional information, so fair value stays at 21.

I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 27.4}

No change: I'm keeping the quote at 14.6 / 27.4.

- **Fair value.** With nothing revealed, the expected sum is 3 × 7 = 21.
- **Spread of the settlement value.** One card has variance 14. Three cards drawn without replacement give a variance of 3 × 14 × 49/51 ≈ 40.4, so the standard deviation is about 6.35.
- **Effect of the history.** Neither earlier quote traded. That gives almost no information because it is symmetric, so fair value stays at 21.
- **Best half-spread.** Set the half-spread as x × 6.4. The expected profit per side is about x·Q(x) − 0.35·φ(x), where Q is the standard normal upper-tail probability and φ is the standard normal density. This is roughly 0.068 at x = 0.8, 0.074 at x = 1.0 and 0.070 at x = 1.2. It peaks near x = 1, which means a half-spread of about 6.4.

{"bid": 14.6, "ask": 27.4}

Card 1 is a 2. The other 51 cards sum to 362, an average of about 7.10 per card. So the expected total is 2 + 2 × 7.10 ≈ 16.2.

Three quotes at 14.6 / 27.4 drew no trade. That slightly favours a total inside that range, so I put fair value at about 16.5.

The two unknown cards add uncertainty with a standard deviation of about 5.2. Noise traders have a standard deviation of 6.4. Given that, I will quote moderately wide around 16.5, leaning slightly towards the upside.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 20.4}

Card 1 = 2, so the other 51 cards average 362/51 ≈ 7.10. That puts the prior expected sum at about 2 + 2×7.10 ≈ 16.2.

**Updating on the buy at 20.4.**
- An informed trader buys only if the sum is above 20.4, which means the last two cards total 19 or more. That has a probability of roughly 0.21.
- A noise trader buys with probability of roughly 0.25.
- So the chance this buyer was informed is about 31%. If informed, the expected sum is about 23.
- That moves the public fair value up to about 0.31×23 + 0.69×16.2 ≈ 18.3.

**Quote.** Two cards are still unknown, so the remaining uncertainty is large. I keep a spread of about ±5 around the new fair value to protect against informed traders, and lean slightly higher because I am short.

{"bid": 13.4, "ask": 23.2}

By my estimate the fair value is now about 20.4, so I'll quote a bid of 17.4 and an ask of 24.4, which is roughly 3 below and 4 above fair.

**Prior value.** Card 1 is a 2, so the other 51 cards sum to 364 − 2 = 362. Each unseen card has a mean of about 7.10. The expected sum is 2 + 2 × 7.10 ≈ 16.2, with a standard deviation of about 5.2.

**First trade.** Someone bought at my ask of 20.4. An informed trader only buys there if the value is above 20.4. A noise trader buys there about 25% of the time. Updating on that buy moves the public fair value to about 18.4.

**Second trade.** Someone then bought at 23.2. A noise trader buys there about 23% of the time, given a fair value of 18.4. After this second buy, the probability mass sits mostly on a high value (around 25+), with a smaller lump near 14. The posterior mean is about 20.4, and the uncertainty is wide.

**Quote.** I'm short 2, so I set the ask further from fair than the bid. That limits how much more short exposure I take on if an informed buyer is hitting me. The bid stays reasonably close, which lets me buy back inventory.

{"bid": 17.4, "ask": 24.4}

The public fair value is now about 24.8, well above the naive 20, so I'm quoting bid 23.0 and ask 26.1.

**Naive value.** With 2 and Jack (11) revealed, 13 is fixed. The remaining 50 cards average 351 / 50 = 7.02. That puts the settlement value at about 20.0 before using the trading history.

**What the history says.** All three stage-2 trades were buys at 20.4, 23.2 and 24.4, made before card 2 was known.
- An informed buyer at 24.4 means the sum is above 24.4. With card 1 = 2 and card 2 = 11, that needs card 3 ≥ 12.
- Noise traders rarely pay that far above the public fair value of about 16 to 18. Three buys in a row is therefore strong evidence of informed buying.
- Bayesian updating on the three buys gives about an 82% chance that card 3 is 12 or 13. The expected value of card 3 is about 11.8, so the expected sum is about 24.8.

**Ask at 26.1.** The highest possible sum is 2 + 11 + 13 = 26. An informed trader therefore never buys at 26.1. Any sale there goes to a noise trader at above fair value.

**Bid at 23.0.** An informed seller only hits this if the sum is 22 or less, which has about a 9% chance. Noise traders still sell fairly often, so the expected edge is positive. A purchase here also cuts my short position of -3, which is badly placed if card 3 turns out high.

{"bid": 23.0, "ask": 26.1}

The third card is the only unknown. Combining the revealed cards with the trading history, its value is most likely a 12 or 13, which puts fair value near 24.

**Base case.** Cards 2 and Jack (11) are revealed. The 50 remaining cards sum to 351, an average of 7.02. Before using the trades, fair value is 13 + 7.02 ≈ 20.0.

**Stage 2 buys.** Counterparties bought at 20.4, 23.2 and 24.4 while only card 1 was known. An informed buyer at those prices means the sum is 21 or more (third card 8 or higher), then 24 or more (11 or higher), then 25 or more (12 or higher). Noise traders rarely buy that far above the public fair value of about 16 to 18.

**Stage 3 sell.** Someone sold at 23, which suggests a third card of 9 or lower. That is a weaker signal, because noise traders also sell there with about 68% probability.

**Bayesian estimate.** Weighting each possible third card by these likelihoods:
- 12 or 13: about 73%
- 11: about 7%
- 10: about 2%
- 9 or lower: about 18%

Fair value is about 24.2.

**Ask.** The maximum possible settlement is 26. An ask of 26.1 can therefore never be lifted by an informed trader. It only fills against noise traders, about 31% of the time, earning roughly 1.9 per fill.

**Bid.** At a bid of 20.5, informed sellers only hit if the third card is 7 or lower (about 9% posterior). Noise traders sell about 18% of the time, each roughly 3.7 below fair. That gives positive expectation, and buying also helps reduce my short position of -2.

{"bid": 20.5, "ask": 26.1}

The third card is still hidden, and the trades in stage 3 point to a fair value of about 20.9. Ask 26.0 and bid 15.0 maximise expected profit on this last quote.

**Starting value.** The 2 and the Jack are gone, so 50 cards remain with a total of 364 − 13 = 351. Their average is 7.02, so before stage-3 trading the expected settlement is 13 + 7.02 = 20.02.

**What the stage-3 trades tell us.** Each step updates the chance of each card-3 value using the probability of the observed trade.
- **Quote 7 (someone sold at my bid of 23):** An informed trader sells there only if card 3 is 9 or lower.
  - A noise trader sells about 68% of the time.
  - So card 3 ≤ 9 explains the trade with likelihood 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.68 ≈ 0.79.
  - Card 3 ≥ 10 explains it with only about 0.44.
  - After this, the estimate drops to about 19.3.
- **Quote 8 (no trade at 20.5 / 26.1):** An informed trader stays out only if card 3 is 8 or higher, giving likelihood about 0.53.
  - If card 3 is 7 or lower, an informed trader would have sold, so a no-trade has likelihood only about 0.18.
  - After this, the expected card 3 is about 7.9, so fair value is about 20.9.

**Choosing the quotes.** This is the last quote, so my position of −2 doesn't constrain anything and I just maximise expected profit.
- **Ask:**
  - At 26.0, an informed trader buys only if card 3 is a King, and the value would then be 26 exactly, so there is no loss.
  - A noise trader buys about 21% of the time at a 5.1 edge.
  - Expected profit is about 0.70, the best of the asks I checked (24.9, 25.9, 26.0, 27).
- **Bid:**
  - At 15.0, an informed trader sells only if card 3 is an Ace, costing 1 point in that case, about 0.02 in expectation.
  - A noise trader sells about 18% of the time at a 5.9 edge.
  - Expected profit is about 0.67, slightly better than bids at 14.9, 15.5, 16 or 17.

{"bid": 15.0, "ask": 26.0}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 17 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 5, 3 cards worth 6, 1 card worth 7, 3 cards worth 8, 2 cards worth 10, 2 cards worth 11, 3 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The expected sum is about 25.6, with a standard deviation of about 5.5. I'm quoting roughly 3.5 either side of that.

**Fair value.** The 17 card values add up to 145, so the average card is 145/17 ≈ 8.53. Three cards therefore have an expected sum of about 25.59.

**Uncertainty.**
- The average squared card value is 1433/17 ≈ 84.3.
- One card's variance is 84.3 − 8.53² ≈ 11.5.
- For three cards drawn without replacement, the variance is 3 × 11.5 × (14/16) ≈ 30.3.
- That gives a standard deviation of about 5.5 for the sum.

**Spread.** About 35% of counterparties know the exact sum. A half-spread of about 3.5 should limit losses to them while still trading with noise traders, whose valuations also spread by about 5.5.

{"bid": 22.1, "ask": 29.1}

Fair value is about 25.6, from 3 × the mean card value of 145/17 ≈ 8.53. The standard deviation of the three-card sum is roughly 5.5. The first quote got no trade, which tells us almost nothing about direction, so I'm keeping the quote centred on 25.6 and narrowing it slightly.

{"bid": 22.8, "ask": 28.4}

Fair value is about 25.2, so I'm quoting roughly symmetric around it with a wide spread.

**Unconditional expectation.** The deck's 17 cards sum to 145. With card 1 = 10, the remaining 16 cards sum to 135, a mean of about 8.44 per card. So with no other information, the expected total is about 10 + 2 × 8.44 ≈ 26.9.

**Updating on the quote-2 trade.** Someone sold to me at 22.8. If an informed trader did that, the total is below 22.8, so cards 2 and 3 sum to 12 or less.
- Only 22 of the 120 possible pairs for cards 2 and 3 sum to 12 or less (about 18%). Those pairs average about 10.2.
- The other pairs average about 18.4.
- Chance of a sell at 22.8:
  - If the total is low: about 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.31 ≈ 0.55. The 0.35 is the informed trader; 0.31 is the chance a noise trader values it below 22.8.
  - If the total is high: about 0.20, noise traders only.
- Updating on this, the chance that cards 2 and 3 are low rises to about 38%.
- Their expected sum becomes about 0.38 × 10.2 + 0.62 × 18.4 ≈ 15.3, so fair value is about 25.2.

**Quote.** The outcome is split between a low and a high case, so informed traders can hurt me on either side. I'm keeping the spread wide.

{"bid": 22.3, "ask": 28.1}

Fair value given card 1 = 10 and the trades so far is about 26.8. Quoting roughly 2.6 either side of it, at bid 24.2 and ask 29.4, protects against the 35% chance of trading with an informed counterparty.

**Fair value from the reveal**
- The 17 cards sum to 145.
- With the 10 removed, the 16 remaining cards sum to 135, an average of 8.4375 per card.
- So the expected settlement is 10 + 2 × 8.4375 ≈ 26.9.
- The two unseen cards have a combined standard deviation of about 4.8.

**Adjusting for the trades**
- **Quote 3 (they bought at 28.1):** a buy above fair value points to a higher settlement. This pushes my estimate up by about 1.6.
- **Quote 2 (they sold at 22.8, before the reveal):** a sell that low points to a lower settlement. This pushes my estimate down by about 1.7.
- The two roughly cancel, leaving fair value at about 26.8.

**Quote**
My position is 0, so I don't need to shift the quote either way.

{"bid": 24.2, "ask": 29.4}

Cards 10 and 11 are revealed, so the known sum is 21.

**Fair value for card 3.** The deck has 15 cards left: 2, 5, 5, 6, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 8, 10, 11, 14, 14, 14.
- These cards sum to 124, so the expected value of card 3 is 124 / 15 ≈ 8.27.
- The fair value of the contract is therefore about 29.27.
- The possible settlements are 23, 26, 27, 28, 29, 31, 32 and 35.

**Ask side.** An informed trader only buys if the settlement is above my ask. If I ask 35.0, no settlement value is above it, so informed traders never buy. Noise traders still buy about 15% of the time, and each of those sales earns about 5.7. The expected profit is about +0.55, which beat the lower asks I tried (31.1, 32.1 and 34.9).

**Bid side.** An informed trader only sells if the settlement is below my bid. If I bid 23.0, the lowest possible settlement equals my bid rather than falling below it, so informed traders never sell. Noise traders still sell about 13% of the time, and each of those purchases earns about 6.3. The expected profit is about +0.52. A bid of 25.9 gives roughly the same expected value but carries some risk from informed traders, so 23.0 is the safer choice.

{"bid": 23.0, "ask": 35.0}

With cards 10 and 11 revealed, 21 points are known. The third card comes from the 15 cards left in the deck, so its expected value is 124/15 ≈ 8.27. That puts public fair value at about **29.27**.

The buy at 35 on quote 5 came from a noise trader. An informed trader values the contract at its true settlement, which is at most 35, so it would only buy if its valuation were above 35. That trade therefore tells us nothing, and fair value stays at 29.27.

Possible settlements are:

| Settlement | 23 | 26 | 27 | 28 | 29 | 31 | 32 | 35 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability (out of 15) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 1 | 3 | 1 | 1 | 3 |

This is the last quote and my position (-1) stays within limits whichever side trades. So I simply choose each side to maximise its own expected profit.

**Ask side**
- At an ask of 35, no informed trader ever buys, because none values the contract above 35.
- A noise trader buys with probability about 0.149, earning about 5.73 per trade.
- Expected profit is about 0.555, which is roughly the best of the asks I checked.

**Bid side**
- At bids from about 24.5 to 25, the only informed seller is the case where settlement is 23 (probability 1/15). That costs only about 0.04 in expectation.
- Noise sellers bring in about 0.60.
- Net expected profit is about 0.56, the best among the bids I checked.

{"bid": 24.7, "ask": 35}

- The variance of a single card is 84.29 − 72.75 = 11.55.

**Choosing the half-spread (h)**
I balanced the expected gain from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders. Both have a standard deviation of about 5.5. The figures below are net expected profit per side for each half-spread.

| Half-spread | Net expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 3 | 0.22 |
| 4 | 0.35 |
| 5 | 0.40 |
| 6 | 0.40 |

The best half-spread is about 5.5. That gives a bid of 20.1 and an ask of 31.1.

The fair value is now about 22.9, so I'll quote around it and skew slightly lower because I'm long.

{"bid": 18.6, "ask": 27.2}

Card 1 is a 6, so the fair value is now about 23.2, and I'm quoting 19.6 / 26.3: roughly symmetric around that, with a slight lean down because I'm long 1.

**Fair value**

- **Bid:** Expected profit from noise traders selling is balanced against informed traders holding 19 or less. The best bid is around 19–19.5, worth roughly +0.28 in expected value.

{"bid": 19, "ask": 26}

Card 1 is 11, and the remaining 15 cards average about 8.07, so with no other information the fair value would be about 19.07. The trading history moves this up a lot:

- **Quote 1:** Someone bought at 21. An informed trader would only do that if card 2 is 13. That makes 13 much more likely.
- **Quotes 2–3:** No trades at 14 / 24.1. This mainly rules out card 2 = 2.
- **Quotes 4–5:** No one sold at a bid of 19. An informed trader would have sold if card 2 were below 8. This makes 2–7 unlikely.

The posterior has card 2 = 13 with about 82% probability and card 2 = 8 or 9 with about 17%. That puts fair value near 23.1, mostly at 24 and otherwise 19–20.

**Ask:** An informed trader never pays more than 24, so the ask only trades with noise traders. Comparing 24.1, 25, 26 and 27, the expected edge is highest around 26.

**Bid:** A bid just under 20 avoids most informed selling when the value is 19–20. It still collects noise sellers with an edge of about 3.
