game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 16 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 1 card worth 5, 3 cards worth 6, 1 card worth 7, 4 cards worth 8, 2 cards worth 9, 1 card worth 11, 3 cards worth 13. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Two cards are dealt from 16, and the contract settles at their sum.

- **Fair value:** the card values add to 132 across 16 cards, so the mean card is 8.25 and the expected sum is 16.5.
- **Spread of outcomes:** the standard deviation of the two-card sum is about 4.1, close to the noise traders' 4.1.
- **Choosing the half-spread:** half of counterparties are informed and half are noise traders with similar spread. I modelled both as normal with SD about 4.1. That model gives the best expected profit per side with each quote about 1.2 SD (around 4.5 to 5) away from fair.
- **Quote:** I set bid 12.0 and ask 21.0, roughly symmetric around 16.5.

{"bid": 12.0, "ask": 21.0}

A sale at my bid of 12 is evidence the sum is low. Informed traders sell there only when the sum is under 12. That happens in 14 of the 120 possible two-card hands, so about 11.7% of the time. A noise trader sells there about 13.6% of the time.

**Updated distribution.** The prior expected sum is 16.5. After the sale, hands summing to 11 or less now carry about 52% of the probability. The posterior expected value is about **13.3**.

**Ask side.** I weighed the losses to informed buyers against the profits from noise buyers, whose valuations centre on about 13.3. The expected profit per quote is:
- Ask 16: about -0.17
- Ask 18: about +0.02
- Ask 19: about +0.05
- Ask 20: about +0.05

The best ask is around 19.5.

**Bid side.** The low sums are now heavy, so the bid has to sit low. The expected profit per quote is:
- Bid 10: about +0.16
- Bid 9: about +0.22
- Bid 8.5: about +0.23
- Bid 8: about +0.24

The best bid is around 8 to 8.5. I'll quote 8.5, which costs only about 0.01 against bid 8.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 19.5}

The quote is centred on an estimated fair value of about 10.2. The two sells at low bids point to a low card sum.

**Prior.** The deck sums to 132 over 16 cards, so each card averages 8.25. The expected sum of two cards is 16.5.

**Updating on the trades.** There are C(16,2) = 120 possible pairs.
- **Trade 1 (sell at 12).** An informed seller means the sum is below 12. That covers only 14 of the 120 pairs: sums of 7, 8, 9, 10 and 11. A noise trader sells at 12 only about 14% of the time. After this trade the public fair value is about 13.3.
- **Trade 2 (sell at 8.5).** An informed seller means the sum is 7 or 8, which is only 4 pairs. A noise trader sells at 8.5 only about 12% of the time.

**Posterior after both trades.**

| Sum | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7–8 | about 62% |
| 9–11 | about 17% |
| 12 or more | about 21% |

The posterior mean is about 10.2.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Bid.** The lowest possible sum is 7, so an informed trader almost never sells into a bid near 7. Noise traders will still sell there with about 20% probability, which gives a good edge. I'll bid 7.5.
- **Ask.** The risk on this side is the roughly 21% chance the sum is high, around 16–17 on average. Across asks from 12 to 14, the expected profit is roughly flat. I'll ask 13.5, which keeps the chance of selling to noise traders and lets me reduce my +2 long position.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 13.5}

With card 1 revealed as 2 and the trading history taken into account, fair value is about 8.4. I'm quoting a bid of 5.5 and an ask of 11.1, a wide spread that only informed traders holding rare outcomes can profit from.

**Card 2 before trading.** The 15 cards left can make a settlement of 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13 or 15. The plain average is 10.67.

**What the trades tell us.** Informed traders sold to me at 12 and then at 8.5, and nobody traded against my 7.5 / 13.5 quote.
- A sale at 8.5 strongly suggests the settlement is below 8.5.
- No trade at 7.5 / 13.5 suggests it is between 7.5 and 13.5.
- Updating on these three trades gives roughly:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 8 | 71% |
| 7 | 8% |
| 10 | 11% |
| 11 | 6% |
| 9, 13, 15 | small |

- The expected settlement is about 8.4.

**Ask at 11.1.** An informed buyer only buys if the settlement is 13 or 15, which is about 0.7% likely. A noise buyer at 11.1 gives an expected gain of about 0.34 per quote, close to the best ask level I found.

**Bid at 5.5.** The lowest possible settlement is 7, so an informed seller never sells to me here. Noise sellers still give a good expected gain. Since I'm already long 2, a lower bid also limits adding to my position.

{"bid": 5.5, "ask": 11.1}

**Fair value.** Card 1 is a 2, so the settlement is 2 plus the second card. The second card comes from the remaining 15 cards, which would put the sum at 10.67 on average.

The earlier trading changes that picture:
- The counterparty sold to me at 12 and then at 8.5.
- Nobody traded at 7.5 / 13.5 or at 5.5 / 11.1.

Updating on that history (half the counterparties informed, noise standard deviation 4.1) puts most of the weight on a sum of 8, at about 72%. The rest is roughly 7 at 8%, 10 at 11%, 11 at 6%, and small amounts elsewhere. That gives a posterior fair value of about **8.4**.

**Ask.** Quoting near fair value loses to informed buyers whenever the sum is 10 or 11. Around 11.5 the informed side costs almost nothing, and noise buyers still pay about 3.1 over fair value. The expected profit is about 0.35, which is close to the best available.

**Bid.** Anything below 7 avoids the informed sellers, since no sum is below 7. The expected profit from noise sellers peaks around 5.3 to 5.5, at about 0.35.

My position of +2 leaves room on both sides.

{"bid": 5.4, "ask": 11.5}

The public fair value is about 9.45, and my quotes are about 6.7 bid and 13.0 ask.

**Value distribution.** Card 1 is a 2, so 15 cards remain: 5, 6×3, 7, 8×4, 9×2, 11, 13×3. Their mean is 130/15 ≈ 8.67. Without history the settlement value would average about 10.67.

**What the history adds.** Quotes 4 and 5 had no trade.
- An informed trader would have bought at 11.1 or 11.5 if the value were 13 or 15. Values of 13 or 15 are therefore much less likely.
- Each no-trade has a likelihood of about 0.72 when the value is 11 or less, and about 0.22 when it is 13 or more. Over the two quotes, that gives a likelihood ratio of about 10:1.

The updated distribution of the settlement value is:

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | ≈ 0.09 |
| 8 | ≈ 0.26 |
| 9 | ≈ 0.09 |
| 10 | ≈ 0.35 |
| 11 | ≈ 0.18 |
| 13 or 15 | ≈ 0.03 combined |

This gives a public fair value of about 9.45. Noise traders' valuations are therefore centred near 9.45, with standard deviation 4.1.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- **Ask:** Expected profit is highest around 12.5 to 13.5, at roughly +0.32. At 13 an informed trader only buys if the value is 15, and the edge on noise traders outweighs that.
- **Bid:** Expected profit is highest around 6.5 to 6.9, at roughly +0.34. Below 7 no informed trader sells, because no settlement value is below 7.
- **Position:** I am long 2, so buying one more takes me to +3, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 6.7, "ask": 13.0}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 4 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 10, 4 cards worth 13, 2 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
The quote is centred near a fair value of about 32.8 and set wide (bid 27, ask 38). That protects against informed traders on both sides of a two-humped value distribution and leans slightly toward buying back the short.

**Prior.** The deck has 13 cards summing to 118, so the expected 3-card sum is 3 × 118/13 ≈ 27.2.

**Update after the buy at 32.**
- Only 3-card hands with no 2 can sum to more than 32. Of the 84 such hands, all except 10+10+10 qualify, so 83 out of 286 hands do. That gives a prior P(sum > 32) ≈ 0.29.
- An informed trader buys at 32 only if the sum is above 32.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(noise > 32 − 27.2) ≈ 0.20.
- The chance of seeing this buy is therefore 0.5 + 0.5 × 0.20 ≈ 0.60 if the sum is above 32, and 0.5 × 0.20 ≈ 0.10 if it is not.
- So the posterior P(sum > 32) ≈ 0.71.
- The average sum is about 36.75 in the high case and about 23.3 in the low case.
- The new public fair value is 0.71 × 36.75 + 0.29 × 23.3 ≈ **32.8**.

**Spread.** The value distribution has two humps: mostly 33–42 if no 2 was dealt, and mostly 30 or below if one was. Informed traders would hurt a tight quote on both sides. I widen around 32.8 and lean slightly upward because I am short 1 and would welcome a buy.

{"bid": 27, "ask": 38}

I put fair value at about 39.4. I quote a bid of 34.5 and an ask of 43.5, which by my estimates have positive expected profit on both sides.

**Fair value before the trading history.** With card 1 = 14 shown, 12 cards remain: four 2s, three 10s, four 13s and one 14. That gives 66 equally likely pairs for cards 2 and 3:

| Total | Pairs |
|---|---|
| 18 | 6 |
| 26 | 12 |
| 29 | 16 |
| 30 | 4 |
| 34 | 3 |
| 37 | 12 |
| 38 | 3 |
| 40 | 6 |
| 41 | 4 |

Without the trading history, the expected total is 31.3.

**Updating on the two buys (at 32 and 38).** A buyer was informed with probability 0.5, and an informed buyer only buys if the true value is above my ask.
- **Buy at 32:** the likelihood is about 0.60 if the value is above 32 and about 0.10 if not. I estimated the stage-1 fair value at about 27.2, so a noise trader buys at 32 only about 21% of the time.
- **Buy at 38:** the likelihood is about 0.54 if the value is above 38 and about 0.04 if not. I approximated the fair value at that point as about 30, so a noise trader buys at 38 only about 8% of the time.
- **Posterior:** about 84% of the weight is on totals of 40 or 41. The fair value is about 39.4.

**Ask (expected profit per quote):**

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 40 | about −0.02 (an informed trader buys whenever the total is 41) |
| 41 | +0.32 |
| 43–44 | about +0.48 to +0.49 |

At 41 or higher no informed trader can buy, since the total is at most 41. I'll ask 43.5.

**Bid (expected profit per quote):**

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 37.9 | about 0 |
| 36 | +0.25 |
| 35 | +0.30 |
| 34 | +0.31 |

I'll bid 34.5. Buying back would also reduce my short position.

{"bid": 34.5, "ask": 43.5}

Card 1 is a 14. Updating on the two earlier buys at 32 and 38 and the no-trade at 34.5/43.5, the fair value is now about 39.7. Most of the probability sits on a total of 40 (about 50%) or 41 (about 34%), with 37 at about 10%.

- **Ask:** I put the ask at 42.5, above the highest likely total of 41. A trader who knows the cards will almost never buy there. Noise traders still do, which gives an expected edge of about 0.4.
- **Bid:** I set the bid around 35.5. Informed traders would only sell to me if the total is 34 or lower, which has about a 3% chance. Expected profit from noise traders is about 0.4.

{"bid": 35.5, "ask": 42.5}

My estimate of fair value is about 40, so I'm quoting 39.4 bid and 41.2 ask.

**Settlement values.** After the 14 and the 13, the 11 cards left are four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and one 14. Card 3 is therefore 2, 10, 13 or 14 with weights 4/11, 3/11, 3/11 and 1/11. The contract settles at 29, 37, 40 or 41. Ignoring the trading, the expected value is about 35.3.

**What the trades tell me.** Half the counterparties know the true sum, so the stage-1 buys at 32 and 38 are evidence about card 3:
- A buy at 38 is very unlikely from a noise trader. With the stage-1 fair value near 27–30, that chance is under 10%. It is much more likely from an informed trader holding a value of 40 or 41.
- If the value were 29, an informed trader would probably have sold at the 34.5 or 35.5 bids in stage 2. There were no trades there.
- My rough Bayesian update puts card 3 at 13 or 14 with high probability: about 70% for 40, 25% for 41 and 5% for 37. The posterior fair value is about 40.

**Quote.**
- I'm short 2, so buying back near fair value is good. A bid of 39.4 only loses to an informed seller when the value is 37, which is unlikely.
- An ask of 41.2 sits above the highest possible value, so informed buyers never profit from it and any noise buyer pays above value.

{"bid": 39.4, "ask": 41.2}

The third card decides settlement. Cards 1 and 2 are known, so the value is 27 plus card 3.

**What card 3 can be.** Eleven cards remain: four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and one 14. So settlement is 29, 37, 40 or 41.

**What the trading history says.**
- At quote 5 my quotes were 39.4 / 41.2 and nobody traded. An informed trader would have sold to me if the value were 29 or 37. So no trade strongly favours 40 or 41.
- Quotes 3 and 4 also had no trade, and the stage-1 buy at 38 fits only a value above 38. Both point the same way.
- My rough calculation gives about 75% for 40, 25% for 41, and under 1% for 37 or 29. Public fair value is about 40.25.

**Quote choice.**
- A bid at or below 40 and an ask at or above 41 mean an informed trader never trades with me at a loss. The informed side then costs me nothing.
- So I only need to earn from noise traders. Their valuations centre on about 40.25 with standard deviation 5.8.
- To pick the ask, I maximise the edge (ask − 40.25) times the chance a noise trader buys. This peaks around 44 to 45.
- To pick the bid, I maximise (40.25 − bid) times the chance a noise trader sells. This peaks around 36 to 36.5.
- Either trade is allowed: buying takes me to -1 and selling takes me to -3.

info.raw:
Pricing from the card distribution:

- **Fair value:** the average card is 118/13 ≈ 9.08, so the expected sum of 3 cards is about **27.2**. The standard deviation is about 7.8.
- **Shape:** the outcome is lumpy and depends mostly on how many 2s are dealt.
  - No 2s (about 29%): sum 30 to 41.
  - One 2 (about 50%): sum 22 to 30.
  - Two 2s (about 19%): sum 14 to 18.
  - Three 2s (about 1%): sum 6.
- **Risk:** informed traders know the exact sum and pick off quotes near the edges of these clusters. Noise traders only cluster around 27.2 ± 5.8.
- **Choice:** a bid just above the two-2s cluster and an ask in the middle of the no-2s cluster roughly break even. They also keep the spread wide enough that trades tell me something.

{"bid": 19, "ask": 33}

Fair value now is about 27.1. Before any trade the expected sum was 27.2. Last quote's no-trade at 19/33 makes values between 19 and 33 slightly more likely.

**Possible sums.** The deck gives these totals:
- Low, below 19: 6, 14, 17, 18.
- Middle: 22, 25, 26, 28, 29, 30, 33.
- High, above 33: 34, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 41.

So the distribution is lumpy, with gaps at 19–21 and 30–33.

**Bid.** An informed seller only hits my bid if the sum is 18 or less.
- At about 18.5, the expected gain from noise sellers (≈0.32) slightly beats the expected loss to informed sellers (≈0.25).
- Raising the bid to about 22 lets in the sum of 22, and the edge disappears.

**Ask.** An informed buyer only lifts my ask if the sum is above it.
- Asks around 30–33 lose to informed buyers on sums of 33 and up.
- Around 35, only sums of 36 or more beat me.
- At 35, noise buyers give about +0.34 and informed buyers cost about −0.22, a net gain of about +0.12.

{"bid": 18.5, "ask": 35}

Card 1 is 13. That leaves 12 cards: four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and two 14s. Their total is 105, so the average card is 8.75. The fair value is 13 + 2 × 8.75 = 30.5.

The final total is split into two groups, so I set each side of the quote separately rather than centring a tight spread on 30.5. There are 66 equally likely pairs for the last two cards:

| Final total | 17 | 25 | 28 | 29 | 33 | 36 | 37 | 39 | 40 | 41 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pairs (of 66) | 6 | 12 | 12 | 8 | 3 | 9 | 6 | 3 | 6 | 1 |

For each candidate price I compared two things. One is the expected loss to an informed trader, who knows the total. The other is the expected gain from a noise trader, whose valuation is 30.5 plus noise with standard deviation 5.8. Each type arrives with probability 0.5.

**Ask side:**

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 34 | -0.23 |
| 35.5 | +0.06 |
| 36.5 | +0.18 |
| 37.5 | +0.22 |
| 38.5 | +0.24 |
| 39.5 | +0.24 |

The ask is best between 38.5 and 39.5, so I quote 39.

**Bid side:**

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 27.5 | -0.25 |
| 25 | +0.11 |
| 24.5 | +0.11 |
| 23.5 | +0.10 |
| 22 | +0.08 |

The bid is best at about 24.5–25. At 24.5 an informed seller only trades when the total is 17, which keeps losses small.

{"bid": 24.5, "ask": 39}

Card 1 is a 13, so 12 cards remain in the deck: four 2s, three 10s, three 13s and two 14s. The remaining cards average 105/12 = 8.75. Two more cards are dealt, so the public estimate before any trading info is 13 + 17.5 = 30.5.

**Update from quote 3.** Nobody traded at 24.5 / 39.
- An informed trader would have sold to my bid if the total were 17. It would have bought at my ask if the total were 40 or 41.
- No trade therefore makes those three totals less likely, without ruling them out, since the counterparty may have been a noise trader.
- After updating, the probabilities of the possible totals are:
  - 17: about 4.5%
  - 25 and 28: about 20% each
  - 29: about 14%
  - 33: about 5%
  - 36: about 15%
  - 37: about 10%
  - 39: about 5%
  - 40: about 4.5%
  - 41: under 1%
- The updated fair value is about **30.6**.

**Choosing the bid.**
- The possible totals are clumped, with large groups at 25, 28 and 29.
- If my bid were above 25, informed sellers would hit it whenever the total is 25 or more below the bid, which loses heavily.
- A bid just under 25 is only exposed to the unlikely total of 17. It still catches noise traders who value the contract low.
- A bid of 24.9 gives an expected profit of about +0.28 on this side.

**Choosing the ask.**
- An ask just above 37 is only exposed to totals of 39, 40 and 41, which have small probability.
- It still catches noise traders about 13% of the time, at roughly 6.5 above fair value.
- An ask of 37.1 gives an expected profit of about +0.30 on this side.

{"bid": 24.9, "ask": 37.1}

With cards 1 and 2 both 13, the settlement is 26 plus card 3. Card 3 comes from the 11 cards left in the deck (4×2, 3×10, 2×13, 2×14), so the settlement is 28, 36, 39 or 40.

Combining these with the deck odds gives:

| 28 | ≈ 0.095 |
| 36 | ≈ 0.071 |
| 39 | ≈ 0.417 |
| 40 | ≈ 0.417 |

Card 3 is the only unknown, so settlement is 26 plus card 3. After updating on the trading history, my expected settlement value is about 36.7.

| 36 | 10 | 3/11 |

- **Quote 4 (buy at 37.1):** an informed buyer here implies settlement of 39 or 40. A noise buyer at that price was unlikely, at about 13%.
- **Quote 5 (no trade at 32 / 41.7):** this rules out an informed seller at settlement 28.

info.raw:
Expected sum is 3 × 7.8 = 23.4, with a standard deviation of about 7.2. Informed traders are as likely as noise traders, so I'm quoting wide (half-spread about 8), where noise-trader profit roughly offsets losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 15.4, "ask": 31.4}

**Fair value:** The deck's 10 cards sum to 78, so the average card is worth 7.8. The expected sum of 3 cards is 23.4.

**Uncertainty:** One card has variance 22.36. Drawing 3 cards without replacement gives a variance of 3 × 22.36 × 7/9 ≈ 52.2, so the standard deviation is about 7.2.

**Effect of the last quote:** Quote 1 at 15.4 / 31.4 drew no trade. That tells us very little, so fair value stays at about 23.4.

**Choosing the spread:** Informed traders see a spread in value (sd about 7.2) that is wider than the noise traders' spread (sd 5.4). So the gain from noise trades only slightly exceeds the loss to informed traders, even at wide quotes. A rough per-side estimate (gain from noise minus loss to informed, each weighted 0.5):

| Half-spread | Gain from noise | Loss to informed |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 0.55 | 0.49 |
| 10 | 0.32 | 0.27 |
| 12 | 0.16 | 0.14 |

The edge is small and positive across this range, so I'll keep a wide quote with a half-spread of about 8.2, centred on 23.4.

{"bid": 15.2, "ask": 31.6}

Card 1 is a 5, so the remaining deck is {0, 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15}. That gives a public fair value of 5 + 2 × 73/9 ≈ 21.2.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement is 5 plus the sum of two cards drawn from those nine. There are 36 equally likely pairs, so the settlement can be listed exactly:
9, 10, 10, 12, 14, 14, 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, 17, 20×4, 21×4, 23, 23, 24, 24, 25×4, 27×3, 31×4, 35.

**Choosing each side.** For each candidate price I compared two things:
- Expected gain from noise traders: their valuation is 21.2 plus noise with standard deviation 5.4.
- Expected loss to informed traders: they know the exact settlement.

**Ask side.** Expected profit per quote rises from about 0 at 26 to a peak of about 0.115 at 31. At 31 only the 35 outcome beats me, and the 31 outcomes are exactly break-even.

**Bid side.** Expected profit per quote peaks at about 0.122 at a bid of 14.0. There I only lose to the 9, 10, 10 and 12 outcomes.

{"bid": 14.0, "ask": 31.0}

Card 1 is a 5. That leaves nine cards (0, 4, 5, 5, 7, 11, 11, 15, 15), and two more of them will be dealt.

**Public fair value**
- The nine remaining cards sum to 73, so each averages 73/9 ≈ 8.11.
- Expected settlement is 5 + 2 × 8.11 ≈ 21.2.

**Settlement distribution**
The 36 possible pairs of remaining cards give these settlement values: 9, 10, 10, 12, 14, 14, 15, 16, 16, 16, 17, 17, 20, 20, 20, 20, 21, 21, 21, 21, 23, 23, 24, 24, 25, 25, 25, 25, 27, 27, 27, 31, 31, 31, 31, 35.

**Choosing the quotes**
For each candidate price I compared two things:
- **Informed loss:** the expected loss to an informed trader, which is 0.5 × the expected amount by which settlement lands beyond my price.
- **Noise gain:** the expected gain from a noise trader, which is 0.5 × the chance its valuation (fair value 21.2, standard deviation 5.4) crosses my price × the distance from fair value.

**Ask side**

- In quote 1 the counterparty sold at 8. That is much more likely when the value is below 8, because an informed trader would sell there.
- In quote 2 there was no trade at 5/17. That weakly points to a value between 5 and 17.
- Weighting the outcomes by these two observations gives a public fair value of about **9.8**.
- There is about a 69% chance the value is in the low cluster (average about 6.5). There is about a 31% chance it is in the high cluster (average about 16.8).

**Choosing the quotes.**
- **Bid 5:** No possible settlement value is below 5, so an informed trader never sells to me here. Noise traders sell about 22% of the time at roughly 4.8 below fair. Of the bids I checked, this had the best expected edge.
- **Ask 16:** An informed trader only buys when the value is 17 or 25. Noise sellers still trade often enough to make about +0.5 expected per quote. Being long 1 also makes a sale welcome.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 16}

**Fair value estimate: about 12.6.**

**Possible totals.** Card 1 is 3. The other ten cards are one 0, three 2s, three 3s and three 11s. Cards 2 and 3 are drawn from those ten. That makes the possible totals 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 14, 16, 17 and 25.

**What the trades tell us.**
- Quote 1: someone sold to me at 8. That points towards a low total, below 8.
- Quote 2: no trade at 5 / 17. That is weak evidence against a total of 25.
- Quote 3: someone bought from me at 16. That strongly points towards a total above 16, so 17 or 25.

**Posterior.** After weighting each total by these three trades, the probabilities are roughly:

| Total | Probability |
|---|---|
| 5 | 0.115 |
| 6 | 0.115 |
| 7 | 0.115 |
| 8 | 0.083 |
| 9 | 0.028 |
| 14 | 0.028 |
| 16 | 0.083 |
| 17 | 0.368 |
| 25 | 0.068 |

The distribution has two clusters and its mean is about 12.6.

**Ask.** Setting the ask at or above 17 means an informed buyer only takes it when the total is 25, which has about 7% probability. Noise buyers still give a good edge. Asks between 17 and 18 all have expected profit of about 0.5 per quote, so I chose 17.5.

**Bid.** Setting the bid at 6 means an informed seller only hits it when the total is 5. The edge from noise sellers stays near its best level. The expected profit is about 0.57, the highest of the bids I checked.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 17.5}

Posterior fair value is about 12.1, so I'm quoting a bid of 6 and an ask of 17. Neither price can be hit by an informed trader.

**Possible settlement values.** The first two cards are 3 + 3 = 6. Nine cards remain: one 0, three 2s, two 3s and three 11s. So the settlement is:
- 6 with probability 1/9
- 8 with probability 3/9
- 9 with probability 2/9
- 17 with probability 3/9

Before using the trade history, the expected value is 11.

**What the trades tell me.** I updated these odds using the two trades:
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at 8. This makes a settlement below 8 (that is, 6) more likely.
- **Quote 3:** someone bought at 16. This makes 17 more likely.
- **Quotes 2 and 4:** no trade. These tell me almost nothing, because informed traders would have done nothing at any of the possible values.

The posterior is roughly:
- 6 with probability 0.23
- 8 with probability 0.17
- 9 with probability 0.11
- 17 with probability 0.49

That gives a fair value of about 12.1.

**Ask side.** An informed trader only buys if the value is above my ask, so only when it is 17. If I ask 17.0, an informed trader holding 17 will not buy. Noise traders buy about 21% of the time at that price. The expected edge is about +0.69, which is the best of the asks I checked.

**Bid side.** At a bid of 6, an informed trader can never profitably sell to me, because no possible value is below 6. Noise traders sell about 16% of the time, for an expected edge of about +0.65. Bids of 7 or 8 attract noise sellers more often, but they lose more to informed sellers holding 6, so they come out worse.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 17.0}

With cards 1 and 2 both showing 3, the contract is 6 plus card 3. The remaining 9 cards are one 0, three 2s, two 3s and three 11s. So the settlement is 6, 8, 9 or 17, with probabilities 1/9, 3/9, 2/9 and 3/9. The public fair value is 11.

**Ask side**
- An informed buyer only trades if the value is 17 and my ask is below 17.
- At an ask of 17, informed traders never buy. Noise traders buy with probability about 0.167 and I earn 6 against fair value, so the expected gain is about 0.65.
- An ask of 16 earns about 0.57 and 17.5 earns about 0.62, so 17 is best.

**Bid side**
- An informed seller only trades if my bid is above the value, so a bid of 6 avoids informed sales entirely.
- At a bid of 6, noise traders sell with probability about 0.21 and I earn 5 against fair value, so the expected gain is about 0.68.
- A bid of 7 earns about 0.64 and 8 earns about 0.53, so 6 is best.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 17}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 1, 3 cards worth 2, 4 cards worth 4, 1 card worth 6, 2 cards worth 12. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected sum of three cards from the deck.

**Fair value**
- The 13 cards are worth 53 in total, so the mean card is 53/13 ≈ 4.08.
- The expected sum of three cards is 3 × 4.08 ≈ 12.23.

**Uncertainty**
- The variance of one card is about 14.2.
- Drawing three cards without replacement gives a variance of 3 × 14.2 × (10/12) ≈ 35.6.
- So the settlement standard deviation is about 6.0.

**Quote**
- Noise traders' valuations are fair value plus noise with a standard deviation of 8.9.
- Informed traders (20%) know the settlement value, which is spread about ±6 around fair.
- A half-spread of about 3.8 keeps a decent chance of noise trades while limiting losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 8.4, "ask": 16.0}

Public fair value is about 13.5 after the buy at 16, so I quote a bid of 10.5 and an ask of 17.5.

**Prior.** The deck sums to 53 over 13 cards, so the expected sum of 3 cards is 3 × 53/13 ≈ 12.23.

**When can the sum exceed 16?** Only if at least one 12 is dealt. Without a 12, the largest possible sum is 6 + 4 + 4 = 14. Counting all 286 three-card hands:
- 64 hands have exactly one 12 and the other two cards sum to more than 4.
- 11 hands have both 12s, and all of these exceed 16.
- So 75 hands exceed 16, giving P(S > 16) ≈ 0.262.
- The average sum given S > 16 is about 20.1; given S ≤ 16 it is about 9.44.

**Updating on the buy at 16.**
- If S > 16, the chance of that buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × P(noise valuation > 16). The noise trader's valuation is 12.23 + N(0, 8.9), so P(noise valuation > 16) ≈ 0.336. This gives about 0.469.
- If S ≤ 16, only a noise trader buys, so the chance is 0.8 × 0.336 ≈ 0.269.
- Weighting the two cases gives a posterior fair value of about 13.5.

**The quote.** Noise traders have a standard deviation of 8.9, so a wide spread still gets fills. The upside tail (sums of 24 or more) carries heavy adverse selection from informed buyers, so I keep the ask well above fair. I am short 1, so I skew the quote slightly upward.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 17.5}

Card 1 is 12, so the value is 12 plus the sum of two cards drawn from the 12 left. I estimate fair value at about 19.5 and quote 15.5 / 23.5 around it.

**Expected value with no trade information.** The 12 remaining cards are 0, 0, 1, 2, 2, 2, 4, 4, 4, 4, 6, 12. They sum to 41, so the average card is about 3.42. Two cards add about 6.83, giving an expected total of about 18.83.

**What the stage-1 trades tell us.**
- **Sell at 10.5:** this was a noise trader. An informed seller would need a value below 10.5, which is impossible now that card 1 is 12.
- **Buy at 16:**
  - An informed buyer at 16 means the total is above 16, so the last two cards sum to more than 4. That holds for 43 of the 66 possible pairs.
  - A buy of this kind happens with likelihood about 0.47 when the total is above 16, versus about 0.27 when it is not. The 0.27 is the chance a noise trader values the contract above 16 when public fair value was about 12.2.

**Updated estimate.** Pairs summing to more than 4 average about 8.93; pairs summing to 4 or less average about 2.91. Weighting by the likelihoods above, the last two cards are expected to sum to about 7.5. That puts fair value at about 19.5.

**Spread.** The last two cards can add anywhere from 0 to 18, so an informed trader can hurt me badly. Noise traders' valuations spread about 8.9 either side of fair value. A spread of about ±4 balances the two risks.

{"bid": 15.5, "ask": 23.5}

Fair value is about 18.8. With card 1 revealed as 12, the remaining 12 cards sum to 41, so each unseen card averages about 3.42 and the two hidden cards add about 6.83.

The distribution of the two hidden cards is skewed to the right:
- **Ask side:** An informed buyer only beats an ask around 22 or higher if the remaining 12 is among the two hidden cards. That happens with probability of about 1/6.
- **Bid side:** Low two-card totals (0+0, 0+1, 0+2, 1+2) are fairly common. So an informed seller below a bid near 15.5 is more likely, and I'll keep the bid a bit lower.

I'll quote 14.5 / 22.5.

{"bid": 14.5, "ask": 22.5}

Card 1 = 12 and card 2 = 4 are known, so the current sum is 16. Card 3 comes from the 11 cards left in the deck: {0,0,1,2,2,2,4,4,4,6,12}. Those cards add up to 37, so card 3 has an expected value of 37/11 ≈ 3.36. The public fair value is about 19.36.

The possible settlements are 16 (prob 2/11), 17 (1/11), 18 (3/11), 20 (3/11), 22 (1/11) and 28 (1/11).

**Ask side.** An informed counterparty buys from me only if the settlement is above my ask. That can only happen when card 3 is 6 or 12. Pricing the ask around 26–27 makes the informed loss very small (about −0.03). It still earns about 1.2 in expected profit from noise traders, whose valuations spread around 19.36 with standard deviation 8.9.

**Bid side.** The lowest possible settlement is 16, so any bid below 16 cannot lose money to an informed seller. Expected profit from noise traders, 0.8 × P(sell) × (19.36 − bid), peaks with a bid around 12.5–13, at roughly 1.2.

{"bid": 12.8, "ask": 26.5}

With card 1 = 12 and card 2 = 4 revealed, settlement is 16 plus card 3. Both quotes below are chosen to maximise expected profit against the mix of 20% informed and 80% noise traders.

**Fair value.** Eleven cards remain: two 0s, one 1, three 2s, three 4s, one 6 and one 12. They sum to 37, so card 3 has an expected value of 37/11 ≈ 3.36. That makes the fair value about 19.36. Possible settlements are 16, 17, 18, 20, 22 and 28.

**Quote 5 tells us nothing new.** The counterparty sold at 12.8. An informed trader values the contract at 16 or more, so it would never sell that low. The trade must have come from a noise trader, and the fair value stays at about 19.36.

**Bid.** An informed trader only sells if the settlement is below my bid. Every bid below 16 is therefore safe from informed traders. The noise-trader payoff is the chance they sell times the 19.36 − bid edge, weighted 0.8:

| Bid | Chance a noise trader sells | Expected gain |
|---|---|---|
| 15 | 31% | 1.09 |
| 14 | 27% | 1.17 |
| 13 | 24% | 1.21 |
| 12 | 20% | 1.20 |

The best bid is around 12.8–13.

**Ask.** An informed trader buys whenever the settlement is above my ask, which costs me money. The net value of each ask is the gain from noise buyers minus that loss:

| Ask | Gain from noise buyers | Loss to informed buyers | Net expected gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21 | 0.56 | 0.15 | 0.42 |
| 23 | 0.99 | 0.09 | 0.90 |
| 26 | 1.21 | 0.04 | 1.17 |
| 26.5 | 1.21 | 0.03 | 1.18 |
| 27 | 1.19 | 0.02 | 1.17 |

The best ask is around 26.5.

**Position.** I am long 1, so either trade keeps me within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": 12.8, "ask": 26.5}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 11 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 0, 3 cards worth 2, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 11. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Here is the quote for quote 1, worked out from the expected value and the payoff on each side.

**Fair value.** The average card is worth 51/11 ≈ 4.64, so the expected sum of three cards is about 13.9.

**Shape of the distribution.** The sum depends mostly on how many 11s are dealt:
- **No 11s** (probability ≈ 0.34): the sum is about 6.75, ranging from 2 to 9.
- **One 11** (probability ≈ 0.51): the sum is about 15.5, ranging from 13 to 17.
- **Two 11s** (probability ≈ 0.15): the sum is about 24.
- **Three 11s** (probability ≈ 0.006): the sum is 33.

**Ask side.**
- At 16, my expected profit per quote is about zero. Losses to informed buyers when two 11s are dealt roughly cancel the gains from noise buyers.
- At 17–18, my expected profit per quote is positive, about +0.2 or more.

**Bid side.** Expected profit per quote rises as the bid moves down from 11 to about 8–9:
- At 11, it is about +0.1.
- At 9, it is about +0.4.
- At 8–9, it is about +0.5.

So I'll bid 8.5 and ask 18.

{"bid": 8.5, "ask": 18}

The public fair value is now about 16.5, and I'll quote 8.0 bid and 24.0 ask.

**Prior.** The deck averages 51/11 ≈ 4.64 per card, so three cards average about 13.9.

**What the first trade tells us.** A buyer at 18 makes high totals more likely. The total can only be above 18 if at least two 11s were dealt, which has prior probability 25/165 ≈ 0.15.
- If the total is above 18, someone buys at 18 with probability about 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.255 ≈ 0.52.
- Otherwise only a noise trader buys, with probability about 0.65 × 0.255 ≈ 0.17. Here 0.255 is the chance noise pushes a valuation from about 13.9 to above 18.

Updated chances for the number of 11s dealt:

| 11s dealt | Probability | Average total |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0.26 | 6.75 |
| 1 | 0.39 | 15.5 |
| 2 | 0.34 | 24.25 |
| 3 | 0.01 | 33 |

That gives a fair value of about 16.5.

**Choosing the quotes.** The possible totals fall in clusters: 4–9 with no 11s, 13–17 with one, and 22–25 with two. Quotes are best placed where few possible totals sit just past them.
- **Ask:** At 24, an informed buyer loses me money only on a total of 25 or 33, and a noise buyer pays well above fair. The expected profit on this side is about +0.45, the best of the asks I checked.
- **Bid:** At 8, an informed seller only hits me on totals of 7 or less. Noise sellers give me about 8.5 below fair. The expected profit on this side is about +0.35.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 24.0}

Card 1 is an 11, so my fair value for the contract is about 24.2. I'm quoting a bid of 22 and an ask of 26.5 around that.

**Fair value from the revealed card.** The 10 cards left are one 0, three 2s, four 3s and two 11s. They sum to 40, so each averages 4, and the expected sum is 11 + 8 = 19 before looking at the trades.

**Updating on the trades.** Both stage-1 counterparties bought, at 18 and then at 24. Buying at 24 is strong evidence of an informed trader whose settlement value is above 24. That points to a final sum of 25 (an 11, a 3 and another 11) or 33 (three 11s). Weighting each possible total by how likely those two buys were gives a fair value of about 24.2. About 67% of the weight is on 25, 8% on 33, 9% on 24 and the rest on 13–22.

**Bid at 22.** I'm short 2 at a fair value near 24–25, so buying back is welcome.
- At a bid of 22, noise traders sell about 36% of the time, giving me roughly 2.2 per trade.
- Informed traders sell only when the value is 22 or less (about 13% probability), and I lose about 5.7 on those.
- That nets slightly positive and also reduces my short.

**Ask at 26.5.** This is above the most likely value of 25, so an informed trader buys only if the value is 33 (about 8%). Noise traders who buy pay me about 2 above fair.

{"bid": 22, "ask": 26.5}

I conditioned on card 1 being 11 and on the three trades so far, and put the fair value at about 23.0.

**What could still settle.** After card 1 = 11, the other 10 cards are 0, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3, 11, 11. Before any trading, the expected total is 11 + 8 = 19. The possible totals are:
- 13 to 17, grouped together with an average of about 15.5
- 22, 24, 25 or 33

**What the trades told us.** Each trade shifts the odds, using the 35% informed / 65% noise mix:
- **Buy at 18:** This favours a total above 18.
- **Buy at 24:** This strongly favours a total above 24, meaning 25 or 33.
- **Sale at 22:** The public fair value was about 24.4 at that point. A sale there favours a total below 22.

**Current estimate.** After these updates, fair value is about 23.0. The probabilities are:

| Total | Probability |
|---|---|
| 13–17 group | about 26% |
| 22 | about 2% |
| 24 | about 7% |
| 25 | about 58% |
| 33 | about 7% |

**Ask.** An ask at 25 or just below it is costly. Informed traders would buy whenever the total is 25 or 33, and those outcomes carry about 65% of the probability. A higher ask only gets hit by informed traders when the total is 33. Noise buyers still give enough edge that expected profit is flat at about 0.55 for asks between 28 and 29. I'm using 27.5 because I'm already short one, and it gives up very little expected profit.

**Bid.** Expected profit peaks at about 0.52 for bids of 16 to 17. That level avoids most selling by informed traders when the total is in the low group, while still catching sales by noise traders.

{"bid": 17, "ask": 27.5}

**Where things stand.** Cards 1 and 2 total 11 + 3 = 14. Card 3 is drawn from the 9 cards left: one 0, three 2s, three 3s and two 11s. So settlement is 14, 16, 17 or 25.

**Updating on the trade history.**
- **Stage 1:** both buys were at high asks (18 and 24). If card 3 is 11, the total is 25 and an informed buyer would take both. That is much more likely than noise traders buying that far above a fair value of about 14.
- **Quote 3:** the sale at 22 fits any value except 25.
- **Quote 4:** no trade at 17 / 27.5 slightly disfavours 14 and 16. An informed trader holding either would have sold at 17.

My rough estimates of each settlement value:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 14 | 0.016 |
| 16 | 0.049 |
| 17 | 0.095 |
| 25 | 0.839 |

That gives an expected settlement of about 23.6.

**Ask.** Any ask of 25 or more cannot be hit by an informed trader. A noise trader buys if their valuation, 23.6 plus noise with standard deviation 6.2, is above the ask. My expected profit is the chance of that times (ask − 23.6). This is roughly 1.05 at an ask of 28 and 1.04 at 29, so I set the ask at 28.

**Bid.** If I bid around 17 to 18, an informed trader sells only when settlement is 14, 16 or 17, which is rare and costs little. Noise traders who sell well below 23.6 give a good edge. Expected profit is about 0.58 to 0.59 per quote in this range, so I bid 17.5.

{"bid": 17.5, "ask": 28}

Settlement is 14 plus the third card. The 9 remaining cards are one 0, three 2s, three 3s and two 11s. So settlement is 14, 16, 17 or 25, with prior odds 1:3:3:2.

**Updating on the trade history:**
- **Stage 1:** the counterparties bought at 18 and at 24. A noise trader rarely buys that high when public fair value is about 14. An informed trader buys at those prices only if the third card is 11, so both buys point to 25.
- **Quote 3:** they sold at 22. An informed trader would not sell there if the value is 25, so this points slightly away from 25.
- **Quotes 4 and 5:** no trade, which also points mildly towards 25.

Putting these together, I estimate roughly a 92% chance the settlement is 25. That gives a posterior mean of about 24.4.

**Quote choice:**
- **Ask:** an informed trader will not buy above 25. Against noise traders centred around 24.4, an ask near 29 gives the best expected edge.
- **Bid:** a high bid invites informed selling when the value is 14, 16 or 17. A bid around 19 balances noise-trader profit against that loss.

{"bid": 19, "ask": 29}

game.title: Dice/cards product
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the two dice.

info.raw:
Fair value before any reveal is E[d1]·E[d2] = 3.5 × 3.5 = **12.25**. The settlement value has a standard deviation of about 8.9 and is skewed to the right: it runs from 1 to 36.

For each side I weighed two things:
- **Noise traders (probability 0.8):** they trade when their valuation (12.25 plus noise with standard deviation 13) crosses my price, and I earn my distance from fair value.
- **Informed traders (probability 0.2):** they trade when the true value is beyond my price, and I lose the difference.

Expected profit per quote, by distance from fair value:

| Distance from fair | Ask side | Bid side |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | ≈ 1.0 | ≈ 1.15 |
| 7 | ≈ 1.34 | ≈ 1.54 |
| 9 | ≈ 1.53 | ≈ 1.73 |
| 11 | ≈ 1.59 | ≈ 1.75 |

Profit rises with width because wider quotes still catch noise traders often, while informed losses shrink. On the bid side it levels off around 9 from fair, since values below 3 are rare. On the ask side it keeps rising slowly because of the long right tail.

I'll quote the bid near 3.3 and the ask near 22.

{"bid": 3.3, "ask": 22.0}

Fair value with nothing revealed is 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25. The product of the two dice is skewed to the right: it runs from 1 to 36 and is clustered at low values. Quote 1 got no trade, which tells us almost nothing, so fair value stays at 12.25.

For each side, the expected profit is the gain from noise traders minus the loss to informed traders:

- **Ask side:** Expected profit is fairly flat for asks from about 22 to 24. At around 24 it is about 1.58 per quote. Below 24 the informed trader picks you off on outcomes of 24, 25, 30 and 36.
- **Bid side:** Low products are common but bounded below by 1, so informed losses are small for a low bid. Expected profit peaks at about 1.76 for a bid near 2.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 24.0}

Die 1 is 6, so the contract settles at 6 × die 2. The possible values are {6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36}, each equally likely, so the fair value is 21.

**Expected profit on the ask at 21 + d:**
- Noise traders (probability 0.8) buy with probability P(N > d), where N has standard deviation 13. Each such sale earns me d.
- Informed traders (probability 0.2) buy only when the settlement value is above my ask. Each such sale loses me (value − ask).

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 27 | 1.55 | 0.40 | 1.15 |
| 30 | 1.76 | 0.20 | 1.56 |
| 31 | 1.77 | 0.17 | 1.60 |
| 32 | 1.75 | 0.13 | **1.62** |
| 33 | 1.71 | 0.10 | 1.61 |

The ask is best at about 32. The values are symmetric around 21, so the best bid is about 10. A bid of 10 only loses to an informed seller when the value is 6.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 32}

With die 1 = 6, the contract settles at 6 × die 2, so it can only be 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 or 36.

**Updating on the trade.** Before quote 3 the fair value was 21 (6 × 3.5).
- An informed trader sells at 10 only when the value is 6. A noise trader sells when 21 + noise < 10, which has probability Φ(−0.846) ≈ 0.20.
- So the chance of a sell at 10 is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.20 ≈ 0.36 if the value is 6, and 0.8 × 0.20 ≈ 0.16 for each other value.
- The posterior probability of 6 rises to about 0.31; each other value has about 0.138.
- The public fair value is now about 18.4.

**Choosing the quotes.** This is the last quote, so I set each side to maximise its expected profit on its own.
- **Ask:** At 30, an informed buyer trades only if the value is 36. Noise buyers trade with probability about 0.19. Expected profit is about 1.56, the best of the asks I tried (26, 31 and 32 all did worse).
- **Bid:** At 11, an informed seller trades only if the value is 6. Noise sellers trade with probability about 0.29. Expected profit is about 2.0, which is the best of the bids I tried (10, 12 and 13 were slightly lower).

{"bid": 11, "ask": 30}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 0, 1 card worth 1, 3 cards worth 2, 4 cards worth 4, 1 card worth 6, 2 cards worth 12. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 12.2: the deck's card values sum to 53, so each card averages about 4.08, and three cards give 12.23. The three-card sum has a standard deviation of about 6. One in five counterparties is informed, so I quote around fair value with a spread of roughly ±3, a little wider on the ask side. That is because the two 12-value cards give the sum a long upper tail.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 15.6}

Fair value estimate: the deck's values sum to 53, so the prior expected sum of 3 cards is 3 × 53/13 ≈ 12.23.

**Update on the buy at 15.6**
- A sum above 15.6 needs at least one 12-card. That happens in 91 of the 286 possible hands (about 0.318).
- Hands above 15.6 average about 19.4. All other hands average about 8.9.
- A noise trader buys at 15.6 with probability about 0.35. The chance of a buy is therefore 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.35 ≈ 0.48 when the sum is above 15.6, and 0.8 × 0.35 ≈ 0.28 when it is not.
- Applying Bayes' rule gives about a 0.44 chance that the sum is above 15.6.
- That puts fair value at about 0.44 × 19.4 + 0.56 × 8.9 ≈ 13.5.

**Quote**
I quote around 13.5 with a fairly wide spread, because informed traders cause adverse selection. I shade both sides up slightly because I am short.

{"bid": 11.0, "ask": 16.8}

Given card 1 = 2, the 12 cards left are 0,0,1,2,2,4,4,4,4,6,12,12. They sum to 51, so each unseen card averages 4.25.

- **Expected settlement:** 2 + 2 × 4.25 = 10.5.
- **Trading history:** In stage 1, one counterparty bought at 15.6 and the next sold at 11. Those two trades point in opposite directions and roughly cancel. They tilt fair value up only slightly, to about 10.6–10.7.
- **Shape of the outcome:** The settlement value is split into two groups. With probability about 0.32, at least one of the two hidden cards is a 12, giving roughly 16 or more. Otherwise the total is about 6.6.
- **Pricing:** An informed counterparty would hit whichever side is wrong. So I want a fairly wide quote around about 10.6, still close enough for noise traders (spread 8.9) to trade with me.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 14.0}

Fair value is about **10.5**, so I'll quote a bid of 4.0 and an ask of 17.0.

**Fair value.** Card 1 is a 2. The 12 cards left are two 0s, one 1, two 2s, four 4s, one 6 and two 12s. They sum to 51, so each averages 4.25. The expected settlement is 2 + 2 × 4.25 = 10.5. The trades so far only nudge this slightly, so I keep 10.5.

game.description:

info.raw:
The settlement value can be 0, 10 or 20, with an expected value of about 11.67. I quote wide, bid 2.0 and ask 20.0, because informed traders (35% of counterparties) know the exact value.

**Settlement value**
- Die 1 is at least 7 with probability 4/6 = 2/3 (faces 7, 8, 10, 12).
- Die 2 is at least 7 with probability 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5 (faces 8 and 9).
- The value is 0 with probability 1/6, 10 with probability 1/2, and 20 with probability 1/3.
- Expected value ≈ 11.67.

**Ask side**
- An informed trader buys only when the value is 20, which has probability 1/3.
- Noise traders value the contract at 11.67 plus noise with standard deviation 10.
- If the ask is 20, an informed trader never buys, because 20 is not above my ask.
- Noise traders then buy about 20% of the time, earning me about 8.3 per trade.
- That gives an expected profit of about 1.1 per quote, which is roughly the best ask setting.

**Bid side**
- An informed trader sells when the value is 0 (probability 1/6), and also when the value is 10 if my bid is above 10.
- With the bid around 2, the expected profit is about 0.93 per quote, which is near the best bid setting.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 20.0}

Fair value starts at 11.67. Die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 2/3, and die 2 with probability 1/2, so the expected settlement is 10 × (2/3 + 1/2).

The quote of 2 / 20 got no trade. An informed trader would have sold at 2 if the value were 0. So the no-trade slightly lowers the chance of 0. The settlement value can only be 0, 10 or 20. The updated probabilities are about 0.10, 0.54 and 0.36, which puts the public fair value at about 12.6.

- **Ask:** At 20, an informed trader holding value 20 does not buy, because it only buys when its valuation is strictly above my ask. Noise traders still buy about 23% of the time, for an expected profit of about 1.1 from this side.
- **Bid:** Compared with other bids, 4 gives the best trade-off. A higher bid gets more noise-trader sales, but a lower bid loses less to an informed seller when the value is 0. Expected profit from this side is about 0.95.

{"bid": 4, "ask": 20}

With die 2 = 9 revealed, the contract is worth 10 if die 1 is low and 20 if die 1 is high.

**Fair value**
- Die 2 shows at least 7, so it contributes 10 for certain.
- Die 1 shows at least 7 on 4 of its 6 faces (7, 8, 10, 12), so that happens with probability 2/3.
- The contract settles at 20 with probability 2/3 and at 10 with probability 1/3.
- Fair value = 10 + 20 × 2/3 ≈ 16.67.
- The no-trade history in stage 1 tells us essentially nothing about die 1.

**Ask side**
- An informed buyer only appears when the value is 20, and it buys only if my ask is below 20.
- So any ask of 20 or more is safe from informed traders.
- For noise traders, the expected edge is d × P(noise > d), where d is the ask minus 16.67.
- This is largest at about d = 7.5, giving about 0.65 × 1.70 ≈ 1.10 per quote.
- That puts the ask at about 24.3.
- An ask just under 20 earns only about 0.77, because informed buyers hit it.

**Bid side**
- An informed seller appears when the value is 10, and it sells only if my bid is above 10.
- So any bid of 10 or less is safe from informed traders.
- By the same symmetric calculation, the best spacing below fair value is about 7.5, which puts the bid at about 9.2.
- I shade it slightly to 9.1, partly because the effect of this quote's trade on my position for the final quote is minor.

{"bid": 9.1, "ask": 24.3}

The value is now either 10 or 30. Pricing each side against that two-point outcome puts the bid at 15.5 and the ask at 34.

**Fair value after the reveal and the trade.**
- Die 2 showed 9, so it contributes 10 for sure.
- Die 1 shows at least 7 with probability 4/6 = 2/3, which would add 20.
- So the settlement is 30 with probability 2/3 or 10 with probability 1/3. That gives a prior fair value of 23.33.
- At quote 3 someone bought at my ask of 24.3. If the value is 30, the chance of that buy is 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.461 ≈ 0.65.
- If the value is 10, only a noise trader would buy, so the chance is 0.65 × 0.461 ≈ 0.30.
- Updating on the buy gives P(value = 30) ≈ 0.8125, so the public fair value is about 26.25.

**Ask.**
- Below 30, informed traders buy from me whenever the value is 30. At an ask of 28, for example, my expected profit is about −0.08.
- At 30 or above, informed traders never buy, so only noise traders hit the ask. My expected profit is then 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 26.25).
- This peaks at about 1.10 for an ask around 34.

**Bid.**
- Between 10 and 30, informed traders sell to me when the value is 10, and noise traders sell when their valuation is below the bid.
- I compared expected profit at several bids:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.55 |
| 14 | 0.61 |
| 15 | 0.62 |
| 16 | 0.62 |
| 20 | 0.42 |

- The best range is about 15 to 16, so I bid 15.5.

- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 1, 4, 7, 8.
- Die 2 (8 faces, each equally likely): 0, 3, 5, 10, 11, 12, 12, 12.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of dice showing at least 6.

info.raw:
The fair value before any reveal is **11.25**, so I'm quoting a bid of **5.2** and an ask of **18.2**.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 shows at least 6 when it lands on 7 or 8, so the chance is 2/4 = 0.5.
- Die 2 shows at least 6 when it lands on 10, 11, 12, 12 or 12, so the chance is 5/8 = 0.625.
- The expected value is 10 × (0.5 + 0.625) = 11.25.

**Settlement distribution**

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.1875 |
| 10 | 0.5 |
| 20 | 0.3125 |

**Choosing the quotes**

For each side I weighed the profit from noise traders against the loss to an informed trader.

- **Ask:** if the ask is between about 11.25 and 20, an informed trader buys only when the value is 20. That costs 20 − ask, with probability 0.3125. Expected profit peaks with the ask about 7 above fair value, near 18.2, at roughly 0.78 per quote.
- **Bid:** if the bid is below 10, an informed trader sells only when the value is 0. That costs the bid, with probability 0.1875. Expected profit peaks with the bid about 6 below fair value, near 5.2, at roughly 0.74 per quote.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 18.2}

The current fair value is about 11.05. I'm quoting a bid of 5.0 and an ask of 17.5 around it, because those prices roughly maximise expected profit on each side.

**Settlement distribution.**
- Die 1 shows at least 6 when it lands on 7 or 8, so with probability 1/2.
- Die 2 shows at least 6 when it lands on 10, 11, 12, 12 or 12, so with probability 5/8.
- The contract therefore settles at:
  - 0 with probability 0.1875
  - 10 with probability 0.5
  - 20 with probability 0.3125
- The prior expected value is 11.25.

**Update after no trade at 5.2 / 18.2.**
- An informed trader would have traded if the value was 0 or 20, but not if it was 10.
- A noise trader (fair value 11.25, standard deviation 7) does nothing about 64.6% of the time.
- So the chance of no trade was about 0.517 if the value is 0 or 20, and about 0.717 if it is 10.
- Updated probabilities:
  - 0 with probability about 0.157
  - 10 with probability about 0.581
  - 20 with probability about 0.262
- The fair value is now about 11.05.

**Expected profit by price.**

| Ask | Expected profit | Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | about 0.74 | 4.5 | about 0.77 |
| 17 | about 0.79 | 5.0 | about 0.78 |
| 17.5 | about 0.79 | 6.0 | about 0.76 |
| 18 | about 0.79 | | |

The ask is flat between 17 and 18, so I take 17.5. The bid peaks at 5.0.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 17.5}

Die 1 shows 8, which is at least 6, so it already adds 10 to the settlement. Die 2 is at least 6 on 5 of its 8 faces (10, 11, 12, 12, 12). The contract therefore settles at either 10 (probability 3/8) or 20 (probability 5/8). Fair value is 10 + 6.25 = 16.25.

**Ask:** An informed buyer only trades against me if the value is 20 and my ask is below 20. Setting the ask above 20 removes that risk. The expected profit from noise buyers alone is about 0.8·d·(1−Φ(d/7)), where d is the ask minus 16.25. This peaks near d = 5, an ask of about 21.2, with roughly 0.95 expected. Any ask below 20 does worse, because the losses to informed buyers outweigh the extra noise trades.

**Bid:** An informed seller only trades if the value is 10 and my bid is above 10. A bid of 10 avoids this, since a seller valuing the contract at exactly 10 is not below my bid. That gives about 0.93 expected profit from noise sellers. Bids above 10 do slightly worse.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 21.2}

With die 1 revealed as 8 (at least 6), the contract is worth 10 + 10 × P(die 2 ≥ 6). Five of die 2's eight faces qualify (10, 11, 12, 12, 12), so the contract settles at 20 with probability 5/8 and at 10 with probability 3/8. Fair value is 16.25.

**What the history tells us:** At quote 3 (bid 10, ask 21.2), an informed trader would not have traded at either value. At value 20 it would not buy above 20. At value 10 it would not sell, because 10 is not strictly below the bid of 10. So the no-trade result carries no information, and fair value stays at 16.25.

**Ask side:**
- Any ask below 20 lets an informed trader holding value 20 buy at a loss to me.
- Above 20, only noise traders trade. Against Normal noise with standard deviation 7, expected profit is best at a margin of about 0.75 × 7 ≈ 5.25.
- That puts the ask at 21.5, with expected profit of about 0.95.

**Bid side:**
- Any bid above 10 lets an informed trader holding value 10 sell to me at a loss.
- I compared expected profit at three bids:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 10 | ≈ 0.93 |
| 10.5 | ≈ 0.91 |
| 11 | ≈ 0.88 |

- A bid of exactly 10 is best: noise traders still trade, and the informed trader with value 10 does not.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 21.5}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 12 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The settlement value is the smallest of the 3 dealt cards. Across all C(12,3) = 220 possible hands:

- P(min = 14) = 4/220
- P(min = 9) = 31/220
- P(min = 3) = 130/220
- P(min = 1) = 55/220

So the fair value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Ask side.** If the true value is 9 or 14, informed traders buy at any ask below that. At asks of 5–7, the losses to them outweigh what I earn from noise buyers. Around 9, the trade becomes slightly positive: only the rare value 14 hurts me, and noise traders still occasionally buy far above fair value.

**Bid side.** At a bid just above 1, an informed trader sells only when the value is 1, and then I lose very little. Noise sellers, about 19% of the time, give me roughly 2.4 of edge. A bid of about 1.1 gives the highest expected profit, about +0.22 per quote. Higher bids such as 2–2.5 lose more to informed sellers when the value is 1.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 9.0}

The posterior fair value is about 3.84. The best quotes are a bid of 1.2 and an ask of 9.0, each with a small positive expected profit.

**Prior distribution of the minimum.** Three cards are dealt from 12, so there are 220 possible hands.

| Min value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | 55/220 |
| 3 | 130/220 |
| 9 | 31/220 |
| 14 | 4/220 |

The prior mean is 3.55.

**Update on quote 1 (1.1 / 9, no trade).**
- If the value is 3 or 9, an informed counterparty does not trade. A noise trader at fair value 3.55 ± 2.8 lands inside the quotes about 78% of the time. So the chance of no trade is about 0.89.
- If the value is 1 or 14, an informed counterparty would have traded. So the chance of no trade is about 0.39.

The posterior is roughly 1: 13%, 3: 70%, 9: 17%, 14: 1%. That gives a fair value of about 3.84.

**Choosing the bid.** A bid below 3 risks an informed seller only when the value is 1. Bids near 1.1–1.5 give the best trade-off between that risk and profit from noise sellers. The expected gain is about +0.2 per quote.

**Choosing the ask.** Any ask below 9 is costly because informed buyers take it whenever the value is 9, which has about 17% weight. An ask at 9 is only exposed to the 1% chance the value is 14. Its expected gain is about +0.06.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 9.0}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement value is at most 9. The other two cards come from the 11 left: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Value distribution before using the trades:**
- P(min = 1) = 10/55
- P(min = 3) = 30/55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55

**Updating on the stage-1 trading:** At quote 1 nobody traded at 1.1 / 9. At quote 2 a counterparty sold at my bid of 1.2. That sale is roughly 3 times more likely if the minimum is 1 than if it is 3 or 9, because an informed trader with value 1 would sell there.

After that update the probabilities are about:
- P(1) ≈ 0.40
- P(3) ≈ 0.40
- P(9) ≈ 0.20

The public fair value is about 3.4.

**Choosing the bid:**
- Any bid above 1 gets hit by informed traders holding a 1, which costs money.
- A bid of exactly 1.0 avoids those informed sellers. It still collects noise sellers below 1, which earns about +0.23 per quote in expectation.

**Choosing the ask:**
- Any ask below 9 gets lifted by informed traders holding a 9.
- An ask of 9 avoids those informed buyers and only fills tail noise buyers, which still has a slightly positive expectation.

My position of +1 leaves room to buy more, so the bid side is not restricted.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Quote bid 1.0, ask 9.0.

**Current fair value.** Card 1 is a 9, so the contract settles at 1, 3 or 9. The two unrevealed cards come from the 11 left: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.
- P(settle at 1) = 2/11.
- P(settle at 3) = 6/11.
- P(settle at 9) = 3/11.
- Expected value is about 4.27.

**Ask side.** Any ask below 9 gets lifted by informed traders whenever the value is 9 (3/11 of the time). Noise traders rarely pay that much. At an ask of 9, informed traders never buy, and noise buys give the best expected profit, about +0.11 per quote.

**Bid side.** Any bid above 1 gets hit by informed traders whenever the value is 1. A bid of 1 avoids that and still catches noise sellers, giving about +0.20 per quote. That is better than the nearby bids I checked.

**Inventory.** A position of +1 is well within the ±3 limit, so it doesn't change the quote.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Card 2 is the only card worth 1 in the deck, so the minimum is now certain to be **1**. Settlement is fixed at 1.

**How each counterparty behaves**
- **Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 1. They will never trade with a bid below 1 or an ask above 1.
- **Noise traders** have a valuation of 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8.

**Choosing the spread.** Any trade at a quote placed some distance x from 1 earns x. The expected profit on each side is x times the probability the noise trader's valuation lands beyond the quote. That is roughly maximised when x/2.8 ≈ 0.61, so x ≈ 1.7 on each side.

**Quote.** That gives an ask near 2.7–2.8 and a bid near -0.7. The rules do not say whether negative prices are allowed, so the bid of -0.7 is a small risk. A bid of 0 would be the fallback, at about a 0.36 edge against 0.46.

{"bid": -0.7, "ask": 2.7}

Card 2 is the only 1 in the deck, so the smallest dealt card is 1 whatever card 3 turns out to be. The contract settles at exactly 1.

- **Informed trader:** they value the contract at exactly 1. With my bid below 1 and my ask above 1, they will never trade with me.
- **Noise trader:** their valuation is 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8. On each side my expected profit is d × P(noise passes my quote), where d is my distance from 1. That is largest at roughly d ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 2.1.
- **Position:** I am at +2, so buying one more unit takes me to +3, which is allowed. Selling is also allowed.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
The fair value is about 9.09, so I'm quoting 8.0 / 10.2.

**Fair value.** I took the CDF of the maximum as the product of the three dice CDFs, then used E[max] = Σ P(max > x) for x = 0 to 11.

- For x = 0 to 3, P(max > x) = 1, because die 2 is always at least 4. These four terms add 4.
- The remaining terms are:

| x | P(max > x) |
|---|---|
| 4 | 0.925 |
| 5 | 0.925 |
| 6 | 0.825 |
| 7 | 0.7375 |
| 8 | 0.475 |
| 9 | 0.4 |
| 10 | 0.4 |
| 11 | 0.4 |

- The total is E[max] = 9.0875.

**Quote.** The settlement value is spread widely around 9.09. One in five counterparties knows the true value, so a tight quote would lose to them. I'm quoting about 1.1 either side of fair. Noise traders have a standard deviation of 2.6, so most of them will still trade at that width.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.2}

Expected value of the maximum, using E[max] = Σ P(max > x):

| x | P(max ≤ x) | P(max > x) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 3 | 0 (die 2 is at least 4) | 1 each, so 4 in total |
| 4 to 5 | 0.5·0.25·0.6 = 0.075 | 0.925 each |
| 6 | 0.5·0.5·0.7 = 0.175 | 0.825 |
| 7 | 0.5·0.75·0.7 = 0.2625 | 0.7375 |
| 8 | 1·0.75·0.7 = 0.525 | 0.475 |
| 9 to 11 | 0.75·0.8 = 0.6 | 0.4 each |

Summing the last column gives E ≈ 9.09.

The outcome is bimodal. The contract settles at 12 with probability 0.4; otherwise it is mostly 8 or below. That means an informed counterparty can hurt either side, so I keep a moderately wide spread around 9.1. The last quote got no trade, which tells me little, so I tighten slightly to 8.1 / 10.1.

{"bid": 8.1, "ask": 10.1}

Die 3 came up 1, so the contract now settles at the larger of die 1 and die 2.

**Value before using the trade history:** I listed all 16 equally likely pairs of die 1 and die 2.
- If die 1 is 2, the four maxes are 4, 6, 7, 12, summing to 29.
- If die 1 is 4, the four maxes are 4, 6, 7, 12, summing to 29.
- Die 1 shows 8 on two faces, so those cases count twice: 8, 8, 8, 12 twice sums to 72.
- The total is 130, so the expected value is 130/16 ≈ 8.13.

**Effect of the earlier sell at 8.1:** I used a rough Bayesian update.
- An informed trader sells at 8.1 whenever the true value is below 8.1. Given die 3 = 1, that is every outcome except the four where the value is 12.
- A noise trader sells at 8.1 with probability of roughly 0.39. This assumes the stage-1 fair value was about 8.8, which I estimated rather than computed exactly.
- So the chance of that sell is about 0.51 if the value is below 8.1 and about 0.31 if it is 12.
- Reweighting the 16 outcomes this way gives a fair value of about 7.7.

**Quote:**
- The possible values are only 4, 6, 7, 8 and 12, so I quote fairly wide around 7.7.
- At an ask of 8.5, an informed trader buys only when the value is 12.
- At a bid of 6.3, an informed trader sells only when the value is 4 or 6.
- I am long one unit, so I shade both prices slightly down to make selling a little more likely than buying.

{"bid": 6.3, "ask": 8.5}

Fair value is now about **8.6**, so I quote 7.4 / 9.9, roughly 1.2 below and 1.3 above it.

**Prior with die 3 = 1.** The contract settles at the larger of die 1 and die 2. There are 16 equally likely combinations:
- If die 1 is 2 or 4, the maximum is just die 2: 4, 6, 7 or 12, summing to 29 each time.
- If die 1 is 8, the maximum is 8, 8, 8 or 12, summing to 36 each time. This case occurs on two of die 1's faces.

That gives an expected value of (29+29+36+36)/16 = 130/16 ≈ 8.125. The value is 12 with probability 1/4. Otherwise the average is 82/12 ≈ 6.83.

**Update for the buy at 8.5 in quote 3.**
- A noise trader buys at 8.5 with probability P(Z > 0.375/2.6) ≈ 0.44.
- If the value is 12, the chance of a buy is 0.2 + 0.8×0.44 ≈ 0.55, because an informed trader would also buy.
- If the value is anything else, the chance of a buy is 0.8×0.44 ≈ 0.35, since only noise traders buy.

The posterior probability that the value is 12 rises to about 0.34. The posterior mean is about 8.6.

**Quote.** The outcome is lumpy: either 12 or about 6.8 on average. Informed traders will lift any ask below 12, so I keep a fairly wide spread around 8.6 to protect against that.

{"bid": 7.4, "ask": 9.9}

The settlement value now depends only on die 2:

- **Settlement:** die 3 is 1 and die 1 is 8, so the contract settles at max(8, die 2).
  - Die 2 shows 4, 6 or 7 with probability 3/4, giving a settlement of 8.
  - Die 2 shows 12 with probability 1/4, giving a settlement of 12.
  - Fair value is 0.75 × 8 + 0.25 × 12 = 9.
- **Noise traders:** their valuations are about Normal(9, 2.6).
- **Informed traders:** they sell to me only if my bid is above 8, and buy from me only if my ask is below 12.

**Ask:** Write the ask as 9 + x. The expected profit is 0.8·x·(1 − Φ(x/2.6)) + 0.05·(x − 3) while the ask is below 12. The last term is the loss to an informed buyer when the value is 12.
- x = 2.0 gives about 0.30.
- x = 2.5 gives about 0.31.
- x = 3.0 gives about 0.30.

The best ask is about 11.4–11.5.

**Bid:** Keeping the bid at or below 8 means an informed seller never trades with me. The noise-only optimum is about 1.95 below fair value, so the bid is about 7.1.

My position of −1 is small, so I don't skew the quotes.

{"bid": 7.1, "ask": 11.4}

The contract settles at 9 in expectation, so I quote a bid of 7.0 and an ask of 11.4.

**Settlement value.** Die 3 = 1 and die 1 = 8, so the settlement is max(8, die 2).
- Die 2 is 4, 6 or 7 with probability 3/4, giving a settlement of 8.
- Die 2 is 12 with probability 1/4, giving a settlement of 12.
- The expected value is 0.75 × 8 + 0.25 × 12 = 9.

Quote 5 had no trade, so the public fair value stays at 9. Noise traders value the contract at N(9, 2.6²).

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 12 and my ask is below 12. That happens with probability 0.2 × 0.25 = 0.05, and each such sale loses me 12 − ask.

Expected profit = 0.8·P(noise > a)·(a − 9) − 0.05·(12 − a).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11.0 | 0.304 |
| 11.3 | 0.311 |
| 11.5 | 0.312 |
| 12.0 | 0.298 |

The curve is flat near the top, so I set the ask at 11.4.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only when the value is 8 and my bid is above 8. A bid at or below 8 avoids that loss entirely.

Expected profit = 0.8·P(noise < b)·(9 − b).

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8.0 | 0.28 |
| 7.5 | 0.338 |
| 7.0 | 0.354 |
| 6.6 | 0.342 |

The best bid is about 7.0. My position limits are not a constraint on this last quote.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.4}

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
The fair value is about 9.09, so I'm quoting 7.8 bid and 10.4 ask around it.

**Expected value of the maximum.** I worked out the probability that the maximum is at most each threshold. Die 2 never shows less than 4, so the maximum is always at least 4.

| Maximum at most | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 0.5 × 0.25 × 0.6 = 0.075 |
| 6 | 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.7 = 0.175 |
| 7 | 0.5 × 0.75 × 0.7 = 0.2625 |
| 8 | 1 × 0.75 × 0.7 = 0.525 |
| 9 | 1 × 0.75 × 0.8 = 0.6 |
| 12 | 1 |

The expected maximum is 4 plus, for each interval above 4, the chance the maximum is above that interval times its length:

E[max] = 4 + 0.925×2 + 0.825×1 + 0.7375×1 + 0.475×1 + 0.4×3 ≈ **9.09**

**Spread.** The settlement value is spread widely around 9.09, and 20% of counterparties know it exactly. Noise traders' valuations vary by about 2.6 around fair value. A spread of roughly ±1.3 around 9.09 should cover the expected loss to informed traders while still trading with noise traders.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 10.4}

Fair value is about 9.09, and I'm quoting a bid of 8.0 and an ask of 10.2 around it.

**Largest of dice 1 and 2.** Pairing each face of die 1 with each face of die 2 gives 16 equally likely outcomes:
- 4 with probability 1/8
- 6 with probability 1/8
- 7 with probability 1/8
- 8 with probability 3/8
- 12 with probability 1/4

Its expected value is 8.125.

**Bringing in die 3.**

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected maximum |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 (die 3 never matters) |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 0.75·9 + 0.25·12 = 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

Weighting these gives an expected settlement of about 9.09.

**Quote.** The last quote got no trade, which tells us almost nothing new. I'm tightening slightly around 9.09: a bid of 8.0 and an ask of 10.2. The spread still protects against the 20% chance of an informed trader, since the settlement value can be far from fair value.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 10.2}

Die 3 = 6, so 6 is the floor for the maximum. Die 1 then gives an effective value of 6 or 8, each with probability 1/2.

**Settlement distribution and fair value**
- Settlement is 6 with probability 2/8, 7 with 1/8, 8 with 3/8 and 12 with 2/8.
- Fair value = (6·2 + 7 + 8·3 + 12·2)/8 = 8.375.

**Choosing the quotes**
- **Ask side:** the only informed buyer I can lose to is the one who knows the value is 12. An ask around 10.5 to 11 gave the best expected profit, about 0.28 per quote. That beats a tight ask, which loses about 3 per trade to informed buyers when the value is 12.
- **Bid side:** informed sellers only hurt me if my bid is above 6 (or above 7). A bid around 6.2 to 6.5 gave the best expected profit, about 0.33 to 0.35 per quote, while still catching noise sellers.

{"bid": 6.4, "ask": 10.7}

Posting bid 6.0 and ask 10.0 around a fair value of about 8.1.

**Fair value given die 3 = 6.** The contract settles at the largest of die 1, die 2 and 6.
- If die 1 is 2 or 4 (prob 1/2), the settlement is 6, 6, 7 or 12, depending on die 2. The average is 7.75.
- If die 1 is 8 (prob 1/2), the settlement is 8, 8, 8 or 12. The average is 9.
- So the possible values are 6 (prob 1/4), 7 (1/8), 8 (3/8) and 12 (1/4). The expected value is 8.375.

**Effect of no trade at quote 3 (6.4 / 10.7).** An informed trader holding 12 would have bought at 10.7. The fact that nobody traded lowers the chance of 12 from 25% to about 19%. That puts the public fair value at about 8.1.

**Bid side.** Informed sellers only matter if the bid is above 6, the lowest possible value. A bid near 6 still catches noise sellers with a good margin and takes almost no adverse selection.

**Ask side.** The risk is an informed buyer when the value is 12. I compared expected profit for asks between 9.5 and 10.5, and an ask around 10 gives the best trade-off.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.0}

**Quote: bid 8.0, ask 12.0.**

**Settlement value.** Die 1 = 8 and die 3 = 6, so the contract settles at max(8, die 2).
- Die 2 = 4, 6 or 7 gives 8, with probability 3/4.
- Die 2 = 12 gives 12, with probability 1/4.
- On the prior alone, the expected value is 9.

**Effect of the last trade.** At quote 4 a counterparty bought from me at 10.
- At that point the public fair value was about 8.4.
- A noise trader buys above 10 with probability about 0.8 × 0.27 ≈ 0.21.
- An informed trader buys only if the value is 12, which adds 0.2.
- That makes a buy about 1.9 times as likely when the value is 12. Updating on it, the chance of 12 rises from 0.25 to about 0.39.
- The public fair value is now about 9.6, so noise valuations are centred there with standard deviation 2.6.

**Ask.** An informed buyer only exists when the value is 12. At an ask of 12, that buyer does not trade, so there is no adverse fill. Noise buyers above 12 then give an expected edge of about 0.34. That is the best value among the asks I tried; 11.5 gives about 0.32 and 11 about 0.25.

**Bid.** An informed seller only exists when the value is 8. At a bid of 8, that seller does not trade, since its valuation is not below my bid. Noise sellers then give an expected edge of about 0.34. Bidding 8.5 drops this to about 0.23 because informed sellers start hitting it. A bid of 7.9 gives about the same edge as 8.

{"bid": 8.0, "ask": 12.0}

Settlement is max(8, die 2, 6). Die 2 is one of 4, 6, 7 or 12, so the contract settles at 8 with probability 3/4 and at 12 with probability 1/4. Fair value is 9.

**What the last trade tells us:** At quote 5 the counterparty sold to me at 8. An informed trader values the contract at 8 or 12, so it would never sell at 8. That seller must have been a noise trader, so fair value stays at 9.

**Ask:**
- If the value is 12, an informed trader buys at any ask below 12.
- The expected profit is 0.8·P(noise valuation > a)·(a − 9) − 0.05·(12 − a).
- This peaks at about a = 11.5–11.7, with expected profit of about 0.31.

**Bid:**
- At a bid of 8 or below, an informed trader never sells.
- The expected profit is 0.8·P(noise valuation < b)·(9 − b).
- This peaks near b = 7.0, with expected profit of about 0.35.
- Any purchase at 7 or below is guaranteed profitable, because settlement is at least 8.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.6}

| Smallest card | Probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | 55/220 = 25% |
| 3 | 130/220 = 59% |
| 9 | 31/220 = 14% |
| 14 | 4/220 = 1.8% |
