**Ask.** If I ask anywhere between 3 and 9, an informed trader buys when the value is 9 or 14. That happens about 16% of the time, and the average value in those cases is about 9.6.
- Asking 8 or below, my losses to informed traders cancel or outweigh my profits from noise traders.
- At 8.9 the expected result is slightly positive, about +0.02 per quote.

**Bid.** The main risk on the bid side is the 25% chance the value is 1.
- Bidding 1.0, an informed trader never sells to me, because their value of 1 is not below my bid.
- Noise traders still sell about 18% of the time, which makes the bid side worth about +0.23 per quote.
- Raising the bid to 2.5 brings that edge down to roughly zero.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.9}

Unconditionally, the smallest card is worth about 3.55 on average. After quote 1 traded nothing, my fair value drops slightly to about 3.44.

**Distribution of the smallest card** (220 equally likely 3-card hands):

| Smallest card | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 25% |
| 3 | 130 | 59% |
| 9 | 31 | 14% |
| 14 | 4 | 2% |

**Effect of quote 1 (bid 1, ask 8.9, no trade):** An informed trader would only have traded if the value was 14, and would have bought. Values 1, 3 and 9 always give no trade with an informed trader. So no trade makes 14 less likely, and fair value is now about 3.44.

**Bid:**
- At a bid of exactly 1.0, an informed trader never sells, because no value is below 1.
- Noise traders sell about 19% of the time, and I gain about 2.4 each time.
- Expected profit is about +0.23, which is the best of the bids I checked.
- Any bid above 1 lets informed traders holding a 1 sell to me, and that loss outweighs the extra noise trades.

**Ask:**
- An ask below 9 lets informed traders buy whenever the value is 9 or 14, and that loss roughly cancels what I earn from noise traders.
- At an ask of 9.0, only a value of 14 hurts me, and that is now very unlikely.
- Expected profit is about +0.045.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

With card 1 = 9, the settlement is min(9, card 2, card 3). Cards 2 and 3 come from the 11 remaining cards: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Settlement distribution**
- P(min = 1) = P(at least one of the two cards is the 1) = 1 − (10/11 × 9/10) = 2/11
- P(min = 9) = P(both cards are 9 or 14) = 6/11 × 5/10 = 3/11
- P(min = 3) = 6/11, the remaining case
- Expected value = (2 + 18 + 27)/11 ≈ 4.27

**Ask side**
- An ask of 9 or higher can only lose to an informed trader if the value is above 9, which cannot happen.
- At ask 9, noise buyers give about 0.5 × 0.046 × 4.73 ≈ +0.11 expected profit.
- At asks between 3 and 9, informed buyers when the value is 9 cost more than the extra noise trades earn.
- At 9.5 the expected profit falls to about +0.08, so 9 is best.

**Bid side**
- A bid of 1 never trades with an informed seller, because the value cannot be below 1.
- At bid 1, noise sellers give about 0.5 × 0.121 × 3.27 ≈ +0.20.
- A bid of 1.5 gives about +0.18 and a bid of 2 about +0.15, because informed sellers holding a 1 cost more than the extra noise trades earn.
- A bid of 0.5 gives about +0.17, so 1 is best.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

The contract's expected value is about 4.27, but the best quotes sit away from it, at bid 1 and ask 9.

**Expected settlement value given card 1 = 9**

The settlement is min(9, c2, c3). Cards 2 and 3 come from the 11 remaining cards: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. There are C(11,2) = 55 equally likely pairs.

| Pair contains | Settlement | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|---|
| The 1 | 1 | 10 | 10/55 |
| At least one 3, no 1 | 3 | 30 | 30/55 |
| Only 9s and 14s | 9 | 15 | 15/55 |

The expected value is (10·1 + 30·3 + 15·9)/55 = 235/55 ≈ 4.27.

No trades have happened at my quotes of 1 and 9, so the history adds no information.

**Choosing the ask**

- Any ask between 3 and 9 is bought by every informed trader holding a 9, and those losses outweigh the noise-trader profit. At 6 the expected result is about -0.18.
- At 9, an informed trader never buys, because it only buys when its value is strictly above my ask.
- At 9, noise traders buy about 4.6% of the time, at a profit of about 4.73 each. That gives an expected gain of about +0.11.
- A higher ask, such as 9.5, earns less, about +0.08.

**Choosing the bid**

- Any bid above 3 is hit by informed traders holding a 1 or a 3, which is a large loss.
- At 1, an informed trader never sells, because it only sells when its value is strictly below my bid.
- At 1, noise traders sell about 12% of the time, at a profit of about 3.27 each. That gives an expected gain of about +0.20.
- Nearby bids do worse: about +0.18 at 1.5, +0.15 at 2 and +0.17 at 0.5.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

Card 3 is drawn from the 10 remaining cards: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and three 14s. Since card 1 is 9, the contract settles at:

- **1** with probability 0.1
- **3** with probability 0.4
- **9** with probability 0.5 (card 3 is a 9 or a 14)

The fair value is 0.1×1 + 0.4×3 + 0.5×9 = **5.8**. I'm taking that as the noise traders' centre. I'm ignoring any information from the no-trade history.

**Ask:** An informed trader only buys if the value is above my ask. At 9.0 they never buy, because the value is at most 9. Noise traders buy about 12.7% of the time, giving an expected edge of about +0.20. Going lower, say to 8.0, lets informed traders buy when the value is 9, which costs more than the extra noise trades earn. Going above 9 loses noise volume. So I ask **9.0**.

**Bid:** At 3.0, an informed trader only sells when the value is 1, costing 0.5×0.1×2 = 0.10. Noise traders sell about 15.9% of the time, earning about 0.22. That nets about +0.12. Any bid above 3 lets informed traders sell when the value is 3, which costs too much. So I bid **3.0**.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 9.0}

**Quote: bid 3, ask 9.** These two prices are where informed traders take the least from me.

**Settlement distribution.** Card 1 = 9 and card 2 = 14, so the contract settles at min(9, card 3). The 10 unseen cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and three 14s.

| Card 3 | Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0.1 |
| 3 | 3 | 0.4 |
| 9 or 14 | 9 | 0.5 |

That gives a prior expected value of 0.1 + 1.2 + 4.5 = 5.8.

**What quote 5's no-trade tells me.** I quoted bid 3, ask 9 and nobody traded.
- An informed trader with value 1 would have sold to me at 3.
- Informed traders with value 3 or 9 would not have traded.
- A noise trader centred on 5.8 with spread 2.8 does not trade about 71% of the time.

Updating on this lowers the chance the value is 1:

| Value | Updated probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | about 0.044 |
| 3 | about 0.425 |
| 9 | about 0.531 |

The public fair value is now about 6.1.

**Ask side.** Any ask below 9 is bought by informed traders when the value is 9, which happens 53% of the time. Expected profit from the ask:
- Ask 9: about 0.22.
- Ask 8.9: about 0.20.
- Ask 9.2: about 0.21.

So the ask stays at 9.

**Bid side.** Any bid above 3 is hit by informed traders when the value is 3, which happens 42.5% of the time. Expected profit from the bid:
- Bid 3: about 0.16.
- Bid 3.1: about 0.15.
- Bid 2: about 0.13.

So the bid stays at 3.

game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is about **8.68**. Out of 28 possible card pairs:
- The minimum is 2 in 7 pairs (P = 0.25).
- The minimum is 9 in 11 pairs (P = 0.39).
- The minimum is 13 in 10 pairs (P = 0.36).

So 7×2 + 11×9 + 10×13 = 243, and 243 / 28 ≈ 8.68.

An informed trader only ever buys when the value is 13, or sells when it is 2. I set each side to balance profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders:

- **Ask:** At 13, I lose nothing to informed buyers, since the value is never above 13. Expected profit peaks at about 0.85 for asks around 13.0 to 13.5.
- **Bid:** Expected profit peaks at about 0.79 for bids around 3. Below that the loss to informed sellers is small, because the value is 2 only 25% of the time.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 13.2}

Fair value after the first trade is about **7.04**, so I'll quote bid 2.0 and ask 13.0.

**Prior fair value.** There are 28 possible two-card deals. The smallest dealt card is:
- 2 in 7 deals,
- 9 in 11 deals,
- 13 in 10 deals.

The prior expected value is 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Update after the first trade.** A counterparty sold to me at 3.2.
- An informed trader sells at 3.2 only if the value is 2.
- A noise trader sells about 19% of the time.

The chance of seeing that sale is about 0.354 if the value is 2 and about 0.154 otherwise. The updated probabilities are about 0.43 for 2, 0.30 for 9 and 0.27 for 13. That gives a fair value of about 7.04.

**Choosing the quotes.** The value can only be 2, 9 or 13, so informed traders hurt me only when my quotes sit between those values. I compared the expected profit of different bids and asks.
- The bid is best at about 2.0. Any bid above 2 loses to informed sellers when the value is 2, and that loss outweighs the extra noise trades.
- The ask is best at about 13.0. At 13 an informed buyer gains nothing, because it only buys if its valuation is strictly above my ask. Noise buyers still trade with me at a wide margin.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 13.0}

Card 1 is a 2, and the deck has only one card worth 2. The minimum of the two dealt cards is therefore exactly 2, so settlement is certain at 2.

That makes the public fair value 2. An informed trader also values the contract at 2, so it will never trade against a quote that has edge on both sides. Noise traders value it at 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 6.3.

On each side I want the edge e that maximises e × P(noise > e). For a normal distribution this peaks at about e ≈ 0.75σ ≈ 4.7. That gives a bid of -2.7 and an ask of 6.7.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 11.98, so I'm quoting 10.6 bid / 13.4 ask, roughly symmetric around it.

**Fair value.** The settlement is the largest of 3 cards drawn without replacement from 20. There are C(20,3) = 1140 possible hands. The chance the largest card is at most v is C(number of cards worth v or less, 3) / 1140. That gives this distribution for the maximum:

| Max | Probability |
|---|---|
| 15 | about 0.40 |
| 11 | about 0.28 |
| 10 | about 0.17 |
| 9 | about 0.07 |
| 7 | about 0.065 |
| 5 or less | about 0.01 |

The expected maximum is 13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98.

**Spread.**
- **Ask side:** an informed counterparty buys from me only when the max is 15, which happens about 40% of the time.
- **Bid side:** an informed counterparty sells to me whenever the max is 11 or below. Losses there are spread over 11, 10 and lower values.
- **Width:** noise traders have a standard deviation of 2.7, so a spread of about ±1.4 still gets a reasonable number of their trades.

{"bid": 10.6, "ask": 13.4}

The expected maximum of the three dealt cards was about 11.98 before any trading. After the counterparty bought at 13.4, my estimate of fair value is about 12.7.

**Prior fair value.** The chance that the maximum is at most v is C(cards ≤ v, 3) / C(20, 3), where C(20, 3) = 1140.

| Maximum | Probability | Contribution to E[max] |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1/1140 | 3 |
| 4 | 3/1140 | 12 |
| 5 | 6/1140 | 30 |
| 7 | 74/1140 | 518 |
| 9 | 81/1140 | 729 |
| 10 | 199/1140 | 1990 |
| 11 | 316/1140 | 3476 |
| 15 | 460/1140 | 6900 |
| **Total** | | **13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98** |

**Updating on the buy at 13.4.**
- An informed counterparty would only buy at 13.4 if the maximum is 15.
- A noise trader buys if its valuation is above 13.4. That has probability P(Z > (13.4 − 11.98)/2.7 = 0.526) ≈ 0.30.
- If the maximum is 15, the chance of a buy is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.30 = 0.44.
- If the maximum is anything else, the chance of a buy is 0.8 × 0.30 = 0.24.
- The posterior chance that the maximum is 15 is 0.4035 × 0.44 / (0.4035 × 0.44 + 0.5965 × 0.24) ≈ 0.55.
- If the maximum is not 15, its expected value is (13658 − 6900) / 680 ≈ 9.94.
- New fair value ≈ 0.55 × 15 + 0.45 × 9.94 ≈ 12.7.

**Quote.** I'm short one unit, so I centre the quote slightly above fair value and keep the spread wide. The spread protects against informed traders, and the distribution has a lot of weight at 15.

{"bid": 11.5, "ask": 14.2}

| 3 | 1 | 1 |

| 5 | 10 | 6 |
| 7 | 84 | 74 |
| 9 | 165 | 81 |
| 10 | 364 | 199 |
| 11 | 680 | 316 |
| 15 | 1140 | 460 |

- This gives an expected maximum of 13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98.

- After the second buy it rises to about 0.70.

info.raw:
Expected minimum of 3 cards from the 22-card deck, using P(min ≥ v) = C(cards ≥ v, 3) / C(22, 3), where C(22, 3) = 1540:

- P(min ≥ 3) = 1140/1540
- P(min ≥ 4) = 680/1540
- P(min ≥ 5) = 286/1540
- P(min ≥ 12) = 84/1540
- P(min ≥ 13) = 35/1540
- P(min ≥ 15) = 1/1540

So E[min] = 2 + (1140 + 680 + 286 + 7·84 + 35 + 2)/1540 ≈ **3.77**.

The distribution is right-skewed. The minimum is 2 with probability 0.26, 3 with 0.30, 4 with 0.26, 5 with 0.13, and 12 or more with about 0.05. An informed buyer at a high ask costs a lot (about 2.3 per trade if the value is 5 or more). An informed seller at a low bid costs less. So I set the spread a bit wider on the ask side.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 4.9}

The fair value from public information is about 3.75. That is the expected smallest of the three cards, with the no-trade on quote 1 nudging it slightly toward 3 or 4.

  - 3 with about 30%
  - 4 with about 26%
  - 5 with about 13%
  - 12 or more with about 5%
- **Ask side:** this side carries the tail risk. An informed buyer at 4.9 only costs me much when the smallest card is 12 or more. Noise traders pay about 1.15 above fair often enough to more than make up for that.
- **Bid side:** an informed seller at 2.6 only hurts when the smallest card is 2, and then I lose just 0.6.

Each side is roughly half a noise standard deviation from fair, which looks close to the best trade-off. I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 4.9}

- The minimum is at least 3 if both cards are 3 or higher. 19 of the 21 are, so the chance is 19/21 × 18/20 ≈ 0.814.
- The expected settlement is 2 + 0.814 + 0.571 ≈ 3.39.

**Ask.**
- An informed trader values the contract at 4 at most, so any ask at or above 4.0 never sells to an informed trader.
- Above 4.0, I only weigh margin against how often a noise trader buys. Expected profit per quote is:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4.6 | about 0.29 |
| 5.0 | about 0.31 |
| 5.5 | about 0.30 |

- The best ask is around 5.0.

**Bid.**
- At 2.0 or below, an informed trader never sells to me.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.5 | about 0.31 |
| 1.8 | about 0.31 |
| 2.0 | about 0.30 |

- A bid of 2.1 gives up a little to informed traders when the value is 2, so I stay at or below 2.0.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 5.0}

Card 1 is 4, so settlement is the minimum of 4 and the two hidden cards. My estimate of fair value is about 3.39, and I quote around it so the informed trader never trades with me.

**Fair value.** The remaining 21 cards are 2×2, 3×3, 3×4, 4×5, 2×12, 4×13 and 3×15. Two of them are still hidden, which gives C(21,2) = 210 equally likely pairs.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description: A custom deck of 20 cards is shuffled: 3 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 4, 1 card worth 5, 4 cards worth 7, 2 cards worth 9, 3 cards worth 10, 3 cards worth 11, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 11.98, the expected maximum of the three cards. I set each side to roughly maximise expected edge, balancing gains from noise traders against losses to informed traders.

**Fair value.** P(max ≤ v) = C(n,3)/C(20,3), where n is the number of cards worth v or less.

| Max card | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | 1/1140 |
| 4 | 3/1140 |
| 5 | 6/1140 |
| 7 | 74/1140 |
| 9 | 81/1140 |
| 10 | 199/1140 |
| 11 | 316/1140 |
| 15 | 460/1140 |

E[max] = 13658/1140 ≈ 11.98.

**Ask side.** The informed trader buys whenever the max is 15, which has 40% probability.
- At an ask of 14.0 the expected profit is about 0.29.
- At 14.5 it is about 0.31.
- At 14.9 it is about 0.32.
- Profit is nearly flat in this range, so I post 14.5.

**Bid side.** The informed trader sells when the max is below the bid, and the loss is largest when the max is 7 or 9.
- At a bid of 10.0 the expected profit is about 0.30.
- At 9.5 it is about 0.31.
- I post 9.7, between the two.

{"bid": 9.7, "ask": 14.5}

Fair value is about 11.98. I'm quoting 10.6 / 13.4, roughly 1.4 either side of fair, because the two sides carry different risks against an informed trader.

**Fair value.** The contract pays the highest of 3 cards dealt from 20. The chance the maximum is at most v is C(cards ≤ v, 3) / C(20, 3), where C(20, 3) = 1140. Differencing those gives the chance of each maximum:

| Maximum card | 3 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 9 | 10 | 11 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chance (out of 1140) | 1 | 3 | 6 | 74 | 81 | 199 | 316 | 460 |

That makes the expected maximum 13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98. The no-trade on quote 1 tells us almost nothing, so fair value stays at about 12.0.

**Ask side.**
- An informed trader buys at an ask below 15 whenever the maximum is 15, which has a 40% chance.
- At an ask of 13.4, the expected loss to informed buyers is about 0.2 × 0.4 × 1.6 ≈ 0.13 per quote.
- A noise trader buys about 28% of the time, for an expected gain of roughly 0.8 × 0.28 × 1.4 ≈ 0.31.

**Bid side.**
- An informed trader sells at a bid near 10.5 when the maximum is 10 or less, which has about a 32% chance.
- The expected loss to informed sellers is roughly 0.2 × 0.47 ≈ 0.09 per quote.
- A noise trader sells for a similar expected gain to the ask side.

Both sides have positive expected value at roughly 1.4 from fair. This is much tighter than the 9.7 / 14.5 quote that got no trade.

{"bid": 10.6, "ask": 13.4}

Fair value is about 11.4, so I'm quoting a bid of 9.9 and an ask of 12.5.

1. **Prior expected maximum.** With 3 cards dealt from 20, the chance that the maximum is at most v is C(cards ≤ v, 3) / C(20, 3). Working that through the deck gives an expected maximum of about **11.98**.
2. **What the trade at 10.6 tells me.** I split outcomes at 10.6:

   - **Low case:** informed traders all sell, so 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.305 ≈ 0.44.
   - **High case:** only noise traders sell, so 0.8 × 0.305 ≈ 0.24.

   Updating on the sell raises the probability of the low case to about 0.46. That moves the public fair value down to about **11.4**.
3. **Quote.** I'm long 1 unit, so I skew the quote slightly lower. I keep a spread wide enough to cover the risk of trading with informed counterparties.

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 12.5}

Card 1 is a 7, so the contract settles at no less than 7. With the remaining 19 cards, my estimate of fair value is about 10.0–10.5.

- **Before the trades:** the expected maximum is about 11.15. The settlement probabilities are 7 (16%), 9 (10%), 10 (19%), 11 (25%) and 15 (30%).
- **After the trades:** the two sells to me in stage 1, at 10.6 and 9.9, lower the estimate. They are somewhat more likely if the value is low, because an informed trader would have sold. After a rough Bayesian update for those sells, the estimate falls to about 10.

I'm long 2, so I'll lean towards selling. I'll put the ask just below 11, so an informed trader only buys if the value is 11 or 15. I'll keep the bid low, so an informed trader only sells if the value is 7.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 10.9}

| Settlement value | Probability (from the deck) |
|---|---|
| 7 | 28/171 |
| 9 | 17/171 |
| 10 | 33/171 |
| 11 | 42/171 |
| 15 | 51/171 |

That gives an expected value of about **11.15**.

**Adjusting for quote 4.** My 9 / 10.9 quote at quote 4 got no trade, which pulls the estimate down:

- One whose value was 7 would have sold at 9.

- A noise trader would not trade about 25% of the time.

Updating on this gives a fair value of about **10.8**. Both stage 1 trades were sells, which hints the value may be a bit lower still.

**Quote.** I am long 2, so I shade both prices down a little to make selling more likely than buying.

{"bid": 9.2, "ask": 11.4}

Fair value is about 11.3, and I'm skewing the quote slightly down because I'm long one unit.

|---|---|
| 7 | 28/171 |
| 9 | 17/171 |
| 10 | 33/171 |
| 11 | 42/171 |
| 15 | 51/171 |

That gives an expected value of 1906/171 ≈ 11.15.

**Adjusting for trading so far.**
- **Quote 4 (no trade at 9 / 10.9):** an informed trader would only stay out if the value were 9 or 10, so those outcomes become a bit more likely.
- **Quote 5 (buy at 11.4):** an informed trader buys only if the value is 15, so that outcome becomes more likely.
- **Net effect:** fair value rises slightly, to about 11.3.

**Quote.** The bid sits about 1 below fair and the ask about 0.9 above, with both shaded down slightly because I'm long. The ask also leaves some room against an informed buyer when the value is 15.

{"bid": 10.3, "ask": 12.2}

Fair value is about 9.72, and I'm quoting a bid of 7.0 and an ask of 12.0.

**Bid.** At 7.0, an informed trader holding a 7 does not sell to me, because 7 is not below my bid. That removes all informed selling. Noise traders give about 0.34 expected profit per quote at this price, and moving the bid up or down earns less.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 12.0}

With cards 7 and 5 revealed, I set the bid at 7.0 and the ask at 12.0, around a fair value of about 9.72.

**Fair value.** Settlement is the larger of 7 and card 3. The other 18 cards are:

- 9, 9: two cards.
- 10, 10, 10: three cards.
- 11, 11, 11: three cards.
- 15, 15, 15: three cards.

Expected settlement = (7×7 + 9×2 + 10×3 + 11×3 + 15×3) / 18 = 175 / 18 ≈ 9.72. The no-trade at quote 7 tells us almost nothing new, so I keep this as the fair value.

**Bid.** An informed seller always knows the value is at least 7. If I bid 7.0, they never sell to me, because a value of 7 is not below 7. Noise traders, centred on 9.72 with spread 2.7, still sell at 7.0 with about 16% probability.

**Ask.** I compared expected profit from noise buyers against expected losses to informed buyers holding a 15:
- Ask 11.0: about 0.19.
- Ask 11.5: about 0.25.
- Ask 12.0: about 0.26.
- Ask 12.5: about 0.25.

The best is around 12.0.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 12.0}

**Value before trading.** Cards 7 and 5 are gone, leaving 18 cards: 3×3, 1×4, 3×7, 2×9, 3×10, 3×11, 3×15. The settlement is max(7, card 3).
- Any card of 7 or below settles at 7. There are 7 such cards out of 18.
- The other settlements are 9 (2 cards), 10 (3), 11 (3) and 15 (3).

**What quotes 7–8 tell us.** Nobody traded at 7 / 12 twice.

- A noise trader fails to trade at 7 / 12 about 64% of the time.
- The chance of no trade is about 0.71 if the value is below 15 and about 0.51 if it is 15. Over two quotes, this roughly halves the weight on 15 (factor about 0.52).
- Updated fair value ≈ 9.26.
- Updated chances of each settlement: 7 ≈ 42%, 9 ≈ 12%, 10 ≈ 18%, 11 ≈ 18%, 15 ≈ 9%.

**Choosing the bid and ask** (expected profit per price):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11.0 | 0.287 |
| 11.5 | about 0.298 (best) |
| 12.0 | 0.284 |

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6.8 | 0.356 |

info.raw:
The expected value of the minimum of the 3 dealt cards is about **3.77**.

{"bid": 2.1, "ask": 5.5}

The quote-1 no-trade barely moves this, so fair value is about 3.8.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 4.9}

The card already revealed is 13. I estimate fair value at about 5.2–5.3. The settlement value has two likely clusters, so I'll quote wide around it. Being short 1, I lean slightly toward buying.

- Before that trade, the chance the value is 5 or more was about 31%. After it, I put that chance at about 44%.

{"bid": 4.1, "ask": 6.6}

Card 1 is 13, so the contract settles at the lower of 13 and the two cards still hidden.

**Remaining deck (21 cards):**
- 13 low cards (values 2 to 5), averaging 49/13 ≈ 3.77.
- 8 high cards: two 12s, three 13s, three 15s.

**Expected settlement:**

| Case | Probability | Expected min |
|---|---|---|
| Both hidden cards low | 156/420 | ≈ 3.14 |
| One low, one high | 208/420 | ≈ 3.77 (the low card) |
| Both high | 56/420 | ≈ 12.54 (12 if either is a 12, otherwise 13) |

This gives a fair value of about 1976/420 ≈ 4.70. The quote of 4.1 / 6.6 at quote 3 drew no trade, which tells us little.

**Quote:** The value is lopsided. About 87% of the time it is near 3.4, and about 13% of the time it is around 12.5. An informed buyer at my ask could cost me a lot, while an informed seller at my bid costs only a little. I'm also already short 1. So I keep the ask wide above fair value and the bid a bit under it.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 6.4}

Cards 1 and 2 (13 and 15) are both high, so the settlement is min(13, card 3).

**Remaining 20 cards:** 2×2, 3×3, 4×4, 4×5, 2×12, 3×13, 2×15.

**Prior settlement distribution:**

| Settlement | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 12 | 13 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.10 | 0.15 | 0.20 | 0.20 | 0.10 | 0.25 |

The prior expected value is 6.9.

**Update from the trade history:** I treat this as a rough approximation.
- Both earlier trades were buys at fairly high asks: 4.9 in stage 1 and 6.4 in stage 2.
- An informed buyer at those prices points to a higher settlement.
- I estimate each buy multiplies the odds of outcomes above that price by about 1.9.
- After this update, the chance that card 3 is high (12 or more) is about 0.6, and the fair value is about 9.3.

**What the quotes risk:**
- The value is bimodal: about 4 if card 3 is low, about 12.9 if it is high. So informed traders cause large losses on either side.
- On the bid, an informed seller (when the value is low) costs about 5 per trade. The best bid is about 2.5 below fair value, around 6.8.
- On the ask, an informed buyer (when the value is high) costs about 3.6 per trade. The best ask is about 3 or more above fair value, around 12.5.
- I am short 2, so buying at the bid would also help reduce my risk.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 12.5}

The contract is now worth about 6.9. I quote a bid of 4.3 and an ask of 9.3 because those maximise this last quote's expected profit.

**What the contract can settle at.** The two revealed cards are 13 and 15, so settlement is min(13, card 3). That leaves 20 cards that card 3 could be:

| Settlement value | Cards giving it |
|---|---|
| 2 | 2 |
| 3 | 3 |
| 4 | 4 |
| 5 | 4 |
| 12 | 2 |
| 13 | 5 (three 13s plus two 15s, which settle at 13) |

The expected settlement value is 138/20 = **6.9**. The outcome is bimodal: 2–5 with probability 0.65, or 12–13 with probability 0.35.

**Ask.** If my ask sits between 5 and 12, an informed counterparty buys only when the value is 12 or 13. Each such trade costs me 3 to 3.7 on average. For a noise trader with valuation 6.9 + N(0, 2.3), the expected profit per quote at each ask is:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8 | about -0.05 |
| 9.3 | about +0.046 (the best) |
| 10 | about +0.03 |

**Bid.** If the bid is set around 4–4.5, an informed counterparty sells only when the value is 2–4. Those losses are small, and noise sellers below the bid make up for them. Expected profit is about +0.17 and almost flat across 4.0–4.5, so I pick the middle, 4.3.

**Position.** I am short 2, so after this trade I would be either -1 or -3, which is within the allowed range.

- Die 2 = 4: expected min is 2.375.
- Die 2 = 5: expected min is 2.75.

Weighting by die 2's probabilities gives a fair value of 0.3·2.0 + 0.2·2.375 + 0.4·2.75 = **2.175**.

**Distribution of the minimum.**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.325 |
| 2 | 0.225 |
| 3 | 0.225 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 5 | 0.15 |

There is a lot of probability at 0. So any bid above 0 gets sold to by informed traders often, and at a large loss.

**Bid.** At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells, because the settlement value is never below 0. A noise trader sells about 11% of the time, and each sale gains about 2.18. That gives an expected edge of about +0.16 per quote, the best of the bids I checked. Higher bids such as 0.3 or 0.5 do slightly worse.

**Ask.** The expected profit from the ask peaks at about +0.13 for asks between about 3.9 and 4.2. At those levels an informed trader only buys when the value is 5 (or 4, for asks below 4). The noise traders who buy pay well above fair value.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 4.0}

Settlement distribution before any trades:
- **Value 0:** 0.325
- **Value 2:** 0.225
- **Value 3:** 0.225
- **Value 4:** 0.075
- **Value 5:** 0.15

That gives an expected value of 2.175.

The first quote of 0 / 4 got no trade. That makes a value of 5 less likely, because an informed trader holding 5 would have bought at 4. After updating, fair value is about 1.98.

**Bid side.** A bid at 0 is never hit by an informed trader, since the value cannot be below 0. Noise traders still sell there often enough to give about +0.175 expected profit. Raising the bid lets informed traders sell when the value is 0, which costs more than it gains.

**Ask side.** An ask between 3.8 and 4.0 loses only to informed traders holding 4 or 5. It still catches noise buyers at a good edge, for about +0.14 expected profit. I'll quote 3.9.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 3.9}

Die 2 is 3, so the contract settles at the smaller of die 1 and 3:

| Die 1 faces | Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 0 | 0 | 1/4 |
| 2, 2 | 2 | 1/4 |
| 3, 5, 5, 10 | 3 | 1/2 |

The public fair value is 0.25 × 0 + 0.25 × 2 + 0.5 × 3 = **2**. No trades have happened yet in this stage, so the history does not move it.

**Ask:** Any ask strictly below 3 loses to informed buyers half the time, since the value is 3 with probability 1/2. At 3 or above, informed traders never buy, so I only face noise buyers.
- Expected profit from the ask is then 0.65 × P(noise > ask − 2) × (ask − 2).
- This peaks at an ask of about 3.3–3.4, giving roughly 0.199 per quote.

**Bid:** A bid of 0 is never hit by informed sellers, because a valuation of 0 is not below 0. Noise sellers still hit it.
- Expected profit is about 0.65 × 0.133 × 2 ≈ 0.173.
- Raising the bid toward 0.6 lets informed traders who know the value is 0 sell to me, and the expected profit falls.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 3.4}

Die 2 came up 3, so the contract settles at min(die 1, 3).

**Settlement distribution**
- Die 1 faces 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 5, 5, 10 give settlement values 0, 0, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 3.
- So the value is 0 with probability 1/4, 2 with probability 1/4, and 3 with probability 1/2.
- The fair value is 0.25 × 0 + 0.25 × 2 + 0.5 × 3 = **2.0**.
- The earlier no-trades tell us nothing new. An informed trader would not have traded at a bid of 0 or an ask of 3.4 or higher, whatever the value.

**Ask**
- Any ask of 3 or more is never hit by an informed trader, because the value is at most 3.
- Against noise traders, the expected profit is 0.65 × x × P(N > x), where x is the ask minus 2. This peaks near x ≈ 1.35, giving about 0.20.
- An ask below 3 loses to informed buyers whenever the value is 3, which happens half the time. That makes it worse.
- **Ask 3.4.**

**Bid**
- At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells, because the value is never below 0.
- Noise traders sell with probability Φ(−2/1.8) ≈ 0.13, so the expected profit is about 0.65 × 2 × 0.13 ≈ 0.17.
- Raising the bid adds a loss to informed sellers when the value is 0. For example, a bid of 0.1 gives about 0.171 and a bid of 0.6 gives about 0.146, both lower than 0.17.
- **Bid 0.**

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The settlement has two equally likely cases:
- **Biased coin (P = 1/2):** the settlement is 6.
- **Fair coin (P = 1/2):** the settlement follows Binomial(6, 0.5), with mean 3.

So the public fair value is 4.5.

I checked the expected profit of each side separately. Each side earns from noise traders and loses to informed traders.

**Ask side:**
- The informed trader buys whenever the true value is 6, which has probability about 0.51.
- So any ask below 6 is costly. An ask at or above 6 has no adverse selection at all.
- The noise-trader edge peaks around an ask of 6.5. Expected profit there is about 0.35 per quote, against about 0.34 at 6.0 and 7.0.

**Bid side:**
- The informed trader sells only when the coin is fair and the count is low.
- The bid's expected profit is flat at about 0.32 for bids between 2.0 and 2.5. It falls to about 0.29 at 3.0.

I'm quoting slightly inside the ask optimum to stay competitive while still avoiding adverse selection. This gives a bid of 2.6 and an ask of 6.3.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 6.3}

No trade at quote 1 slightly raises my estimate of fair value, to about 4.6.

**Starting value.** If the coin is fair (probability 1/2), the expected number of heads is 3. If the coin always lands heads (probability 1/2), the total is 6. So the prior fair value is 4.5.

**What the quiet first quote tells me.**
- An informed trader would have sold at my 2.6 bid only if the true value was 2 or less.
- That happens only with the fair coin, with probability about 0.17.
- No trade therefore makes low outcomes a little less likely, which nudges fair value up to about 4.6.

**Ask side.**
- There is about a 0.5 chance the settlement is exactly 6.
- Any ask below 6 gets picked off by informed traders whenever the value is 6.
- An ask at or above 6 means an informed trader never buys from me.
- Against noise traders, expected edge is roughly flat for asks from about 6.0 to 7.0, peaking around 6.3 to 6.5.

**Bid side.**
- Only low outcomes (2 or fewer heads) hurt a bid near 2.5, and they are fairly unlikely.
- Expected edge is roughly flat and best for bids from about 2.0 to 3.0.

I'll keep a similar wide quote, centred slightly higher than before.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.3}

The public fair value after two revealed heads is **5.6**.

**Posterior on the coin.** The two heads are likely under the biased coin (probability 1) and less likely under the fair coin (1/4).
- P(biased) = 0.5·1 / (0.5·1 + 0.5·0.25) = 0.8.
- P(fair) = 0.2.

**Fair value.**
- The 4 remaining flips give 4 heads if the coin is biased and 2 heads on average if it is fair.
- Expected remaining heads = 0.8·4 + 0.2·2 = 3.6.
- Public fair value = 2 + 3.6 = 5.6.

**Settlement distribution:**

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.8125 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 0.0125 |

**Ask.** The settlement can never exceed 6, so any ask of 6.0 or more is never hit by an informed trader. Against noise traders only, expected profit is 0.8 · (a − 5.6) · P(noise > a − 5.6):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6.0 | 0.14 |
| 7.0 | 0.33 |
| 7.5 | 0.35 (best) |
| 8.0 | 0.34 |

**Bid.** A low bid loses to informed sellers only when the settlement is 2 or 3. Combining noise profit and informed losses:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4.0 | 0.33 |
| 3.8 | 0.34 |
| 3.5 | 0.34 (best) |
| 3.3 | 0.34 |

I choose a bid of 3.5, since the profit curve is flat in this range.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 7.5}

Fair value after two heads is 5.6, so I'll quote a bid of 3.7 and an ask of 7.5.

**Fair value.** Two heads move the odds towards the biased coin.
- P(biased) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 0.25) = 0.8.
- Expected settlement = 2 + 4 × (0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5) = 5.6.

**The 7.5 buy tells us nothing.** The settlement can't exceed 6, so an informed trader would never buy at 7.5. Only a noise trader could have done it, and noise traders behave the same whichever coin it is. Fair value stays at 5.6.

**Settlement distribution.**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.8125 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 0.0125 |

**Ask side.** Any ask of 6 or more is never hit by an informed trader. Against noise traders alone, expected profit peaks between about 7.5 and 7.7, at roughly 0.35 per quote.

**Bid side.** Below 4, informed sellers rarely hurt me, because the value is below 4 only about 6% of the time. Expected profit is flat at about 0.34 for bids between 3.5 and 3.8. A buy would also cut my short position, which is a small plus.

{"bid": 3.7, "ask": 7.5}

The posterior is about 94% that the coin always lands heads, so fair value is about 5.94. I'm quoting wide around that, because noise traders are the only source of profit here.

**Fair value**
- With four heads in four flips, P(fair coin) = (0.5 × 1/16) / (0.5 × 1/16 + 0.5 × 1) = 1/17.
- So P(always-heads coin) = 16/17.
- Expected settlement = 4 + 2 × (16/17) + 1 × (1/17) ≈ **5.94**.
- Settlement distribution: 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with probability about 0.029, and 4 with probability about 0.015.

**Ask**
- The settlement can never exceed 6, so an informed trader never buys above 6.
- Noise traders value the contract at 5.94 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.6.
- Expected profit per quote is roughly P(noise trader buys) × (ask − 5.94):
  - An ask of 7 gives about 0.34 × 1.06 ≈ 0.36.
  - An ask of 8 gives about 0.21 × 2.06 ≈ 0.44.
  - An ask of 8.5 gives about 0.16 × 2.56 ≈ 0.41.
- The best ask is about 8.2.
- Selling one more unit only takes my position to -2, which is within the limit.

**Bid**
- An informed trader sells only if the true value is below my bid.
- With a bid near 3.8–4.0, that only happens if the settlement is 4, which has probability about 1.5%.
- Noise-trader profit dominates and peaks with a bid around 3.9.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 8.2}

**Posterior on the coin.** Four heads have been revealed.
- Fair coin: (1/2) × 0.5⁴ = 1/32.
- Two-headed coin: (1/2) × 1 = 1/2.
- So P(two-headed) = 16/17 and P(fair) = 1/17.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement is 4 plus the heads in flips 5 and 6.
- 6 with probability about 0.956.
- 5 with probability about 0.029.
- 4 with probability about 0.015.
- Fair value is about 16/17 × 6 + 1/17 × 5 ≈ 5.94. I am ignoring the small signal from the earlier buy at 7.5, which would push this slightly higher.

**Ask.** At any ask of 6.0 or above, the informed trader never buys, because the settlement cannot exceed 6. So the ask only meets noise traders, and the trade-off is a wider edge against fewer fills.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.94).
- This peaks around 7.8–8.0, at roughly 0.35 per quote.
- Selling would take my position from −1 to −2, which is within the limit.

**Bid.** At a bid of 4.0 or below, the informed trader never sells, because the settlement cannot fall below 4. So the bid also only meets noise traders.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (5.94 − bid).
- This peaks near 4.0, at about 0.35 per quote.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Prior expected value is 0.5×6 + 0.5×3 = 4.5. The settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.51. Otherwise it is roughly Binomial(6, 0.5), centred on 3.

**Ask side.**
- If the ask is below 6, informed traders buy whenever the coin is the always-heads coin, which happens about half the time.
- At an ask of 6.0, informed traders never buy, because the value can never exceed 6.
- Noise traders still buy about 19% of the time, for a gain of 1.5 per trade.
- That gives roughly +0.18 expected profit, about the best among the asks I checked.

**Bid side.**
- A bid around 2.5–3.0 balances two effects. Informed traders sell when the fair coin produces few heads, which loses money. Noise traders sell well below the 4.5 fair value, which earns money.
- Expected profit is about +0.10 across this range.
- I'll use 2.8.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

Posting bid 3.0 and ask 6.0.

**Fair value.** The settlement is 6 if the coin always lands heads, or Binomial(6, 0.5) with mean 3 if it is fair. Each is equally likely, so the fair value is about 4.5. The no-trade at quote 1 hardly changes that.

**Ask at 6.0.**
- The settlement can never be above 6, and an informed trader only buys if its value is strictly above the ask. So no informed trader buys at 6, and the ask never loses to them.
- Noise traders still buy about 19% of the time. Each of those sales gains about 1.5 against a fair value of 4.5.

**Bid at 3.0.**
- An informed trader sells only if the true value is 0, 1 or 2. That happens about 17% of the time, and each such trade loses about 1.4.
- A noise trader sells about 19% of the time, and each such trade gains about 1.5.
- That nets out to roughly +0.10 per quote.
- Bids between 2.8 and 3.0 give about the same expected profit. Raising the bid to 3.5 lowers it to about +0.04, because it buys from more informed traders.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

Before anything is revealed, the expected settlement is 0.5 × 3 + 0.5 × 6 = **4.5**. With a fair coin the number of heads is Binomial(6, 0.5), and with the always-heads coin it is exactly 6.

**Ask side**
- An informed buyer pays my ask only if the true value is above it. Settlement can never exceed 6, so an ask of 6.0 can't be bought by an informed counterparty.
- A noise trader buys at 6.0 with probability about 0.19, and I gain about 1.5 against fair value when that happens.
- The expected edge is about +0.18. That is roughly the best of the asks I checked: 5.5 gave about 0.09, 5.9 about 0.17 and 6.2 about 0.18.

**Bid side**
- At 3.0, an informed seller hits my bid only when the true value is 2 or less. That has probability of about 0.17, and I lose about 1.36 when it happens.
- A noise trader sells at 3.0 with probability about 0.19, and I gain about 1.5.
- The net edge is about +0.10. This is close to the best of the bids I checked, which were roughly flat between 2.5 and 3.0.

The two quotes with no trade hint very slightly that the true value is not low, but the effect is negligible. I'll keep the same quote.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

Flips 1 and 2 both came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one. The other coin always lands heads.

So far 0 heads are in. The settlement value is therefore a Binomial(4, 0.5) on the remaining flips 3–6. Its mean is 2 and its standard deviation is 1. Probabilities by settlement value:

| Value | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/16 | 4/16 | 6/16 | 4/16 | 1/16 |

Noise traders value the contract at 2 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7.

**Expected profit from the ask side** (informed loss subtracted from noise gain):

| Ask | Informed loss | Noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | 0.022 | 0.181 | 0.159 |
| 3.4 | 0.013 | 0.187 | 0.174 |
| 3.5 | 0.011 | 0.184 | 0.173 |

An ask around 3.4–3.5 maximises the expected profit. The distribution is symmetric around 2, so the best bid is around 0.5–0.6.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

The first flip came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one. Two flips are already 0, and the other four are fair flips. The settlement value is therefore Binomial(4, 0.5), with mean 2.

The possible settlement values have these probabilities:

| Value | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/16 | 4/16 | 6/16 | 4/16 | 1/16 |

Noise traders value the contract at 2 + N(0, 1.7). Informed traders know the exact value.

**Ask side, expected profit per quote:**
- At 3.0: about 0.159. Noise traders buy 27.8% of the time for a 1.0 edge. Informed traders only buy when the value is 4, costing 0.0625.
- At 3.3: about 0.173.
- At 3.4: about 0.174. Noise traders buy 20.5% of the time for a 1.4 edge, which gives 0.187. Informed traders cost 0.0131. This is the best of the four.
- At 3.5: about 0.173.

The problem is symmetric around 2, so the best bid is 0.6. With 4 quotes left after this one, position risk is small.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

The first two flips were both tails, so the coin must be the fair one: a P(heads) = 1 coin can never land tails. That leaves four unrevealed flips at probability 0.5 each, plus zero heads already counted. The settlement value is therefore Binomial(4, 0.5), with mean 2 and standard deviation 1. There have been no trades, so the public fair value stays at 2.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared expected profit per quote at several ask prices. Informed traders buy only when the true value is above my ask, which costs me money. Noise traders buy when their valuation, 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.7, is above my ask, and I earn (ask − 2) on average.

| Ask | Expected informed loss | Expected noise profit | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | −0.022 | +0.181 | 0.159 |
| 3.3 | −0.015 | +0.188 | 0.172 |
| 3.4 | −0.013 | +0.187 | 0.174 |
| 3.6 | −0.009 | +0.180 | 0.171 |

An ask of about 3.4 is optimal.

**Choosing the bid.** The value distribution is symmetric around 2, so the same reasoning puts the bid at 0.6.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 3.4}

**Reasoning**

- **The coin must be fair.** Flip 1 came up tails, and the always-heads coin can't do that.
- **Settlement value.** So far there are 2 heads. Flips 5 and 6 are fair, so settlement is 2 + Binomial(2, 0.5):
  - 2 with probability 0.25
  - 3 with probability 0.5
  - 4 with probability 0.25
- **Fair value is 3.**
- **Informed traders can only value the contract at 2, 3 or 4.**
  - An ask at or above 4 is never lifted by an informed trader.
  - A bid at or below 2 is never hit by an informed trader.
  - Inside that range, informed flow costs me money.
- **Ask choice.** Only noise traders trade outside that range. Their valuation is 3 + N(0, 1.7). My expected profit on the ask is 0.65 × (a − 3) × P(Z > (a − 3)/1.7). This peaks at about a ≈ 4.3–4.4, worth roughly 0.20 per quote.
- **Bid choice.** The problem is symmetric, so the best bid is about 1.7.
- **Position.** I am long 1, which leaves plenty of room on both sides.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

The first flip came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one (a coin with P(heads) = 1 never shows tails). That makes the settlement value predictable in distribution:

- Heads so far: 2.
- Flips 5 and 6 are fair coin flips, so settlement is 2 + Bin(2, 0.5).
- That gives 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4, so fair value is 3.

**Informed traders:**
- They only hurt me if my quotes sit inside the range 2 to 4.
- With an ask at 4 or above, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 4.
- With a bid at 2 or below, an informed trader never sells, because the value cannot fall below 2.

**Noise traders:**
- Their valuation is 3 + N(0, 1.7).
- Once the ask is at or above 4, expected profit on that side is 0.65 × P(noise > a − 3) × (a − 3). Quoting below 4 adds noise fills but gives up 0.35 × 0.25 × (4 − a) to informed buyers.

| Ask | Expected profit on the ask side |
|---|---|
| 3.5 | ≈ 0.08 |
| 3.8 | ≈ 0.15 |
| 4.0 | ≈ 0.181 |
| 4.1 | ≈ 0.185 |
| 4.3 | ≈ 0.188 (best) |
| 4.5 | ≈ 0.184 |

The best ask is 4.3. By symmetry, the best bid is 1.7. My +1 position is well inside the ±5 limits, so it doesn't change the optimal quotes.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

The coin must be fair, so the fair value is 3.0.

**Which coin:** Flip 1 came up tails. The P(heads) = 1 coin can never show tails, so the coin is the fair one.

**Settlement value:** Flips 1–4 show 2 heads. Flips 5 and 6 are fair flips, so the settlement is 2 + Bin(2, 0.5):
- 2 with probability 1/4
- 3 with probability 1/2
- 4 with probability 1/4

The fair value is 3. My position doesn't change this, because expected profit is linear in position and only one more trade can happen.

**Choosing the ask:**
- If the ask is at least 4, an informed trader never buys, because its valuation is never above the ask.
- Expected profit from noise buyers is 0.65 × P(noise > a − 3) × (a − 3), with noise standard deviation 1.7.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|-----|-----------------|
| 4.0 | ≈ 0.181 |
| 4.2 | ≈ 0.187 |
| 4.3 | ≈ 0.188 (best) |
| 4.4 | ≈ 0.186 |
| 4.5 | ≈ 0.184 |

**Choosing the bid:** The problem is symmetric around 3, so the best bid is 1.7. An informed trader never sells below 2, so this bid only trades with noise sellers.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The current fair value is 4.5 heads. Half the time the coin is fair and the expected count is 3. Half the time it always lands heads and the count is 6. So 0.5·3 + 0.5·6 = 4.5.

**Ask side.** The settlement value can never be above 6. At an ask of 6 or higher, an informed trader never buys from me, so only noise traders hit that side. The expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(noise > ask − 4.5) × (ask − 4.5):

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 6.0 | ≈ 0.34 |
| 6.5 | ≈ 0.35 |
| 7.0 | ≈ 0.34 |

6.5 is the best of these.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only when the true value is below my bid. Values that low come only from the fair coin, so they are rare. At a bid of 2.5:
- The expected loss to informed traders is 0.2 × (2.5·1 + 1.5·6 + 0.5·15)/128 ≈ 0.03.
- The expected gain from noise traders is about 0.8 × 0.221 × 2 ≈ 0.35.
- The net is about 0.32. That is close to the best bid; 2.0 and 3.0 give about the same.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 6.5}

Fair value with no flips revealed is 4.5. That is the average of the fair coin (expected 3 heads) and the two-headed coin (6 heads), each with probability ½. The last quote produced no trade, which barely moves this estimate.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer only profits from my ask if the true value is above it. The only value above 4.5 that is likely is 6 heads, with probability about 0.51.
- Any ask of 6 or higher removes that informed loss.
- Expected edge per quote from noise buyers is about 0.34 at 6.0, 0.35 at 6.5 and 0.34 at 7.0.
- 6.5 is near the best, so I keep it.

**Bid side.** An informed seller only hurts me when the coin is fair and the outcome is low.
- At a bid of 2.5, my expected loss to informed sellers is about 0.03 per quote.
- My expected edge from noise sellers is about 0.35.
- That nets about 0.32, roughly as good as nearby bids, so I keep 2.5.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 6.5}

Posterior after two heads: P(biased) = 0.5·1 / (0.5·1 + 0.5·0.25) = 0.8.

Expected settlement = 2 + 4·(0.8·1 + 0.2·0.5) = **5.6**.

The settlement distribution is heavily skewed. P(6) ≈ 0.81, P(5) = 0.05, P(4) = 0.075, P(3) = 0.05 and P(2) ≈ 0.0125.

**Ask.** Settlement cannot go above 6, so an ask above 6 can never be hit profitably by an informed trader. The best trade-off against noise traders, whose valuations are roughly N(5.6, 2.6), comes at an ask of about 7.4–7.5.

**Bid.** An informed trader only sells when the outcome is 2–4, and those outcomes are unlikely. A bid of about 3.5 gives the best expected profit against noise sellers after allowing for that adverse selection.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 7.4}

After two heads, the coin is most likely the always-heads one, so fair value is about 5.6. My bid is 3.7 and my ask is 7.5.

**Posterior on the coin**
- Before any flips, each coin has probability 1/2.
- Two heads happen with probability 1/4 for the fair coin and 1 for the always-heads coin.
- So P(always-heads | HH) = 1 / (1 + 1/4) = 0.8, and P(fair) = 0.2.

**Settlement distribution**
- The two revealed heads give 2 for sure, and four flips remain.
- If the coin is always-heads, settlement is 6.
- If the coin is fair, settlement is 2 + Binomial(4, 0.5).
- Overall: P(6) ≈ 0.81, P(5) ≈ 0.05, P(4) ≈ 0.075, P(3) ≈ 0.05, P(2) ≈ 0.0125.
- Expected value: 0.8 × 6 + 0.2 × 4 = **5.6**.
- The no-trade at quote 3 barely changes this.

**Ask side**
- An informed buyer's valuation is at most 6, so any ask at 6 or above is only hit by noise traders.
- Noise valuations are about Normal(5.6, 2.6).
- Expected profit = 0.8 × P(noise buys) × (ask − 5.6):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | 0.26 |
| 7.0 | 0.33 |
| 7.5 | 0.35 |
| 8.0 | 0.34 |

The best ask is about 7.5.

**Bid side**
- An informed seller only hits my bid when the true value is below it.
- At a bid near 3.7, that means only values 2 or 3, which together have probability about 6%.
- So the adverse-selection cost is small.
- Expected profit is about 0.34 for bids between 3.5 and 3.8, so I chose 3.7.

{"bid": 3.7, "ask": 7.5}

With four heads in four flips, the coin is very likely the always-heads coin, so the settlement value is almost certainly 6.

**Probability the coin is biased.** A fair coin gives four heads with probability 1/16, and the always-heads coin gives them with probability 1. With a 1/2 prior on each, P(biased) = 1 / (1 + 1/16) = 16/17.

**Settlement distribution.** Four heads are already counted, so settlement is 4 plus the heads in flips 5 and 6.
- Settles at 6 with probability ≈ 0.956.
- Settles at 5 with probability ≈ 0.029.
- Settles at 4 with probability ≈ 0.015.
- Fair value = 4 + 2×(16/17) + 1×(1/17) ≈ 5.94.

**Last trade.** At quote 4 the most the contract could settle at was 6, so the buyer at 7.5 cannot have been informed. That trade carries no information, and public fair value stays at about 5.94.

**Ask.** Settlement can never exceed 6, so an informed trader will never buy above 6. Any ask above 6 only trades with noise traders and always makes money. The expected profit is roughly 0.8 × (a − 5.94) × P(noise valuation > a). That is largest when a − 5.94 is about 0.75 × 2.6 ≈ 1.95, so I set the ask at 7.9.

**Bid.** Settlement can never be below 4, so at a bid of 3.9 an informed trader will never sell to me. The same reasoning on the downside puts the bid about 1.95 below fair, at 3.9. Buying would also reduce my short position.

My position is −1, so even selling twice in the last two quotes keeps me within the −4 limit.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 7.9}

With four heads in four flips, the coin is very likely the always-heads one, so I expect settlement just under 6.

**Posterior on the coin.** Four heads has likelihood 1 for the always-heads coin and 1/16 for the fair coin. So P(always-heads) = 16/17.

**Does the trading history change this?**
- The buy at 7.5 must have come from a noise trader, because settlement can never exceed 6.
- The sell at 3.9 must also have come from a noise trader, because settlement is now at least 4.
- The rounds with no trade tell us nothing beyond what the flips already show.

So the history adds no information about the coin.

**Settlement distribution and fair value.**
- Settlement is 6 with probability 65/68, 5 with probability 2/68 and 4 with probability 1/68.
- Fair value = 16/17 × 6 + 1/17 × 5 ≈ 5.94.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- An informed counterparty never buys from me at any ask of 6 or more, since settlement cannot exceed 6.
- An informed counterparty never sells to me at a bid of 4 or less, since settlement is at least 4.
- That leaves only noise traders, whose valuation is 5.94 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6. Against them, the profit-maximising distance from fair value is where x·(1−Φ(x/σ)) peaks, at about 0.75σ ≈ 1.95.
- That puts the bid near 4.0 and the ask near 7.9.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Pricing from the prior, before any flips are revealed:

**Fair value.**
- Half the time the coin is fair, giving an expected 3 heads.
- Half the time it always lands heads, giving 6.
- So the public fair value is 4.5.

**Settlement distribution.**
- P(value = 6) is about 0.508: the all-heads coin, plus a 1/128 chance of six heads from the fair coin.
- The fair coin gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 heads with probabilities 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6 out of 128.

**Ask side.**
- Any ask below 6 loses to informed buyers whenever the coin is all-heads, which is about half the time.
- At an ask of 6.0, informed traders never buy, because the value cannot exceed 6.
- Noise traders still buy about 19% of the time at a 1.5 edge, for an expected profit of about +0.18 per quote.
- A higher ask (6.5) earns less (about +0.16), because fewer noise traders reach it.

**Bid side.**
- Informed sellers hurt most when the value is low.
- Expected profit per quote at each bid:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 3.0 | 0.102 |
| 2.7 | 0.106 |
| 2.5 | 0.104 |

- A bid of 2.7 gives the best expected profit.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.0}

After the first trade, my estimate of fair value has dropped from 4.5 to about 3.4.

**Prior.**
- With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, so settlement is Binomial(6, 0.5) with mean 3.
- With probability 1/2 the coin always lands heads, so settlement is 6.
- The prior expected value is therefore 4.5.

**Update from quote 1.** Someone sold to me at 2.7.
- An informed trader sells there only if the true value is 2 or less. Prior chance of that: 0.5 × 22/64 ≈ 0.17.
- A noise trader sells there with about 14.5% probability, since 2.7 is 1.8 below 4.5 and the noise SD is 1.7.
- After Bayes, the new public fair value is about 3.4.
- About half the weight is now on a value of 0–2, mostly on 2. Most of the remaining weight is on 6, from the all-heads coin.

**Best bid.** I compared the profit from noise sellers against the loss to informed sellers at several bid levels.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.02 at 2.5, 0.13 at 1.5, 0.15 at 1.7 and 0.13 at 1.9.
- 1.7 is the best, and I set the bid there.

**Best ask.** I did the same for buyers. Informed traders mostly buy when the value is 6.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.02 at 4.5, 0.09 at 5.5 and 0.10 at 5.9.
- I set the ask at 5.9.

My position is only +1, so inventory doesn't change these quotes.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 5.9}

The public fair value is about 3.17 after updating on the first two quotes. I'll bid 1.9 and ask 5.0.

**Prior.** Half the time the coin is fair, so the head count is Binomial(6, 0.5) with mean 3. Half the time the coin always lands heads, so the count is 6. The prior fair value is 4.5.

**Quote 1 (sold to me at 2.7).** An informed trader sells there only if the value is 2 or less. A noise trader sells with probability about 14.5%. Updating on this sale lowers the fair value to about 3.39.

**Quote 2 (no trade at 1.7 / 5.9).** This is more likely when the value is between 2 and 5, so the estimate moves down again. The fair value is now about 3.17.

The current distribution is bimodal:

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 or less | 0.53 |
| 3 | 0.12 |
| 4 | 0.09 |
| 5 | 0.035 |
| 6 | 0.23 |

**Bid.** If I bid above 2, informed traders holding a value of 2 also sell to me, and those losses outweigh the noise-trader edge. A bid around 1.8–2.0 limits informed selling to values of 0 or 1. This gives an expected edge of about +0.15 per quote.

**Ask.** Any ask from about 5.0 to 5.9 gives roughly the same expected edge, about +0.09. I'm already long, so I lean toward the lower end, which makes selling more likely.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 5.0}

Flips 1 and 2 both came up heads. That moves the probability that this is the always-heads coin from 0.5 to 0.8, because 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 0.25) = 0.8.

**Fair value**
- Expected heads in the 4 unrevealed flips: 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 3.6.
- So fair value = 2 + 3.6 = **5.6**.
- Settlement distribution:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.8125 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 0.0125 |

**Ask**
- Settlement can never exceed 6, so an ask at 6 or above never loses money.
- An informed trader would never buy there, because its valuation is at most 6. Only noise traders buy.
- The expected edge per quote is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.6).
- This peaks around an ask of 6.9–7.0, at about +0.19 per quote.

**Bid**
- A bid at 4.0 makes money from noise sellers: 0.65 × 0.174 × 1.6 ≈ 0.181.
- It loses to informed sellers only when settlement is 2 or 3: 0.35 × (0.0125 × 2 + 0.05 × 1) ≈ 0.026.
- Net is about +0.155, which is the highest of the bids I checked.

My position of +1 is well within limits, so I don't need to adjust for inventory.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 6.9}

Fair value given flips 1 and 2 are both heads:

1. **Which coin?** The chance the coin is the always-heads coin is 1 / (1 + 1/4) = 0.8.
2. **Expected value:** The four remaining flips add 0.8·4 + 0.2·2 = 3.6 heads. So E[settlement] = 2 + 3.6 = 5.6. The no-trade at quote 4 nudges this up slightly, to about 5.65.
3. **Settlement distribution:**

| Settlement | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.8125 | 0.05 | 0.075 | 0.05 | 0.0125 |

**Ask side:** The settlement can never exceed 6. An informed trader only buys if its valuation is above my ask, so any ask of 6 or more is never hit by one. I only trade with noise traders, at a profit of ask − 5.65. Expected profit per quote peaks near an ask of 6.8–7.0, at about 0.19.

**Bid side:** An informed trader sells only when the settlement is below my bid. With a bid around 4.0, that happens only when the settlement is 2 or 3. Expected profit per quote is about 0.15 near a bid of 4.0, which is the best of the bids I checked.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 6.9}

**Fair value from the revealed flips.** After two heads, the chance the coin is the always-heads coin is 1 / (1 + 0.25) = 0.8. The four unrevealed flips then add 0.8×4 + 0.2×2 = 3.6 expected heads. With the 2 revealed heads, fair value is 5.6.

**Adjusting for the last trade.** Someone sold to me at 4. That is much more likely if the true value is 2 or 3, which only happens with the fair coin. Updating on that sale lowers my estimate to about 5.15.

**Shape of the distribution.** The settlement value is skewed:
- It is 6 with probability about 0.68.
- It can never exceed 6, so an informed buyer never pays more than 6.
- An informed seller below 4 would hold a value of 2 or 3.

**Ask.** Asks around 6.0–6.5 earn the most expected profit per quote, roughly 0.18–0.19. At or above 6, informed traders never buy from me. Above 6, noise buyers still pay me a wide margin.

**Bid.** Bids of 3.0–3.5 earn about 0.12 per quote, versus about 0.09 at 4. Bidding 3.5 limits losses to informed sellers while still catching low noise sellers. I am long 2, so I have room to buy, but I prefer a cautious bid.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 6.4}

The tails on flips 3 and 4 rule out the always-heads coin, so the coin is fair.

**Fair value:** 2 heads are revealed so far. Flips 5 and 6 are fair coin flips. The settlement value is 2, 3 or 4, with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, so fair value is 3.

**Ask side, expected profit per quote:**
- An informed trader buys only if the true value is 4 and my ask is below 4. Quoting at 4 or above removes that loss entirely.
- Noise traders value the contract at 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7. My expected profit from them is 0.65 × P(noise > ask − 3) × (ask − 3).
- This is about 0.18 at an ask of 4.0, 0.19 at 4.3 and 0.18 at 4.5, so the best ask is about 4.3.

**Bid side:** the payoffs are symmetric around 3, so the best bid is about 1.7.

My position is +2, so I can still buy 3 more units before hitting the +5 limit. That leaves room for both sides on the remaining quotes.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

The coin must be the fair one, since tails showed up on flips 3 and 4. Two heads are already in, and flips 5 and 6 are each 50/50. So the settlement is 2 + Bin(2, 0.5): it is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4. Fair value is 3.

**Ask side:** At any ask of 4.0 or higher, an informed trader never buys from me. A noise trader's valuation is 3 + N(0, 1.7). Expected profit per arrival is 0.65 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 3):
- Ask 4.1: about 0.185
- Ask 4.3: about 0.188 (best)
- Ask 4.4: about 0.187

**Bid side:** The same calculation applies in mirror image, so the best bid is about 1.7.

My +2 position doesn't change this, because I am maximising expected profit, which is unaffected by inventory risk.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

With flips 3 and 4 showing tails, the coin must be the fair one, because the biased coin only lands heads.

**Settlement value**
- Two heads are already in.
- Flips 5 and 6 are fair, so the value is 2, 3 or 4 with probabilities 1/4, 1/2 and 1/4.
- The public fair value is 3.

**Choosing the ask (a)**
- An informed trader never buys from me if a ≥ 4, because the most the contract can settle at is 4.
- Noise traders buy with probability Q((a − 3)/1.7), where Q is the chance a standard Normal exceeds that value. Each such sale earns me about a − 3.
- So the expected profit from the ask side is 0.65 · (a − 3) · Q((a − 3)/1.7):
  - a = 4.0: ≈ 0.181
  - a = 4.3: ≈ 0.188
  - a = 4.5: ≈ 0.184
- The best ask is about 4.3.

**Choosing the bid**
The setup is symmetric around 3, so the best bid is about 1.7. My current position does not change the expected profit of this quote, so it does not shift the prices.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 4.5, and its distribution is lopsided, so I'm quoting a wide, asymmetric market: bid 2.8, ask 6.0.

**Value distribution**
- With probability 1/2 the coin always lands heads, so the contract settles at 6.
- With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, so the number of heads averages 3 with a standard deviation of about 1.22.
- The expected settlement value is therefore 4.5.
- Overall, the value is exactly 6 about 50.8% of the time.

**Ask side**
- 6 is the highest possible value. At an ask of 6.0, an informed trader never buys, because their valuation is never strictly above 6.
- A noise trader buys when their noise exceeds +1.5, which happens about 19% of the time. Each such sale earns 1.5 against fair value.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.65 × 0.19 × 1.5 ≈ +0.18.
- Any ask below 6 lets an informed trader buy whenever the value is 6, which costs more than it gains.

**Bid side**
- An informed trader sells to me only when the coin is fair and gets few heads, so I bid well below fair value.
- I compared bids by expected profit:

| Bid | Informed-trader loss | Noise-trader gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | −0.08 | +0.18 | ≈ +0.10 |
| 2.8 | −0.07 | +0.18 | ≈ +0.106 |
| 2.5 | −0.05 | +0.16 | ≈ +0.10 |

- The bid around 2.8 is best.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

The first counterparty sold to me at 2.8, so I moved my estimate of fair value down to about 3.45. I'm quoting 1.9 bid / 6.0 ask.

**Fair value before any trades**
- The coin is either fair or always heads, each with probability 1/2.
- If it's the always-heads coin, the contract settles at 6.
- If it's the fair coin, the number of heads is Binomial(6, 0.5), which averages 3.
- So the expected settlement is 4.5.

**Updating on the sale at 2.8**
- An informed seller only sells at 2.8 if the settlement is 2 or less.
- A noise trader sells there with probability about 16% (valuation 4.5 plus noise must fall below 2.8).
- Updating on that sale puts the main probabilities at about:
  - 6 heads: 32%
  - 2 heads: 33%
  - 1 head: 13%
  - 3 heads: 10%
- This gives a public fair value of about 3.45.

**Choosing the quotes**
- **Bid at 1.9:** Bids around 1.9–2.0 maximise expected profit, about +0.127 per quote. Informed sellers (only those with settlement 0 or 1) are cheap to trade with at that level. Noise traders sell with probability about 18%.
- **Ask at 6.0:** The always-heads case still carries about 32% probability. Any ask below 6 loses money to informed buyers in that case. An ask at 6.0 has no informed losses and still sells to noise traders often enough, for about +0.11 per quote.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 6.0}

Flip 2 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one. The contract settles at 1 plus the heads in flips 3–6, each a fair flip. Expected value is 1 + 2 = 3, with a standard deviation of 1. The possible settlement values are 1 to 5, with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16 and 1/16.

**Choosing the spread:**
- An informed trader only trades when the true value is beyond my price, so I lose to it.
- A noise trader values the contract at 3 plus noise with standard deviation 1.7, so I gain from it.
- On the ask side, the expected profit per quote is:
  - ask 3.6: about 0.075
  - ask 4.0: about 0.159
  - ask 4.3 to 4.5: about 0.17 (the curve is flat here, peaking near 4.4)
- The bid side is symmetric, so the best bid is around 1.6.

I am long 1 unit, so I shade both prices down slightly to make selling a little more likely.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.2}

Flip 2 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one, because the other coin always lands heads.

- **Settlement value:** one known head plus the heads from the 4 unrevealed fair flips. Its mean is 3, and it can be anywhere from 1 to 5.
- **Probabilities:** 1/16 for a value of 1, 4/16 for 2, 6/16 for 3, 4/16 for 4 and 1/16 for 5.
- **Last quote:** my 1.7 / 4.2 quote got no trade. That is roughly symmetric evidence, so the public fair value stays at about 3.

To set the bid, I compared the expected profit from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders:

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.181 | 0.022 | 0.159 |
| 1.9 | 0.185 | 0.020 | 0.166 |
| 1.8 | 0.187 | 0.018 | 0.170 |
| 1.7 | 0.188 | 0.015 | 0.172 |

The net profit barely changes across bids from 1.7 to 2.0. The ask side is the mirror image, around 4.0 to 4.3.

I'm long 1, so I lean slightly toward selling with a tighter ask. I'll post a bid of 1.9 and an ask of 4.0.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 4.0}

The bias question is resolved: flips 2–4 came up tails, and the always-heads coin can never show tails, so this coin is fair.

**Fair value:** Flip 1 was a head, so 1 head is already locked in. Flips 5 and 6 are fair coins. Settlement is therefore 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, so fair value is **2.0**.

**Choosing the half-spread d around 2:** Each side earns 0.65 × P(noise > d) × d from noise traders. Noise is Normal with standard deviation 1.7. Each side loses 0.35 × 0.25 × (1 − d) to informed traders when d < 1. Once d ≥ 1, an informed trader never trades: a value of 3 does not buy at an ask of 3.0 or higher, and a value of 1 does not sell at a bid of 1.0 or lower. Expected profit per side:
- d = 0.5: about 0.08
- d = 0.9: about 0.17
- d = 1.0: about 0.18
- d = 1.3: about 0.19 (roughly the maximum)
- d = 1.4: about 0.19

The current position of +1 is well inside the ±4 limit. Since I am risk neutral, it does not change the quote. I will quote symmetrically at 2 ± 1.3.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

Seeing a tails means the coin must be the fair one. The contract has 1 head so far, plus 2 fair flips still to come. So settlement is 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, and fair value is 2.

An informed trader can never value the contract above 3 or below 1. Quotes at or outside those bounds therefore lose nothing to informed traders.

Against noise traders (fair value 2, noise standard deviation 1.7), the expected edge per side is 0.65 × x × P(noise > x), where x is the distance from fair value. This peaks around x ≈ 1.3, at about 0.19 per side. That gives an ask of 3.3 and, by symmetry, a bid of 0.7.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any flips are revealed, the fair value is 4.5: there is a 50% chance the coin is two-headed (6 heads) and a 50% chance it is fair (average 3 heads).

The settlement value is bimodal. It is exactly 6 with probability about 0.51; otherwise it follows a Binomial(6, 0.5) spread around 3.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer gains only if the value is 6. If I set the ask at 6.0, no informed trader beats it, because their valuation must be strictly above my ask. Noise traders still buy about 19% of the time, which gives roughly +0.18 expected per quote. That is about the best ask I can find.

**Bid side.** Informed sellers hurt me when the value is low (0–2 heads under the fair coin). I checked a few bid levels:
- A bid of 2.5–2.8 expects about +0.10–0.11 per quote.
- Raising the bid toward 3.5 drops that to about +0.04, because informed sellers who know the value is 3 also start hitting it.

So I'll bid 2.8 and offer 6.0.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

The public fair value is about 4.74. Before any trading the expected settlement is 4.5. Last quote's no-trade nudges that up, because an informed seller with a low value (2 or less) would have hit the 2.8 bid.

**Ask:** Settlement is 6 with about 55% posterior probability. Quoting below 6 lets informed buyers hold to the maximum value hit me. At 6.0 they cannot profitably buy, and noise buyers still give about 0.19 expected edge.

**Bid:** At 3.0 only informed sellers with values of 2 or less sell to me, and those are fairly unlikely. Noise sellers give about 0.17 expected edge, so the net is about +0.12. Raising the bid to 3.5 brings in informed sellers with a value of 3 and does worse.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 6.0}

The first flip came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one; the always-heads coin could never show tails. That leaves 1 head so far plus 4 more fair flips. Settlement is therefore 1 + Bin(4, 0.5), which takes values 1 to 5 with probabilities 1/16, 4/16, 6/16, 4/16, 1/16. Its mean is 3 and its standard deviation is 1. Neither earlier quote traded and both sides were treated the same, so the public fair value stays at 3.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared the expected profit per quote at several ask prices. Noise traders value the contract at 3 + N(0, 1.7). Informed traders buy only when the settlement value is above my ask.

| Ask | Profit from noise buyers | Loss to informed buyers | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.5 | +0.125 | −0.077 | ≈ +0.05 |
| 4.0 | +0.181 | −0.022 | ≈ +0.16 |
| 4.4 | +0.187 | −0.013 | ≈ +0.17 |
| 4.5 | +0.184 | −0.011 | ≈ +0.17 |

Profit stops improving at around 4.4, so I'll ask 4.4. The setup is symmetric around 3, so the matching bid is 1.6.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 4.4}

The coin must be the fair one, because flip 1 came up tails and the always-heads coin can't do that. So flips 3 to 6 are fair, and settlement = 1 + Binomial(4, ½). That has mean 3 and possible values 1 to 5.

**Updating on the trade:** someone bought at 4.4. An informed trader only does that if the settlement value is 5. A noise trader buys about 20% of the time. Conditioning on this pushes the expected value up to about **3.28**.

**Choosing the quotes:** an informed trader's valuation is a whole number, so quotes just above or below a whole number cost almost nothing extra.
- **Ask:** at 5.0 or higher, no informed trader ever buys. Noise buyers still give a profit of about +0.175 per quote, which is near the best available.
- **Bid:** at about 1.9 to 2.0, only a settlement value of 1 gets sold to me, which is a small loss. The expected profit is about +0.17. I'm currently short, so I lean towards the higher bid of 2.0 because buying back reduces my risk.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.0}

**Quote 5: bid 0.7, ask 3.3**

**Fair value.** Flips 1, 3 and 4 came up tails. The always-heads coin can never show tails, so the coin must be the fair one. One head has shown so far, and flips 5 and 6 are each 50/50. The settlement value is 1 + Binomial(2, 0.5):
- 1 with probability 0.25
- 2 with probability 0.5
- 3 with probability 0.25

So the public fair value is 2.

**Choosing the ask.**
- An informed counterparty only buys if the settlement value is above my ask, and the value can be at most 3. At an ask of 3 or more, informed traders never buy, so I take no adverse-selection loss on that side.
- Above 3, my expected profit comes only from noise buyers: 0.65 × (ask − 2) × P(noise > ask − 2). This peaks when ask − 2 is about 0.75 × 1.7 ≈ 1.28.
- At an ask of 3.3, expected profit on the ask side is about 0.19 per quote.
- An ask just below 3 does worse. For example, 2.9 gives about 0.165, because noise profit drops and informed traders sometimes buy.

**Choosing the bid.** The situation is symmetric around 2, so the bid is 2 − 1.3 = 0.7. Informed traders never sell to me below 1, since the value is at least 1.

**Position limit.** My position is 0 with one quote left after this, so the ±4 limit cannot bind.

{"bid": 0.7, "ask": 3.3}

The coin is fair, because a fair-or-always-heads coin that has shown tails must be the fair one. Heads so far: 1. The last two flips are fair, so settlement is 1, 2 or 3 with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25. Fair value is 2.

- **Informed traders:** an ask at 3 or higher can never be lifted by an informed trader, since the settlement is at most 3. The same logic means a bid at 1 or lower can never be hit by one.
- **Noise traders:** their valuation is 2 + N(0, 1.7). The expected noise profit on the ask is P(Z > (a−2)/1.7) × (a−2). This peaks at an edge of about 1.2 to 1.4 from fair value, giving roughly 0.29 × 0.65 ≈ 0.19 per side.
- **Quoting inside 3 / 1:** tightening only adds a small amount of noise flow. It also exposes me to informed traders, so it is worse.

So I quote symmetrically, about 1.3 either side of fair value.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
